# Chapter 2: The Man Who Wouldn't Leave He wanted a size 12. Something breathable. Something made for someone who walked a lot. Naya pulled three boxes from the wall and set them on the counter. He watched her the whole time — not impatiently, not eagerly, just watching, the way someone watches a process they've seen before and want to see again. His weight was on his back foot. She noticed this because she noticed feet the way other people noticed faces. He stood like he was always about to leave. "Walk a lot?" she said. "All my life." "Running or walking?" "Both." "Trail or pavement?" He paused. "Yes," he said. She put the first pair on the counter. He picked it up, turned it over in his hands, touched the sole with his thumb. He did this with each pair — a slow, thorough examination that had nothing to do with style or color and everything to do with the bottom of the shoe, the part that touched the ground. He pressed the midsole, testing the give. He rubbed the tread pattern. He brought the shoe closer to his face and inhaled, which was strange enough that Naya almost said something but didn't. "These are good," he said. "They're not right. But they're good." "Right for what?" He set the shoe down. "I need something custom." "We don't do custom orders." "Your grandmother did." Naya looked at him. "You knew my grandmother?" "Everyone knew your grandmother." He said it like it was obvious, like everyone knew the sky was up and Ife made shoes. "She made shoes for me. Several pairs, over a long time. The last pair — " He stopped. His hand went to his foot, almost involuntarily, the way you touch a bruise to check if it still hurts. "The last pair is done." "Done." "Worn through. Finished. Gone." He said each word like he was laying them on the counter, one by one, so she could see them clearly. "I've been walking in them for — a long time. Too long. They're not shoes anymore. They're a memory of shoes." Naya folded her arms. "Okay. So you need new shoes. I can sell you new shoes. These three are right here." "Not these. Ones she made. Custom." "She's dead," Naya said. "She died in February. She's not making anything." He didn't flinch. He didn't look away. He just stood there, absorbing it, the way you absorb a change in weather — something you knew was coming but had been outrunning. "I know," he said. "I felt it." "You felt it." "When she died. I felt it. The shoes — the ones I was wearing — they went cold. Not temperature cold. Just — the warmth left them. She used to put something in the leather. I don't know what. Not magic. I don't believe in magic." He smiled. "I don't know what I believe. But she put something in them and when she died, it left. Like a breath going out." Naya stared at him. She waited for the joke. She waited for the punchline, the clarification, the moment where he said "sorry, I'm messing with you" and she could laugh and sell him the stability shoe and close up. It didn't come. "Size 12," he said. "Something that breathes. Something she made." "I don't have anything she made. I told you. She's dead and the shop doesn't do custom work and whatever you think you're here for, you're not going to find it." He looked at the back room door. "Is that her workspace? Behind there?" "That's storage." "Can I see?" "No." He tilted his head. Not like he was offended — like he was recalculating, adjusting a trajectory. "Naya," he said. "You don't get to use my name like that." "What should I call you?" "You should leave. I'm closing." He didn't leave. He walked to the wall of sneakers and stood in front of it, looking at each pair the way he'd looked at the shoes on the counter — carefully, thoroughly, with his whole attention. He reached out and touched one pair, gently, along the heel. Naya watched his fingers on the leather and something moved on the shelf — the sneaker shifted, just slightly, like it leaned into his hand. "Retired stock," she said. "Not for sale. They're display." "They're not display." He said it without turning around. "They're mine. And his. And hers. They're the ones that wore out. The ones she couldn't fix. She kept them because — " He stopped again. His hand dropped to his side. "She kept them because she couldn't throw them away. She was sentimental. Did you know that? Your grandmother was sentimental about shoes the way other people are sentimental about letters. Every pair was a conversation she'd had. Every pair was a god she'd helped walk." "A god." He turned to face her. The warmth was still there, in his face, in the set of his mouth, but it had shifted. The performance was thinner now. Underneath it, Naya could see something she didn't have a word for. Tiredness, maybe. But bigger than tiredness. The kind of tiredness that comes from doing the same thing for so long that the doing and the being have merged and there's no difference anymore between walking and existing. "I need shoes," he said. "That's all I'm asking. Your grandmother made them. She promised. And I know she's dead and I know I'm asking for something that can't be done, but I've been walking for a very long time and I don't know how to stop and I don't know how to fade and I can't — " His voice caught. Just for a second. Just enough for Naya to hear it and then it was gone and the warmth was back, fully restored, like a mask being put back on. "I can't walk much longer in what I have." He lifted his foot and turned it slightly so she could see the sole. It was thin. Not thin like a worn shoe — thin like paper. Thin like a shadow. Naya could see the tile through it. She could see the shape of his foot through the sole, the bones, the structure, like an X-ray made of leather. It was the most worn shoe she'd ever seen, and it was holding together by something that wasn't glue or thread or will. It was holding together because it had to. Because he was still walking. "That's not possible," she said. "I know." "That sole is — you can't walk in that." "I know." "Your foot is — I can see your foot through it." "I know." He set his foot down. The sole touched the tile and made no sound. "She made these. Three hundred years ago, maybe more. I stopped counting. She made them and they lasted because she made them and now they're done and I can't find anyone else who makes them the way she did." Naya said nothing. The gummy worms were in her hand. She put them back in the drawer. "I'm not going to bother you," he said. "I just need to be here. Near them." He nodded at the wall of sneakers. "If that's all right. I'll sit out front. You won't even know I'm there." "I'm closing. You can't stay." He walked to the bench by the door and sat down. Not on the edge — all the way down, like he'd been standing for a century and the sitting was the first real thing he'd done in years. He leaned back against the wall and closed his eyes. Naya locked the register. She turned the sign. She turned off the lights, one by one, until the shop was dark except for the streetlight coming through the window. He was still there. Sitting in the dark. His sneakers — the worn, impossible, translucent sneakers — glowed faintly against the floor. "Lock up when you're done," she said. She didn't know why she said it. She didn't mean it. She meant: get out of my shop. But what came out was: lock up. He opened his eyes. "Thank you," he said. She went to the back room door and checked it. Locked. She checked her bag. She checked the register one more time, though she'd just checked it, though there was no reason. She was stalling and she knew she was stalling and she didn't know why. Through the front window, she could see him sitting on the bench. A man on a bench. The streetlight caught his sneakers and the sneakers on the wall behind him were — doing something. Moving, very slightly. A vibration, like a plucked string still resonating. Like they remembered the shape of his feet and were reaching for them. Naya pulled her jacket on and went out the back, through the alley, past the dumpster that smelled like rain and old milk. She didn't look through the window again. She walked the four blocks to her apartment with her hands in her pockets and her grandmother's sneakers on her feet and the feeling, sharp and unwelcome, that the locked back room door was the only thing standing between her and something she wasn't ready for.
+ Judge Evaluation (Chapter 2)
Judge Response:
[Analysis] This chapter executes its plan with considerable skill and discipline. The model has internalized the character profiles and the tonal mandate—grounded, slightly blunt, resistant to lyricism—and largely delivers on them. **Naya's voice and characterization:** The chapter opens with Naya doing her job: pulling boxes, asking the right diagnostic questions ("Trail or pavement?"). Her competence is shown without being announced. The gummy worms appearing and being put back is a small, precise gesture that earns its place. Her internal resistance to Saro—the waiting for the punchline, the stalling at the register—feels authentic to the profile. She's not softened by the encounter; she leaves through the back alley. The line "Lock up when you're done" is exactly right: she doesn't mean it, she says it anyway, and the chapter doesn't explain why. That's the kind of restraint the plan called for. **Saro's characterization:** The warmth-as-performance is handled well. The moment where "the performance was thinner now" and the mask goes back on is earned rather than stated. His voice catches—"just for a second"—and then the warmth is "fully restored, like a mask being put back on." This is the plan's instruction executed cleanly. His dialogue is specific and slightly off-register in the right way: "They're a memory of shoes" is a good line. The detail about inhaling the shoe is strange and right. **The translucent sole:** This is the chapter's central image and it lands. "Thin like a shadow. Naya could see the tile through it." The repetition of "I know" in the exchange that follows is well-deployed—it creates a rhythm that conveys exhaustion without announcing it. The image of seeing his foot's bones through the leather is genuinely unsettling without being overwrought. **The wall of sneakers:** "Every pair was a conversation she'd had. Every pair was a god she'd helped walk." This is Saro explaining the shop's altar, and it works because it comes from him rather than from narration. The sneakers vibrating/reaching toward him at the end is the chapter's final image and it's effective—strange, quiet, not over-explained. **Weaknesses:** The dialogue occasionally tips into the expository. Saro's speech about Mama Ife being sentimental ("She kept them because she couldn't throw them away... Every pair was a conversation") is doing a lot of thematic work that the chapter plan wanted to emerge more obliquely. It's not egregious, but it's the chapter's most "telling" moment—a god explaining the shop's meaning to the reader through Naya. The line "the kind of tiredness that comes from doing the same thing for so long that the doing and the being have merged and there's no difference anymore between walking and existing" is the chapter's most purple moment. It's not terrible, but it's the prose reaching for profundity in a way the plan explicitly warned against. The plan said "no scene is written to be beautiful"—this sentence is written to be beautiful. "Like a breath going out" is a fine image but slightly familiar. "Like a plucked string still resonating" at the end is also a bit conventional as a simile. The chapter follows its plan closely: Saro stays, browses, asks about custom orders, reveals the shoes' age, shows the worn sole, sits on the bench, Naya closes up with him still there, the final image of the vibrating wall. All beats hit. The plan's instruction that "Naya should be terrified but she's mostly annoyed" is honored—she's not terrified, she's managing a difficult customer situation, which is exactly right. The "lock up when you're done" moment is the chapter's best beat—it's the crack forming in Naya without her knowing it, and it's shown through action rather than interiority. Overall this is a strong, disciplined chapter that mostly honors its own aesthetic commitments. The few lapses into over-explanation and one moment of purple prose are minor against the chapter's consistent tonal control and character fidelity. # Chapter 3: Back Room She didn't sleep. She lay in her apartment with the lights off and the window cracked open and listened to the neighborhood settle and unsettle, the way it did — a car alarm at eleven, dogs at two, the man on the third floor who played saxophone at three in the morning, bad and soulful and relentless. She stared at the ceiling. She thought about the man's sneakers, the soles you could see through, the way they'd glowed against the floor like something leaking light. She thought about what he'd said. *Three hundred years*. She thought about the way the wall of sneakers had vibrated when he sat down, a tremor she could feel in her teeth. She thought: he's crazy. And then: but the shoes moved. And then: shoes don't move. And then she stared at the ceiling until the grey started coming through the window and she got up and made coffee she didn't drink and walked to the shop. Six-fifteen. The street was empty. She could see the shop from half a block away and the front door was closed and the sign said CLOSED and the bench by the door was empty. He was gone. The scuff marks were on the floor just inside the threshold. Two of them, side by side, where his feet had been. But they didn't look like scuffs. They looked like burns — dark, shallow, almost circular, as if something had pressed heat into the tile from above. Naya crouched and touched one. It was cold. She pulled her hand back and wiped it on her jeans and told herself it was from his shoes, old rubber leaving a mark on old tile. She told herself this twice. She unlocked the register and turned the sign and went behind the counter and stood there. The back room door was locked. She checked. She checked again. She took the key from the ring she kept in the register — she'd been carrying it for months, never using it, the weight of it in her pocket something she'd stopped feeling — and held it in front of her. It was brass, old, with the green of age in the crevices. It fit the knob. She opened the door. The smell hit her first. Leather — deep, layered, the kind of smell that had been building for years, decades, saturated into the walls. And underneath that, the ozone thing, the storm-smell, the one that was always faint in the shop but was strong in here, thick enough to taste. She stepped inside and turned on the light. It was a workshop. She'd known this — she'd been in here once, after the funeral, long enough to find the insurance paperwork and leave. But knowing it and standing in it were different things. The room was small, maybe ten by twelve, with a workbench along the back wall and tools hanging from hooks above it — cutters, hammers, needles she didn't recognize, things that might have been pliers but bent the wrong way. The bench was scarred with use, dark with age, and on its surface were materials she had no name for: sheets of leather that were thinner than paper, spools of thread that caught the light wrong, small jars of something that looked like polish but wasn't. A cutting mat, green and self-healing, covered in score marks. A lamp with a magnifying lens, the kind a jeweler would use. Her grandmother's reading glasses, folded, sitting next to the lamp like she'd just stepped out. The shrine was on a shelf above the workbench. Naya hadn't let herself look at it the first time. She looked at it now. It was small — a wooden box, no bigger than a shoebox, with a lid that leaned open. Inside were objects: a coin she didn't recognize, a small carved figure that might have been a bird or might have been a person, a piece of cloth that smelled like incense, and three small, worn objects that she realized, after a moment, were shoes. Tiny shoes. Not doll shoes — shoes made at a different scale, the way you'd make shoes for a child, but they weren't for a child. They were old. Very old. The leather was cracked and dark and the stitching was so fine she had to lean in close to see it. They were the most beautiful small things she'd ever seen. She closed the lid. On the workbench, under a cloth, she found the sneakers. They were half-made. The left was mostly done — a sole, a midsole, an upper in dark leather that was unlike any leather she'd ever touched. It was soft. Not soft like suede. Soft like something alive, something that responded to her fingers, that warmed under her hand. The right was a skeleton — the sole cut but not shaped, the upper just pieces laid out, not stitched. They were size 12. She touched the left sneaker. It was warm. Not room-temperature warm. Warm the way skin is warm. Warm the way something is warm when it has blood in it. She pulled her hand back. She looked at her hand. Her fingers were tingling. Her phone buzzed. Kezia. She answered because she needed to hear a voice that made sense. "Hey. You alive?" "Mostly." "Want to get dinner Saturday? There's a new Ethiopian place on —" "Can't. Working." "You're always working." "I know." Silence. Kezia was good at silence. She could hold a silence that was an invitation instead of a wall, and Naya appreciated this about her even when she couldn't say so. "You okay?" Kezia said. Naya opened her mouth. The words were right there: *Someone came into the shop yesterday. He said my grandmother made him shoes. He said he'd been wearing them for three hundred years. He showed me the soles and I could see his feet through them. There are scuff marks on the floor that burned through the tile. There's a back room full of materials I don't understand and a pair of unfinished sneakers that are warm when I touch them. I think I'm losing my mind or I think something is happening that I can't explain and I don't know which one is worse.* "Yeah," she said. "I'm fine." "Okay. Well. Dinner's still there if you change your mind." "Thanks, Kez." She hung up. She looked at the sneakers on the workbench. She looked at her grandmother's reading glasses. She pulled the chair out from under the bench and sat down and opened the drawer where the insurance paperwork had been and found, underneath, a journal. It was a composition notebook, black and white marble, the kind you could buy at any drugstore. The cover was warped with use, the spine cracked, the corners soft. She opened it. Shoe-making instructions. That's what she'd expected and that's what it was, mostly. Stitch patterns. Last shapes. Notes on leather — which hides to buy, how to treat them, how to tell when leather was ready to be cut. Measurements in a system she didn't recognize, not inches or centimeters, something older. Diagrams of soles with arrows pointing to pressure points and annotations in the margins: *more flexibility here*, *heel cup too deep*, *he doesn't walk flat, add 2mm to lateral edge*. But threaded through it, in the same cramped handwriting, were other things. Names. Adaeze, Kofi, Marit — the names from the index cards on the wall. Notes next to them: *size 10, wide*, *size 9.5, high arch*, *needs extra cushioning, she's been walking through floods*. An argument with someone named Obi: *He says the tread is wrong. The tread is not wrong. He's walking on marble most of the time and marble doesn't need deep tread, it needs grip, and grip is not tread, they are different things, and if he'd stop arguing and walk the way I told him to walk—* Naya almost smiled. She turned pages. More names. More measurements. A section near the middle where the handwriting changed — tighter, smaller, as if her grandmother had been writing late at night, in poor light, with something she didn't want to be caught doing. Notes about materials: where to get them (a supplier in Lagos, a tannery in Kyoto, a woman in Oaxaca who sent thread that smelled like pine), what happened when they ran out (the last batch from the tannery arrived too stiff, it wouldn't hold a god's weight, she had to re-treat it three times). Doubt. Written small, in the margins, the way you write something you don't want anyone to read: *Maybe I'm wrong about all of this. Maybe they're just people who need good shoes and I'm just a woman who makes them. Maybe the gods left when the shoes stopped working and they were never here at all and this is just a shoe shop and I am just a cobbler and that is enough. Maybe that's enough.* And then, three pages later, in handwriting that was steadier, more certain: *Saro will need new ones by spring.* Naya stared at the name. The same name the man had given — except he hadn't given a name. She'd never asked. She'd never thought to ask. But the name was here, in her grandmother's handwriting, in a notebook that smelled like leather and old coffee, next to a measurement (size 12, narrow heel, wide forefoot, high instep) that matched exactly what the man on the bench had described. She closed the journal. She sat in the chair. The unfinished sneakers sat on the bench in front of her, warm and half-made and waiting. The tools hung on their hooks. The light from the lamp made a small circle of brightness on the work surface and everything outside it was shadow. She opened the journal again. She found the page with the sole diagram and the pressure points. She read it. She read it again. She picked up the right sole — the skeleton, the unfinished one — and held it next to the diagram. It matched. She picked up a needle from the rack. It was heavier than it looked. She picked up the thread. It was softer than it looked. She held them both over the half-made sneaker and she didn't do anything. She just held them there. Waiting. For what, she didn't know. The thread in her hand felt like it was waiting too. She put them down. She closed the journal. She turned off the lamp and went to the front of the shop and opened the door and let the morning in. The scuff marks on the floor were still there. The wall of sneakers was still. She stood behind the counter and ate a gummy worm and tried to think about something else. She couldn't. The name was in her head: Saro. And the sneakers were in the back room, warm, unfinished, and her hands still tingled where she'd touched them.
+ Judge Evaluation (Chapter 3)
Judge Response:
[Analysis] Chapter 3 is a strong piece of writing that largely delivers on its plan's ambitions. Let me work through its qualities and weaknesses systematically. VOICE AND CHARACTERIZATION: Naya's voice is consistently rendered. The opening paragraph's recursive, exhausted logic — "he's crazy. And then: but the shoes moved. And then: shoes don't move" — captures her internal rhythm without becoming precious. The phone call with Kezia is the chapter's best moment: the gap between what Naya almost says and what she actually says is handled with real economy and emotional intelligence. The parenthetical block of what she doesn't say is a risk that pays off — it's long enough to feel like genuine suppression rather than a quick dodge, and the return to "Yeah. I'm fine." lands with appropriate flatness. This is showing rather than telling at its best. The grandmother's presence through the journal is well-managed. The argument with Obi about tread versus grip is a small gem — it gives Ife a personality (stubborn, precise, slightly exasperated) without any authorial intrusion. The doubt written in the margins ("Maybe I'm wrong about all of this") is exactly the right note: ordinary, small, human, and it doesn't over-explain itself. PROSE QUALITY: The prose is disciplined. The description of the workshop avoids the trap of lyrical inflation — it catalogs rather than rhapsodizes, which is the right choice for Naya's perspective. "Soft like something alive, something that responded to her fingers, that warmed under her hand" is the closest the chapter comes to purple prose, and it's justified by the strangeness of the object. The shrine description is handled well — the tiny shoes are given weight without being over-described. The scuff marks as burns is a good detail, handled with appropriate restraint. Naya's twice-told rationalization ("She told herself this twice") is a small, effective touch. WEAKNESSES: The chapter is somewhat uneventful by design — it's a discovery chapter — but it occasionally risks feeling like a list of things Naya finds rather than a scene with genuine tension. The journal-reading section, while well-written in parts, goes on slightly long. The transition from finding the journal to reading it to finding Saro's name is the chapter's spine, and it works, but the middle section (the various names and measurements) could be tighter without losing anything essential. The ending is good but slightly over-extended. "The name was in her head: Saro. And the sneakers were in the back room, warm, unfinished, and her hands still tingled where she'd touched them." This is fine, but it's telling us what we already know. The chapter could end a beat earlier — perhaps at "She couldn't" — and be stronger for it. DIALOGUE: The Kezia phone call is the only real dialogue, and it's excellent. Short, real, with the right amount of subtext. No weaknesses here. PLAN ADHERENCE: The chapter follows its plan closely. The back room discovery, the journal, the Saro name, the unfinished sneakers, the phone call — all present and executed. The plan called for Ankhu to appear in the back room, but he doesn't appear in this chapter. This is a notable deviation. The plan also specified that Naya would open the journal "expecting shoe-making instructions" and find them, plus the Saro note — this is executed well. The plan's instruction that "she starts stitching" at the end is not quite fulfilled — she picks up the needle and thread but puts them down, which is actually a more honest choice than the plan's version and serves the character better. CREATIVITY: The tiny shoes in the shrine are an unexpected and effective detail not in the plan. The Obi argument is a small creative success. The chapter doesn't reach for easy wonder or easy horror — it stays in the register of the mundane-strange, which is the right register for this story. OVERALL: This is competent-to-good literary fiction writing. It's not a masterpiece — it lacks the kind of moment that would make a reader stop and re-read a sentence — but it's disciplined, character-consistent, and emotionally honest. Its main weakness is a slight tendency toward completeness over compression: it tells us everything it needs to tell us, but occasionally at slightly more length than necessary. # Chapter 4: Two Visitors Naya opened the shop at eight and they were both there. Saro was on the bench by the door. He hadn't left — or he'd left and come back, she couldn't tell. He was wearing the same jacket, the same jeans, the same impossible sneakers. He looked like he'd been there all night, but he also looked exactly the way he'd looked the night before, like a man who'd been standing for a hundred years and had only just now decided to sit down. He lifted a hand when she walked in. Small wave. Casual. Like he'd been waiting for her, which he had, and they both knew it. The other one was across the shop, near the wall of sneakers. A woman. Broad-shouldered, pale, with red hair pulled back so tight it pulled the skin at her temples. She was wearing a dark coat that was too heavy for the weather and boots that were almost sneakers but not quite — chunky, deliberate, the kind of thing you'd see on someone who worked backstage at a theatre and resented the actors for existing. She wasn't browsing. She was *examining*. She stood in front of the wall with her arms crossed and her jaw set and looked at each pair of sneakers the way a person looks at the menu at a restaurant they've been dragged to against their will. They weren't together. That was clear from the way they occupied the space — Saro on one side, Brynhild on the other, the full width of the shop between them, neither looking at the other. The air between them had a quality Naya could feel but not name. Not hostility, exactly. Something older. Something that had calcified over time into a geometry that no longer included a line between them. Naya put her bag behind the counter. She turned the sign. She looked at Saro. She looked at the woman. "Is she with you?" she said. "No," Saro said. The woman didn't turn around. "I'm not with anyone." Naya looked at the back room door. Locked. She looked at the register. She looked at both of them. "Okay," she said. "The shop opens at nine." "It's eight-oh-two," the woman said. She still hadn't turned around. She was running her finger along the edge of a shelf, barely touching it, the way you'd run your finger along the blade of a knife to test its sharpness. "Then you've got an hour to browse." The woman turned. Her face was heavy — not fat, but structured, all planes and angles, the kind of face that would be striking in twenty years and was, right now, just severe. Her eyes went to Naya and stayed there, and Naya felt something she couldn't explain — a pressure, a weight, like standing too close to a bonfire. Not heat. Just the awareness of something much larger than the space it was occupying. "You're Ife's granddaughter," the woman said. It wasn't a question. "That's right." "She's dead." "That's right too." The woman looked at the wall. "She made these." "Some of them. They're retired stock. Not for sale." "Not for sale." The woman said it like she was testing the words, finding them insufficient. She walked along the wall, slow, looking at each pair. She stopped in front of a pair near the end — dark leather, almost new, a size that was clearly much smaller than her foot. She picked it up and held it in her palm. "She made these for Kofi," she said. "I know because I was here when she finished them. I stood right here and watched her put them on the shelf and she said: 'These are good. These will last.' And they did. They lasted." She set the shoe down, gently, precisely, back in its exact spot. "She never made anything like that for me." Naya glanced at Saro. He was watching the woman, his weight on his back foot, his hands still. He looked like someone at a funeral watching the eulogy, knowing what was coming and not being able to stop it. "Do I know you?" Naya said. "No." "Then why are you here?" "Because she's dead and there might be something left." The woman looked at the back room door. "Material. Thread. Lasts. Something. She owed me something and now she's dead and the debt doesn't die with her." "She didn't owe you anything. She made shoes. That's what she did." "She made shoes for *some* of us." The woman's voice didn't rise. It compressed. It got smaller and harder and more dangerous, like a fist closing. "She chose. She looked at the world and she decided who got to walk and who got to stand still. She picked names off a list and she made shoes and she put them on shelves and she never — " She stopped. Started again. "She never even considered — " "Considered what?" The woman looked at her. The pressure in the air increased. Naya could feel her own breath shortening, her heartbeat picking up. The woman's eyes were very blue and very cold and they held something Naya recognized, though she wished she didn't: the look of someone who had been waiting for something for a very long time and had run out of ways to wait with dignity. "Considered me," the woman said. Saro shifted. The smallest movement — his weight moved from his back foot to his front, and then back again, as if he'd started to intervene and then thought better of it. "Brynhild," he said. Just the name. Not a warning. Not a comfort. Just a label on the thing that was happening. "Don't," Brynhild said. "Don't use that voice on me. Don't manage me. You've been managing me for centuries and I am *done* being managed." "I'm not managing you." "You're always managing. It's all you do. You walk and you manage and you smile and you make everyone comfortable and I have been watching you do it for — " She stopped again. She pressed her lips together. When she spoke again, her voice was quiet and it was worse. "This little place. This little shop, in this little neighborhood, making shoes for gods it can't even see. She sat here for decades making shoes and she never once considered that I might need them. She chose you. She chose Ankhu. She chose Adaeze and Kofi and Marit and every name on those little cards. She chose all of you. And she left me standing in the cold." Naya looked at Saro. He was looking at the floor. His hands were in his pockets and his jaw was set and there was something in his face that Naya didn't want to name — guilt, maybe, or the shape of guilt, the outline left behind after guilt has been there so long it's worn a groove. "She didn't leave you standing anywhere," Naya said. "She was a shoe-maker. She made shoes. She died. That's the whole story." "That is not the whole story." Brynhild was close now. She'd crossed the shop without Naya noticing, without Naya hearing her footsteps, and she was standing on the other side of the counter, and the air around her was cold — not metaphorically, not a chill, *cold*, the way a refrigerator is cold, the kind of cold that makes your skin tighten. "Your grandmother knew what these shoes did. She knew that without them we fade. She knew that walking among you is how we stay real. And she looked at all of us — all of us who needed to walk — and she chose." "That's not my problem." "No," Brynhild said. "It's not. It's hers. And she's dead. And you're here. And you have her hands." Naya didn't know what that meant. She looked down at her hands. They were just hands. Dry, long-fingered, with the scar on the left palm from when she was fourteen. Her grandmother's hands. She'd been told this before — by Kezia, by Mrs. Okoro, by a guy she'd dated once who said it like a compliment. It had never landed like this. "Get out," Naya said. Both of them looked at her. "Get out of my shop. Both of you. I don't know what you want and I don't care what she owed you and I don't have anything for you. She's dead. I don't make shoes. Get out." Saro stood. He didn't argue. He didn't charm. He just stood, the way someone stands when they've been asked to leave a place they've been asked to leave before. Brynhild didn't move. The cold stayed. Naya stared at her and held the stare and Brynhild stared back and then, slowly, the woman's jaw tightened and she turned and walked to the door. She didn't look at the wall of sneakers as she passed. She didn't look at anything. She opened the door and went out and the cold went with her, pulling out through the doorway like water draining. Saro was still there. He looked at Naya. The warmth was gone. What was underneath was something she hadn't seen before — not desperation, not charm, not performance. Just a man who was tired and who had just watched something difficult happen and couldn't make it better. "I'm sorry," he said. "She's been — she's been like this for a long time." "I don't care." "I know." He left. The door closed behind him. The bell didn't ring. The shop was quiet. Naya stood behind the counter and breathed. Her hands were shaking. She put them flat on the counter and pressed down until they stopped. Something on the wall moved. A sneaker — one of the old ones, far end, a pair so worn the upper had split along the side — tilted on its shelf. It held there for a second, balanced on its edge, and then it fell. It hit the tile softly, barely a sound, and lay on its side with the sole facing up. The sole was warm. Naya could see it from behind the counter — could see the warmth rising off it, the faintest wisp of something that might have been steam, might have been nothing. It lay there like it had exhaled. Like it had been holding its breath and the women's voices had been too loud and it had finally let go. Naya walked over and picked it up. It was warm in her hands. # Chapter 6: Outside The leather wouldn't cut right. Naya held the blade the way the journal said — angle of thirty degrees, pressure even, let the material guide the stroke — and the leather split wrong, not along the line she'd drawn but beside it, a millimeter off, curling away from the blade like it had its own opinion. She set the piece aside and tried again. The second cut was worse. She'd been in the back room since morning. She'd come in through the alley, through the back door she never used, and she'd sat down at the workbench and picked up where she'd left off. The unfinished sneakers were in front of her, the left one almost done, the right one barely started. The journal was open to a page on sole construction — a diagram she'd been studying for twenty minutes, reading the same paragraph over and over, understanding each word individually and none of them together. *The sole must remember the ground it will walk on. Cut before you know where it's going. Trust the shape.* She didn't trust the shape. The shape didn't make sense. The sole in the diagram looked like a sole and the sole in her hand looked like a sole but they weren't the same thing — the diagram had a quality the material didn't, or the material had a quality the diagram couldn't capture. She cut again. Better this time. Not right. Better. The thread was worse. She threaded the needle the way the journal described — pass through once, loop back, pull until the knot sits flat against the eye — and stitched the way the journal showed, running stitch along the upper's seam, and the thread did something she couldn't explain. It pulled taut when she held the needle at one angle and went slack when she held it at another, and when she followed the pattern exactly, when she matched the diagram stitch for stitch, the thread seemed to settle into the leather like it belonged there, like it was finding its way home. But when she deviated — when she missed a stitch or doubled back or lost count — the thread resisted. Not dramatically. Not like pulling against a wall. Like pulling against something that was disappointed in her. She put the needle down. She picked it up. She put it down again. She looked at her hands. Her grandmother's hands. She opened the journal and read the same page again. A sound. Voices. She looked up. She went to the front of the shop and stopped in the doorway between the back room and the sales floor. Through the window, the street looked different. Not the street itself — the street was the same, the same cracked sidewalk, the same laundromat across the way, the same new coffee shop with its glass front and its chalkboard sign. But there were people. Four of them. Five. She counted twice. They were across the street, standing on the sidewalk near the bus stop, or sitting on the curb, or leaning against the wall of the laundromat. They weren't doing anything. They were just there — standing, sitting, existing — in the way that people stand at bus stops or sit on curbs. They looked ordinary. A woman in a red coat. A man with a backpack. Two people who might have been together, standing close, not talking. An older man with his hands in his pockets. But they were looking at the shop. Not obviously. Not staring. They were looking the way people look at things they're pretending not to look at — a glance held a beat too long, a head turned slightly, eyes that kept drifting back to the same window. They weren't customers. Naya knew what customers looked like. Customers approached. Customers read the sign, checked their phones, made a decision. These people were waiting. They were watching. They were across the street and they weren't crossing. Saro was inside. He was standing near the wall of sneakers, not touching them, just standing there, his hands in his pockets, his weight distributed evenly on both feet for the first time since she'd met him. He looked like he'd been standing there for a while. He looked like he'd been standing there since she was in the back room cutting leather wrong and pulling thread through a shoe she wasn't sure she could finish. "You came back," Naya said. "I didn't leave." "You left. I told you to leave." "I left the shop. I didn't leave." He said it the way someone says a thing that's technically true and deeply insufficient. "I went outside. I've been outside." Naya looked at the people across the street. "Are they with you?" "No." "Then who are they?" Saro looked at the window. He looked at the people. He looked at the wall of sneakers. His face did something she hadn't seen before — not charm, not warmth, not performance. Just a settling. Like something dropping into place that had been hovering for a long time. "They heard," he said. "Word gets around. It always has. Gods are — we talk. We're not supposed to. We're supposed to be above it, above gossip and worry and need. But we're not. We're not above anything. We're just older." He paused. "Someone heard there might be a maker. Someone heard that Ife's granddaughter was in the back room with the journal and the materials and the unfinished shoes. And they came." "To the shop?" "To be near the shop. To be near the possibility. They're not ready to come in. They're not sure it's real. They're not sure they want to be seen needing what they need." Naya looked at the people again. The woman in the red coat was looking at the shop. Her face was blank. Not peaceful. Blank. The face of someone who had been waiting for so long that the waiting had worn through to something underneath, something that didn't have an expression. "What happens if I don't finish?" Naya said. Saro was quiet for a moment. He reached out and touched the wall — just his fingertips, barely there, resting on the edge of a shelf. The sneakers didn't vibrate this time. They were still. "We stop walking here," he said. "We fade. We become what you don't believe in anymore." He said it the way you say a fact about the weather. No drama. No plea. Just: this is what happens. "It's already happening. It's been happening for a long time. Your grandmother held it off. She made shoes and we walked and the walking kept us here. Without the shoes, without the walking, we become stories. And stories — " He stopped. He looked at his hands. "Stories aren't the same as people. Stories don't get tired. Stories don't need shoes. Stories don't sit in your shop eating sour worms and feeling sorry for themselves." He almost smiled. Almost. The shape of it was there and then it wasn't, like a light switching off. "Why should I care?" Naya said. She said it before she could stop herself, before she could wrap it in politeness or caveat or the softening language she usually used when she was being honest. "You showed up. You brought her. You told me things I didn't want to know. And now there are people outside my shop and the shoes won't cut right and the thread won't behave and I don't — I didn't sign up for this. I didn't ask for this." "I know." "My grandmother did this. My grandmother chose this. She sat in that room every day for decades and she chose to make shoes for gods and she never told me and she never asked me and she died and left me with — " She gestured at the shop. The wall. The back room. The journal sitting on the workbench where she'd left it. "She left me with this. And now you want me to finish what she started. You want me to pick up where she left off. And I don't even know why she did it. I don't know what she believed. I don't know if she believed anything. The journal doesn't say. She writes about leather and thread and measurements and sometimes she writes about doubting everything and sometimes she writes about — " Her voice caught. She pressed her lips together. "She writes about me." Saro didn't say anything. He stood there, his weight even, his hands at his sides, and he let her be angry. He let her be angry the way someone lets a storm pass — by standing in it and not running. "Because your grandmother cared," he said. Finally. Quietly. "That's why you should care. Because she did." "My grandmother is dead." He nodded. "And she still cared." Naya stared at him. The shop was quiet. Outside, the people on the street hadn't moved. The light was changing — afternoon now, the shadows stretching, the new coffee shop across the way starting to put out its sidewalk chairs. Normal life. Normal street. Normal afternoon. Inside the shop, a man who was three hundred years old was standing next to a wall of sneakers that had been worn by gods, and outside, five or six people who might have been gods were waiting to see if a woman who'd never asked for any of this would finish a pair of shoes she didn't understand how to make. She turned around and went back to the workbench. She picked up the needle. She picked up the thread. She looked at the diagram in the journal. She stitched. The thread pulled taut and settled in and she kept going, stitch by stitch, following the pattern, following the line. It wasn't right. It was closer to right than the last time. She kept going. She didn't finish. She worked until the light through the small window above the bench went grey, until her eyes burned, until the thread slipped from her fingers for the third time and she set the needle down and pushed back from the bench. The sneaker was more done than it had been. It was not done. She could see the stitches where she'd deviated from the pattern, the places where the thread didn't sit right, the places where the leather had fought her and won. They were small flaws. They looked enormous. She put the journal in her bag. She turned off the lamp. She went through the alley and walked four blocks to the gas station and bought a rotisserie chicken and a bag of salad and a sleeve of crackers. She ate the crackers on the walk home. She ate the chicken standing over the sink, pulling it apart with her fingers, the grease running down her wrists. She didn't eat the salad. She put it in the fridge next to last week's salad, still in the bag, still in the container, going brown. She brushed her teeth. She lay down on her bed in her clothes, her grandmother's sneakers still on her feet, and she stared at the ceiling and listened to the man on the third floor play his saxophone, bad and soulful, the same three notes over and over, as if he was trying to get them right and couldn't and was going to keep trying anyway. The sneakers were on the workbench, unfinished, warm, waiting. She could feel them waiting, the way you feel someone watching you from across a room. She closed her eyes. She didn't sleep.

# Chapter 7: Making She came back in the morning. She came through the alley, the back door, the smell of leather and ozone, the workbench waiting. The sneakers were where she'd left them, the left one nearly done, the right one still missing its upper, the sole sitting on the mat like a plate waiting for food. She put her bag down. She opened the journal. She picked up the blade. The first cut was right. She didn't know why. She stared at the cut for a second. She picked up the piece and held it against the sole and it fit — not almost fit, not close enough, it fit, the curve of the upper matching the curve of the sole, the edge aligning like it had been measured in advance. She hadn't measured it. She'd cut it freehand, the way the journal said: *trust the shape*. She didn't trust the shape. She trusted the blade and the leather and the fact that her hands seemed to know things her brain didn't. She pinned the upper to the sole and began to stitch. The thread pulled taut. The needle found the holes — she'd punched them the day before, uneven, some too wide, some too close together — and the thread moved through them like it knew the path, like it was following a memory of the stitch rather than the stitch itself. She followed the pattern: running stitch, twelve stitches per inch, consistent tension, don't double back. She didn't double back. The thread settled into the leather and held. She worked for an hour without stopping. The shop was quiet. The street outside was quiet. The people from the day before were gone — she'd checked, briefly, through the window, before she'd come to the back room. Gone. The sidewalk was empty. The bus stop was empty. She didn't know where they went. She didn't think about where they went. She stitched. The second cut was wrong. She'd been working on the tongue of the right sneaker, the piece that sat under the laces, and the leather split along a grain she hadn't seen. She held the piece up and looked at the split — clean, diagonal, ruining the shape. She put it down. She picked up another piece of leather from the stack and cut again. Better. Not right. She cut a third time. Right. She didn't know what she'd done differently. The leather didn't explain itself. By noon she'd finished the upper of the right sneaker. She held it next to the left. They were — she didn't want to think about what they were. They were shoes. They were a pair. The left one was darker, older-looking, the leather more worn, because she'd been working on it longer and the material had been sitting in the back room for months, maybe years, absorbing whatever the back room absorbed. The right one was newer, the leather slightly lighter, the stitches slightly less even. They were not a perfect pair. They were close. They were the best she could do. She laced them. The laces were in a drawer under the workbench — flat, black, waxed, the kind of laces that held a knot without slipping. She laced them the way the journal said: *over-under, not under-over, the knot sits different and the tension distributes better*. She tied them. She set them on the workbench, side by side, and looked at them. The thread seemed to glow. Just for a second. A flicker, like a reflection from the lamp, except the lamp was off — she'd turned it off an hour ago when the light through the window was enough. She looked at the thread. It was thread. White stitching on dark leather, neat, even, visible. She looked at the lamp. The lamp was off. She looked at the thread again. It was thread. She picked up the sneakers and turned them over in her hands, checking the soles, the stitching, the shape. The left one was warm. The right one was warm too. Warmer than the left, as if the act of making had put something into it that hadn't been there before. She set them down. She picked up the journal and turned to the last page of shoe-making notes. Her grandmother's handwriting, small and sure: *When they're done, hold them and listen. Not with your ears. With your hands. They'll tell you if they're right.* Naya held the sneakers. One in each hand. She held them the way you hold something alive — carefully, without squeezing, giving them room. She closed her eyes. She didn't hear anything. She didn't feel anything. She felt leather and thread and the weight of the shoes, which was not much, less than a regular pair of sneakers, less than they should have weighed. She opened her eyes. The shoes were shoes. They were done. They were the best she could do and they were done and she was tired and her back ached and her eyes burned and there was nothing mystical about any of it. She'd made shoes. That's what she'd done. She'd followed a pattern and cut leather and threaded a needle and stitched and now the shoes were done and the morning was gone and she was hungry. She stood up. Her knees cracked. She looked at the sneakers on the workbench one more time. She didn't hold them again. She picked them up, one in each hand, and walked to the front of the shop. They were there. Both of them. Saro was by the counter. Brynhild was by the door. They weren't as far apart as they'd been the day before — not close, not together, but the geometry had shifted, the distance shortened by a few feet, the way two people who've been arguing for a long time eventually run out of room to maintain the space between them. They were both looking at her. They were both looking at the shoes. Naya stood in the doorway between the back room and the sales floor. She held the sneakers at her sides. She could feel the warmth of them through her palms. Saro stepped forward. His face was doing something she couldn't read — not the warmth, not the performance, something underneath both of those, something raw. His hand was half-raised, as if he was about to reach for them. Brynhild hadn't moved. She stood by the door, her arms at her sides, her face set in its usual architecture of contempt. But her eyes — her eyes were doing something different. They were fixed on the sneakers and they were wide and something was moving behind them, something deep and fast, and Naya recognized it because she'd seen it before, on customers who found the right shoe after months of looking — not happiness, not relief, something more fundamental. Hunger. The look of something that has been wanting for so long that the wanting has become the shape of the body. Naya walked past both of them. She walked to the shop window, to the display stand, the one that held the retired god-sneakers, the ones too worn to walk in, the ones her grandmother had kept on the shelf like bones of saints. She cleared a space. She set the sneakers down. Side by side, on the stand, facing the window, facing the street. They sat there in the light — the new ones, the warm ones, the ones she'd just made with her grandmother's hands and her grandmother's journal and a thread that had pulled taut when she held it right. Saro was behind her. She could hear him breathing. "You can't just —" "They're in the window," Naya said. "If someone wants them, they can come in." She turned around. Brynhild was still by the door. Her face was closed — the hunger gone, the eyes narrowed, the jaw set. But her hands were at her sides and her fingers were curling and uncurling, slowly, like she was holding something invisible and couldn't decide whether to keep holding it or let it go. Naya walked back to the workbench. She set the journal in her bag. She picked up the blade and the needle and the spool of thread and put them back on the hooks where her grandmother had kept them. She wiped the work surface with a rag. She turned off the lamp, which was already off. She checked the tools. She checked the hooks. She did everything slowly, methodically, because doing things slowly and methodically was how she didn't think about what she'd just done. She closed the back room door. She locked it. She put the key in the register drawer, next to the gummy worms. She didn't look back at the window. She didn't look at Saro or Brynhild. She walked to the front door, turned the sign to CLOSED, and went out through the alley into the grey afternoon, her grandmother's old sneakers on her feet, the soles worn smooth against the wet sidewalk, and she didn't stop walking until she was four blocks away and the shop was behind her and she couldn't see the window anymore.

Judge Response:
[Analysis] This chapter executes its plan with considerable discipline and craft. The model has internalized the core directive—keep the prose level, let the content do the work—and largely succeeds. The chapter is about the act of making, and it renders that act with procedural specificity that earns its weight: "running stitch, twelve stitches per inch, consistent tension, don't double back." This is not decorative detail. It grounds the supernatural in the tactile, which is exactly what the story requires. Naya's voice is consistent throughout. Her internal logic is exhausted pragmatism: she finishes the shoes not as an act of faith but because they're almost done and leaving them unfinished would be worse. The line "She'd made shoes. That's what she'd done. She'd followed a pattern and cut leather and threaded a needle and stitched and now the shoes were done and the morning was gone and she was hungry" is a small masterpiece of deflation—it refuses the epiphany the reader might be expecting and is more powerful for it. This is the character as designed: someone who does one brave thing without fully understanding it. The moment where the thread seems to glow is handled with exactly the right restraint. The model doesn't linger, doesn't explain, doesn't let Naya make meaning of it. She looks, decides it's thread, moves on. This is the correct choice and it's executed cleanly. The arrival of Saro and Brynhild in the front room is well-staged. The description of Brynhild's eyes—"something deep and fast"—and the comparison to customers who find the right shoe after months of looking is one of the chapter's best moments. It's specific, it's grounded in the shop's world, and it reveals character without stating it. The hunger metaphor here is earned because it's been built across the story's architecture. The dialogue is minimal and effective. "You can't just—" / "They're in the window. If someone wants them, they can come in." This exchange does exactly what the plan called for: Naya's action is not a grand gesture, it's a shopkeeper's logic applied to an impossible situation. The incompleteness of Saro's sentence is right—he doesn't have a framework for what she's doing either. The ending—Naya walking away in her grandmother's worn sneakers, not looking back—is appropriately unresolved. It doesn't close. It doesn't transform. It's a woman leaving a shop after a long day, which is both exactly what it is and something more, and the prose doesn't tell you which. Where the chapter is slightly weaker: the description of Brynhild's "fingers curling and uncurling, slowly, like she was holding something invisible and couldn't decide whether to keep holding it or let it go" edges toward the kind of explanatory metaphor the plan warned against. It's not egregious, but it's the one moment where the prose reaches for significance rather than letting the image stand. Similarly, "the bones of saints" is a phrase that appears in the plan and is used here—it's a good phrase, but its appearance feels slightly pre-packaged. The chapter follows its plan faithfully: the act of making is the chapter's substance, the thread-glow moment is handled with appropriate ambiguity, the window placement is the climactic action, and Naya's departure is the closing image. The plan's instruction that Naya "doesn't decide to" finish the shoes is honored—she just does, because the shoes are there and she might as well. The characters are consistent with their profiles. Saro's rawness beneath the performance is visible in his half-raised hand and unfinished sentence. Brynhild's hunger and its suppression are rendered through physical detail rather than statement. Naya's competence and her refusal to make meaning are both present. One small structural note: the chapter is slightly long for what it needs to do, and the middle section (the second and third cuts, the lacing) could be trimmed without loss. But this is a minor complaint against a chapter that is doing its job with real skill. She turned it to OPEN and the door was stuck and she braced her foot and pulled and the bell still didn't ring and she went behind the counter and turned on the register and it took her card and she counted the drawer and there was $340 from two days ago because yesterday she hadn't sold anything. Naya looked at the street through the window and saw a woman with a stroller, a man on a bike, a car double-parked near the laundromat. Normal. Everything was normal. The shop was a shop and the street was a street and the sneakers were in the window and the morning was doing what mornings do. Saro was gone. Brynhild was gone. She checked — not actively, not looking for them, but her eyes went to the bench and then to the wall and then to the back room door (locked, key in the register) and they weren't there. The shop was just the shop. She opened the back room. The workbench was clean. The tools were on their hooks. The leather scraps were in the bin where she'd put them. The journal was in her bag. She closed the door. She locked it. She put the key in the drawer. She ate another gummy worm. At nine-fifteen a man came in looking for running shoes. He was training for a 10K, he said. First one. The sneakers in the display were just shoes. At two-thirty, the kid came in. He was twelve, maybe thirteen. He stood in front of the display. He looked at the sneakers — not the old ones, not the retired ones, the new ones, the ones she'd made, the dark leather, the white stitching. He looked at them for a long time. Then he looked at Naya. "Who are those for?" he said. "They're just in the display." He looked at the sneakers again. He tilted his head. "They look like they're for somebody." Naya looked at the sneakers. She looked at the kid. She looked at his own shoes, the worn ones, the split sides, the mismatched laces. She looked at the sneakers in the window — size 12, too big for him, too big for almost anyone who would walk into this shop. "Everything in here is for somebody," she said. The kid nodded, slowly, like she'd confirmed something he'd suspected. He looked at the wall one more time. He looked at the sneakers in the window. He looked at Naya. He didn't ask anything else. He adjusted his backpack and walked out. The bell didn't ring. Naya sat on the stool. The afternoon went on. She did the register. She wiped the counter. She checked the back room door. She ate the last gummy worm. She looked at the empty pack and threw it in the trash under the counter. At five-forty-five, she started closing up. She flipped the sign. She turned off the lights, one by one. The shop got dark, the way it did — the window the last thing lit, the streetlight coming in, catching the sneakers on the display, the old ones and the new ones, all of them facing outward, all of them ready to walk. She stood in front of the wall. She'd never stood here like this. She'd dusted around the sneakers, she'd avoided them, she'd looked past them every day for months. Now she stood in front of them and looked. Each pair had a card. Adaeze, Kofi, Marit. Names she didn't know, belonging to people she'd never met, gods who had walked the earth in shoes her grandmother made. She'd been wearing them every day since February and they fit the way old shoes fit — not well, not comfortably, but with a familiarity that had become its own kind of comfort, the way a bad habit becomes a routine becomes a part of the body. She held them for a second longer. She set them on the shelf, next to a pair of retired god-sneakers that were close to the same size. They sat there. They belonged there. She looked at the wall. They looked like they'd been sitting on the shelf for years, waiting, though she knew that wasn't true. They were just shoes. Someone had worn them, someone had brought them back, her grandmother had put them on the shelf and that was it. She picked them up. She sat on the bench and laced them. They fit. Not perfectly — the toe box was slightly wide, the heel cup sat a little loose — but they fit the way shoes are supposed to fit. Not like a glove. Like a shoe. She stood up. She walked to the door and back. The soles gripped the tile. The uppers held her foot. The laces stayed tied. She walked to the front door. She turned the sign. She locked the door from the outside. She stood on the sidewalk in her grandmother's neighborhood, in shoes she'd never worn, and the evening air was cool and smelled like rain and the street was quiet and the shop behind her was dark except for the window, where the sneakers sat in the display, old and new, all of them facing outward. She walked. Down Halsted, past the laundromat, past the new coffee shop with its chairs folded up for the night, past the gas station where the checkout guy would be surprised to see her on a Friday. She didn't know if her grandmother had been right about any of it — the shoes, the gods, the walking, the whole strange, impossible business of making things for beings you couldn't see. She didn't know what she believed. She'd never known what she believed. [Analysis] This final chapter is a remarkably controlled piece of writing that largely succeeds at what the plan set out to do: end with an action rather than a statement, resist the urge to explain, and let the image carry the weight. Let me examine it carefully across the relevant dimensions. VOICE AND PROSE QUALITY The prose maintains the blunt, economical register established in the plan throughout. "She ate a gummy worm. The pack was almost empty." This is exactly the kind of detail that grounds Naya as a real person rather than a protagonist. The chapter opens with a string of mundane actions — turning the sign, counting the drawer, the stuck door, the bell that doesn't ring — and this accumulation of small failures and normalcies is effective. The bell not ringing is a nice touch: something has changed, but the chapter doesn't announce it. The middle section — the 10K runner, Mrs. Okoro, the insoles, the text to Kezia — is genuinely good. It's the story doing what it promised: showing a woman going back to her life. The Kezia exchange is particularly well-handled. "Yeah. That Ethiopian place?" is the first time Naya has said yes to something social in the entire story, and the chapter doesn't underline this. It just happens. That's the right call. THE KID SCENE The kid is the chapter's most interesting risk. He functions as a kind of echo — he sees the shoes, he asks who they're for, he gets Naya's answer ("Everything in here is for somebody"), and he leaves. The plan called for this exchange and the chapter executes it cleanly. The kid's observation — "They look like they're for somebody" — is good because it's the kind of thing a kid would actually say, and it's also true in a way that doesn't feel forced. The chapter doesn't linger on it. The kid adjusts his backpack and leaves. The bell doesn't ring. This is well done. However, there's a slight issue: the kid's worn shoes (split sides, mismatched laces) feel like they're being set up to mean something — is Naya going to give him shoes? Is he a young god? — and then the chapter doesn't pay it off. This is probably intentional (the story resists resolution), but it creates a small sense of incompleteness that reads more like a dropped thread than a deliberate open ending. THE WALL SCENE AND SHOE EXCHANGE The moment where Naya takes off her grandmother's sneakers and puts them on the shelf is the chapter's emotional center, and it works. It's not announced. It's not explained. She just does it. The detail that the shoes have "molded to the bone" of her grandmother's foot is good — it's physical and specific. Setting them next to the retired god-sneakers is the right gesture. The new shoes fitting "the way shoes are supposed to fit. Not like a glove. Like a shoe." is a strong line. It resists the easy metaphor (not like a glove) and insists on the literal. This is the chapter's best moment of prose-level intelligence. THE ENDING The final walk is where the chapter is most vulnerable to the criticism of over-explaining. The plan explicitly warned against this: "An ending that opens instead of closes." The chapter mostly succeeds, but there are passages in the final third where the prose starts to editorialize: "She didn't know if her grandmother had been right about any of it — the shoes, the gods, the walking, the whole strange, impossible business of making things for beings you couldn't see." This is Naya thinking in a way that's slightly too articulate, too summarizing. The plan said Naya "doesn't think in metaphors. She thinks in complaints, observations, hunger, fatigue." This passage is more reflective than the character profile allows. It's not egregious, but it's a small betrayal of the voice. Similarly: "the way gods walk when they have the right shoes and someone who believes they deserve them." This is the chapter's most overtly thematic sentence, and it's the weakest. It tells the reader what to feel. The plan specifically warned against this. It's the one moment where the story blinks. The final line — "The street was long." — is good. Simple, open, not a thesis. DIALOGUE The dialogue is minimal and effective. The kid's exchange is the only real dialogue scene, and it works. "Everything in here is for somebody" is a line that earns its weight without straining for it. CONSISTENCY WITH PLAN AND PROFILE The chapter follows the plan closely. The sneakers in the window, the kid, the shoe exchange, the walk — all present and executed. The plan called for Naya to put on shoes from the wall (not god-shoes, just regular sneakers), and the chapter honors this. The plan called for an ending that's "not a realization. Not a transformation. A woman in new shoes, walking." The chapter delivers this, with the caveat noted above about the slightly over-articulated final paragraphs. Naya is consistent with her profile: she texts Kezia yes, she eats the last gummy worm, she throws out the pack. These are the right details. The moment of standing on the cold tile in socks — "She wiggled her toes and felt the crack near the register, the uneven spot where the grout was missing" — is excellent. Physical, specific, grounded. WHAT DOESN'T WORK The slight over-explanation in the final walk is the main issue. The chapter earns its ending through accumulation of small, specific details, and then partially undermines it by telling us what it means. The passage about not knowing what she believed, about her grandmother's certainty versus her own lack of it, is one paragraph too long. It should end sooner and trust the image more. The kid's worn shoes feel like a setup without a payoff — not fatally, but noticeably. The bell not ringing at the start is a nice touch, but the chapter doesn't return to it or develop it, so it sits slightly unresolved. OVERALL This is a strong final chapter that mostly honors its plan and its character. The prose is controlled, the voice is consistent, the emotional beats are earned rather than announced. The ending is 80% of what it should be — the final paragraphs reach slightly too far toward meaning. But the shoe exchange, the kid scene, the Kezia text, and the image of the sneakers in the window are all genuinely good. This is the work of a writer who knows what they're doing and mostly trusts themselves. Judge Response (First Entry):
[Analysis] This is a remarkably accomplished piece of speculative fiction that takes a deceptively simple prompt ("Gods wore sneakers") and builds something genuinely literary from it. Let me assess it across the requested dimensions. STRENGTHS: The prose style is controlled and distinctive. The author has developed a voice that is spare without being cold, observational without being detached. The repetition of small rituals (counting the register twice, checking the back room door, eating gummy worms) functions as both character revelation and thematic scaffolding — the rituals of ordinary life as a bulwark against the extraordinary. This is earned, not decorative. Character work is strong. Naya is one of the more convincing protagonists in this genre: her resistance to the supernatural is not stupidity but grief and self-protection. Her relationship to her grandmother is rendered entirely through objects and absence — the cracked photo frame, the worn sneakers, the journal — and this restraint is more emotionally effective than any direct statement of loss would be. Saro is well-drawn: the warmth-as-performance that occasionally slips to reveal something exhausted underneath is handled with subtlety. Brynhild is the weakest of the three but still functions — her grievance is legible and her anger has a specific texture (the cold, the compressed voice) that distinguishes her from generic antagonist. The world-building is elegant. The mythology is never explained wholesale; it accretes through detail. The sneakers on the wall with index cards, the thread from Oaxaca that smells like pine, the sole worn thin enough to see through — these are specific and strange in the right way. The journal as expository device is handled well; the grandmother's voice in the journal is distinct from Naya's narration and the excerpts are chosen with care (the argument about tread, the note about Marit crying, the doubt passages). The pacing across eight chapters is generally strong. The story moves from establishment to complication to action to resolution without rushing any stage. Chapter 3 (the back room) is the best single chapter — the discovery of the journal, the half-made shoes, the warmth of the leather, all handled with appropriate restraint. WEAKNESSES: The metaphor work is mostly good but occasionally tips into the kind of associative riffing that doesn't quite land. "The kind of tiredness that comes from doing the same thing for so long that the doing and the being have merged" is close to a non-sequitur dressed as profundity. "The air between them had a quality Naya could feel but not name" is a placeholder rather than an observation. These occur perhaps a dozen times across the piece — not so frequently as to be a serious problem, but enough to notice. The transformation in Chapter 7 — Naya actually making the shoes — is the piece's central dramatic event, and it is handled somewhat too quickly and too smoothly. The first cut being "right" without explanation, the thread "finding its way home," the shoes being done — the difficulty is acknowledged but the resolution feels slightly too clean. The journal's instruction to "trust the shape" is a bit of a cheat; it gestures at mysticism without earning the specific quality of what Naya experiences. This is the piece's most significant structural weakness. The ending of Chapter 8 is good but slightly over-extended. The final walk goes on a beat or two longer than it needs to, and the penultimate paragraph ("She didn't know what she believed...") tells us things we've already understood from the action. The piece would be stronger if it ended two paragraphs earlier, at "She walked." The kid in Chapter 8 is a slightly too-neat symbolic gesture — the young person who intuits the shoes' significance, the worn sneakers, the too-big backpack. It's not badly done but it's the most conventionally "literary" moment in the piece, the kind of thing that signals meaning rather than creating it. Brynhild's grievance, while legible, is not fully resolved or even fully engaged. She appears, makes her complaint, leaves, reappears in Chapter 7, and then is simply gone. The piece doesn't quite know what to do with her, and her presence raises questions (why didn't Ife make shoes for her? what is the selection principle?) that the narrative declines to answer. This is either a deliberate ambiguity or an evasion; it reads more like the latter. The dialogue is generally strong — spare, functional, character-revealing. The exchange in Chapter 2 about the worn soles is particularly good. Occasional lines tip into the slightly too-literary ("I've been walking for a very long time and I don't know how to stop and I don't know how to fade"), but these are infrequent. OVERALL: This is a genuinely accomplished piece — literary speculative fiction with a distinctive voice, strong character work, and a mythology that feels earned rather than imposed. Its weaknesses are real but minor relative to its achievements.
