Judge Response (First Entry):
[Analysis] This is a genuinely accomplished piece of speculative fiction that demonstrates considerable craft across multiple dimensions. Let me work through its strengths and weaknesses systematically. CHARACTER WORK Ben is the most fully realized character. His grief is rendered through specific, concrete details: the net he doesn't need to mend, the whiskey bottle he looks at every night but doesn't open, the ring in the glove compartment, the knuckle-cracking ritual (left pinky, left ring, left middle—this repetition is excellent). His relationship with Cisco functions as emotional shorthand without becoming cloying. The phone call with Steph is one of the story's best scenes—the dialogue is restrained and true, capturing the specific pain of caring about someone you can no longer have. "You won't." "No. Probably not." This is earned. Elara is well-drawn as a scientist whose professional caution is in constant tension with her intuitive leaps. The thumbnail-pressing habit is a good physical tic. Her relationship with Tom and June is efficiently sketched. Her decision to send the true transmission rather than the curated lie is the story's moral climax, and it's handled with appropriate understatement—she doesn't feel heroic, she feels tired and certain. This is psychologically accurate. Lena is the most ambitious character and the most uneven. The sections written from her perspective are stylistically distinctive—fragmented, sensory, present-tense—and largely successful. The block-sorting, the pencil-holding in bed, the yogurt tasting "like the color pink" (synesthesia rendered simply and effectively). However, Lena risks becoming a mystical-disabled-person trope: the nonverbal autistic woman who serves as a conduit for alien communication. The story is aware of this risk (Maria's "She's not a subject. She's not a data point") but doesn't fully escape it. Lena's interiority is rendered with care, but she remains primarily a plot device—a human antenna—rather than a fully autonomous character. PROSE QUALITY The prose is consistently strong and occasionally excellent. The writer has a good ear for rhythm and knows when to use long sentences and when to cut short. "Overfishing is a slow drain. This was a plug pulled." This is clean and effective. The description of the dead harbor—the GREENWELL'S SEAFOOD sign still lit, the boats sitting like cars in a parking lot—is evocative without being overwrought. There are some instances of forced or strained metaphor. "The institutional weight settle on her shoulders like a physical thing" is a cliché dressed up as observation. "A stone in a stream and the water moves around it" in the Lena section is competent but not distinctive. The recurring "flat line" metaphor for the dead ocean is used well but perhaps once too often. "Like a horizon with no land on it" is the kind of image that sounds profound but doesn't quite cohere on examination—horizons by definition have no land on them. The Lena sections occasionally tip into purple prose: "a building that is not a building. A home for something very large and very old and very far away." This is doing a lot of atmospheric work with very little specificity. It's evocative but also somewhat evasive. PACING The pacing is generally well-managed. The story moves between three perspectives without losing momentum, and each chapter advances both plot and character. The early chapters (1-3) establish the world and characters effectively. Chapter 4 is the intellectual heart of the story—the discovery that the signal is structured around the acoustic signature of a healthy marine ecosystem—and this is genuinely creative and well-executed. The "scaffold built to hold a choir, and the choir was missing" is one of the story's best images. The later chapters (6-8) are somewhat less tightly controlled. Chapter 6 (Lena Draws) is the longest and most diffuse. The ending of Chapter 8 is deliberately open, which is appropriate for the story's themes, but it risks feeling unresolved rather than resonant. The final image—Elara writing "Don't know" and then starting to write underneath it—is a good ending, but the chapter as a whole meanders slightly before arriving there. WORLD BUILDING The world-building is excellent and restrained. The megastructures are never over-described—we get impressions, angles, the way they affect people rather than detailed specifications. This is the right choice. The biomechanical organisms are a genuinely interesting invention: not toxic, not predatory, but integrative—overwriting cellular processes with their own rhythm. "The fish didn't die of poisoning. They died of being gradually, mechanically overwritten." This is both scientifically plausible-feeling and thematically resonant. The new growth in Chapter 8 is handled well—strange, not quite right, but not threatening. The new fish species that are "too symmetrical, too coordinated" is a nice detail. The story resists the temptation to explain too much, which is the right instinct for this kind of first-contact narrative. PLOT AND CREATIVITY The central conceit—that the signal is structured around the acoustic signature of a healthy marine ecosystem, with gaps where extinct or depleted species' frequencies would be—is genuinely creative and emotionally resonant. It reframes the first-contact scenario as an ecological elegy, which is both original and thematically coherent. The question "Asking? Or inventorying?" is the story's best line. Elara's decision to send the true transmission is the plot's moral fulcrum, and it's handled with appropriate weight. The consequences are deliberately ambiguous—we don't know if it was the right choice, and the story doesn't tell us. WEAKNESSES The story's main weakness is that it occasionally tells us what to feel rather than letting us feel it. "She felt the weight of the assessment" is weaker than showing us Maria's face. The Lena sections, while stylistically distinctive, sometimes substitute atmosphere for specificity. The Rostova character is functional but thin—she's the institutional antagonist, the voice of strategic caution, and she doesn't have much texture beyond that. The aide who never gets a name is a missed opportunity. The ending is perhaps too comfortable in its ambiguity. The new growth, the new fish, the second hum in Lena's drawing—these feel like gestures toward hope that haven't been fully earned by the preceding darkness. The story has done excellent work establishing grief and loss; the tentative renewal in Chapter 8 arrives somewhat quickly. DIALOGUE The dialogue is generally strong. The Ben/Steph phone call is the best scene in the story. The Elara/Tom/June dynamic is efficiently rendered. The Rostova call is functional. The community meeting scene is slightly on-the-nose—the fishermen's grievances are real but the dialogue is a bit too perfectly representative of the type. OVERALL This is a sophisticated, emotionally intelligent piece of speculative fiction. Its central conceit is original, its prose is controlled, and its characters (particularly Ben and Elara) are genuinely realized. Its weaknesses are real but not fatal: occasional purple prose, a Lena who risks being a trope, an ending that arrives at hope slightly too easily. It's a strong piece that falls short of masterpiece primarily because it doesn't fully trust its own darkness. Of course. Here is a comprehensive writing plan for your darkly comic British YA story. ### **Brainstorming** **The Core Concept: The Nature of the Threat** 1. **The Literal Threat:** The emojis are a warning from a friend about a real, physical threat. This is more of a straight thriller, but the comedy could come from the group's incompetent attempts to solve it, like in *The Inbetweeners* or *Shaun of the Dead*. The threat could be a local serial killer, a gang, or something more mundane but scary (e.g., a dangerous, escaped animal). 2. **The Social Threat:** The emojis are a coded message about a social catastrophe. In the brutal hierarchy of a British sixth form, this could mean a massive secret is about to be leaked, a devastating rumour is spreading, or someone is about to be the victim of a truly epic prank or cyberbullying campaign. The "blood" is metaphorical. The comedy comes from the overblown, hyper-dramatic reaction of the teenagers. 3. **The Ghost Story/Urban Legend:** The emojis are the signature of a ghost or a figure from a local urban legend. Perhaps the "Stoke-on-Trent Slasher" or "Old One-Blood-Pete." The story follows the kids investigating a local haunting or legend, and the emojis are a classic trope of the genre, used with modern tech. Think *The Frighteners* but with iPhones and Greggs. 4. **The Elaborate Prank/Game:** The text is the opening move in a massive, immersive game (like a murder mystery or ARG) that one of their friends has set up. The protagonist thinks it's real, leading to a series of escalating, darkly funny misunderstandings as they try to "solve" the "murder" while their friends are just playing a game. 5. **The Combination:** The emojis are sent by a friend who has faked their own disappearance/disaster to get attention. The group then has to "investigate," slowly realising the truth, but in doing so, they stumble upon a *real* secret or a *real* danger that the prank was covering up. **Characters** * **Protagonist (P):** Our main character. Cynical, observant, and a chronic overthinker. Probably uses humour as a defence mechanism. They are the one who receives the text. Let's call them **Leo**. * **The Sender (S):** The friend who sends the text. Impulsive, a bit dramatic, and always in some sort of mess. The story's central question revolves around them. Let's call them **Finn**. * **The Voice of Reason (V):** The pragmatic friend. Tries to apply logic to every situation. Their suggestions are often the most sensible but the least fun, and therefore ignored. Let's call her **Maya**. * **The Chaos Agent (C):** The friend who embraces the drama. They don't want to solve the problem; they want to see where it goes. They suggest the most ridiculous and potentially disastrous courses of action. Let's call him **Callum**. **Setting & Tone** * **Setting:** A distinctly British, slightly grim suburb. Think a rain-soaked cul-de-sac, a 24-hour Tesco as a meeting point, a grotty park with a single flickering streetlamp, and the pervasive smell of damp. * **Tone:** The comedy comes from the clash between the mundane reality of their lives and their melodramatic teenage reactions. The "dark" comes from the slow-burn reveal that something is genuinely, unsettlingly wrong. The dialogue is sharp, sarcastic, and full of British slang and pop culture references. The horror/thriller elements should be played straight, which makes the characters' flippant reactions even funnier. **Plot Beats & Pacing** * **Chapters 1-2:** The setup. The text is received. The group gathers. Initial theories are wild and comedic. * **Chapters 3-5:** The investigation. They actively start looking for clues. This section is a mix of red herrings, dead ends, and moments of genuine tension. The friendship dynamic is tested. * **Chapters 6-7:** The twist. The true nature of the situation is revealed. It should be something unexpected but logical based on the clues. The tone shifts, becoming more serious. * **Chapter 8:** The confrontation and resolution. They have to deal with the reality of the situation. The ending should be satisfying but not overly neat, leaving a lingering question or a darkly humorous final beat. --- ### **Reflection** Looking at the brainstorming ideas, the most compelling path seems to be a combination of a few concepts. The "Literal Threat" (serial killer, etc.) feels a bit too generic for a YA story and might not allow for enough comedy. The "Ghost Story" could work, but the prompt's modernity (the emojis) feels better suited to a more grounded, human-centric threat. The "Social Threat" is the most realistic and relatable for a YA audience. The sheer terror of a social media meltdown or a devastating secret being exposed is something that age group understands viscerally. The "Elaborate Prank" is also strong and very much in the spirit of British comedy (think *Misfits* or *Stath Lets Flats* in tone). What feels like it has the most potential is the **combination**: **The Elaborate Prank that accidentally uncovers a Real, Social Threat.** This structure works perfectly for the prompt: 1. **It starts darkly comic:** The initial reaction is to treat Finn's text as a silly, dramatic cry for attention. The investigation begins as a joke, with Callum wanting to buy balaclavas and Maya making a spreadsheet of likely causes (from "dumped his girlfriend" to "ate a dodgy kebab"). 2. **The investigation deepens the mystery:** They follow clues that seem like part of a game or a cry for help. They might try to track Finn's phone, only to find it's been left in a ridiculously obvious place like a park bin. This reinforces the idea that it's all a prank. 3. **The twist raises the stakes:** The prank is a cover. Finn didn't just fake a crisis; he did it to get out of sight because he discovered something truly nasty about a trusted adult, a popular student, or a dark secret within their own friend group. Maybe he witnessed a crime, or he's the victim of blackmail. The "blood" emojis are no longer a joke; they are a literal or metaphorical representation of the danger he's in. 4. **The comedy comes from the contrast:** The protagonists are now in way over their heads, still reacting with teenage sarcasm and incompetence even as they face a genuinely perilous situation. Imagine them trying to blackmail a real criminal while arguing about whose turn it is to buy the crisps. This perfectly nails the "darkly comic British YA" tone. The characters I've brainstormed—Leo (the protagonist), Finn (the sender), Maya (the logic), and Callum (the chaos)—are a classic, functional ensemble. Their dynamic will be the engine of the story. The conflict between Maya's pragmatism and Callum's desire for chaos will provide natural comedy, while Leo's journey from cynical observer to reluctant hero will provide the narrative drive. The scope of 8 chapters at 1000 words each is ideal. It allows for a tight plot without rushing. We have enough space to establish the characters and their world (Ch 1-2), build the mystery with red herrings and genuine clues (Ch 3-5), execute a compelling twist (Ch 6-7), and bring it to a darkly humorous, impactful conclusion (Ch 8). The setting of a mundane British suburb will make the dark events feel more immediate and unsettling, grounding the horror in a recognisable reality. The final story will feel like a high-stakes game of "Cluedo" played by sarcastic teenagers, which is exactly what the prompt calls for.

# Intention **The Core Concept:** A prank that uncovers something real. Finn sends the bloody emojis in genuine terror, but the group's initial assumption—born from experience—is that he's being his usual dramatic self. The comedy lives in the gap between their flippant, bumbling teenage investigation and the genuinely disturbing truth they slowly uncover: a beloved teacher has been systematically bullying and manipulating students, and Finn is his latest target. The story is about the moment teenage games become real, and the friendship that holds when they do. **Plot Choices:** - The villain is Mr. Davies, a charming assistant headteacher everyone loves. This makes the twist land harder and raises the stakes: who will believe a group of teenagers over a respected adult? - The blood emojis are literal but misleading. Finn drew blood from himself in a panic during a physical confrontation with Davies. He sent the emojis as a desperate, coded cry for help—the only thing he could think to send in the moment. - The story unfolds as an amateur detective thriller driven by the group's incompetence, mutual bickering, and occasional flashes of genuine bravery. - The resolution involves the group presenting evidence to the headteacher as a united front. Davies faces real consequences but the story doesn't end neatly—the police investigation is ongoing, the school is shaken, and the kids are changed. **Voice and Style:** - First-person narration through Leo. Dry, observational, self-deprecating. Leo deflects with humour but underneath cares deeply. The voice should feel like a teenager who reads too much and says too little. - Dialogue-driven. The comedy comes from how these specific people talk: Callum's escalating crime-drama narration, Maya's deadpan pragmatism, Finn's chaotic energy (even in absentia), and Leo's internal monologue undercutting everything. - Distinctly British: the weather, the settings (Greggs, bus stops, a lock-up garage on a rough estate), the emotional repression, the way the characters say "it's fine" when it absolutely is not. - The tone should balance warmth with unease. The reader should feel the comedy of the friendship AND the creeping dread of what Davies actually is. Neither should overwrite the other. **What I Aim For:** - A story that earns its darkness by grounding it in authentic characters and real-world dynamics (the power imbalance between teacher and student, the terror of not being believed). - A villain who is chilling precisely because he's ordinary and well-liked. - A group of friends whose dynamic feels lived-in—messy, loving, argumentative, loyal. - A final chapter that sits with the emotional aftermath rather than rushing to a tidy conclusion. - At least three moments per chapter where the reader laughs out loud. - An ending line that lands with weight. **What I Avoid:** - Gratuitous violence or trauma. The darkness is in the situation and the power dynamics, not in graphic description. - A perfect resolution. Davies faces consequences but the story acknowledges that this kind of damage doesn't just "get fixed." - Making the characters too competent. They are teenagers. they get things wrong, argue about snacks, and make terrible decisions. That's the point. - Preachiness. The story doesn't lecture about safeguarding or bullying—it shows it through characters who are flawed and funny and brave in spite of themselves. - Over-explaining the humour. The comedy should arise naturally from character and situation, not from the narrator winking at the reader. --- # Chapter Planning **Chapter 1: "🩸🩸🩸" (~1000 words)** Leo is in bed at midnight, doomscrolling through TikTok, when the text arrives from Finn. Three bloody knife emojis. No words. Leo's first reaction isn't fear—it's exhaustion. Flashback montage of past Finn emergencies: the Facebook Marketplace goat, the time he accidentally joined a cult for a free pizza, the incident with the fire extinguisher and the head of year. Leo tries to call. Phone off. Texts go blue. He sits up. Something prickles at the back of his mind—Finn was weird at school today. Quieter than usual. Didn't steal a chip off Leo's plate at lunch. Leo gets dressed and bikes to Finn's house in the rain. Finn's mum answers. She says Finn's sleeping at a friend's house. Her face says she's been crying. She closes the door a beat too fast. Leo stands on the doorstep, soaked. He texts the group chat: "Finn's in trouble. The actual kind." Maya responds in four seconds. Callum responds with three fire emojis. The three meet at the bench behind the Greggs on High Street—their unofficial headquarters. They go to Finn's house while his mum is at work (Finn's older sister lets them in, barely glancing up from her phone). Finn's room is chaos, as expected—but there are wrong notes. A notebook hidden under his mattress with coded entries. His laptop search history: "how to record conversations legally UK," "evidence gathering school," "what is gaslighting." # How a Human Would Write This (And How an LLM Wouldn't) ## Telltale LLM Writing Approaches Before critiquing the plan, it's worth identifying the deep patterns in how language models approach creative writing, because these patterns are insidious—they feel like good craft decisions but they produce fiction that reads as *engineered* rather than *lived*. **The Symmetry Problem.** LLMs build fiction the way they build arguments: with balance, parallelism, and clean architecture. Characters slot into roles like chess pieces. The cynic observes, the pragmatist plans, the chaotic one provides comic relief. Every character has a function that complements the others. Real friend groups don't work this way. Real groups have redundancies, contradictions, people who contribute nothing useful, people who actively sabotage things in ways that aren't charming. The LLM ensemble is a sitcom writer's room; a human writer draws from the mess of actual relationships. **Linear Escalation.** LLM stories climb a steady staircase from Setup → Complication → Crisis → Climax → Resolution. Each chapter turns the dial one notch further. But real stories breathe. They stall. They wander into dead ends that aren't narratively efficient. They have scenes in the middle of a crisis where two characters stop to argue about whose turn it is to buy milk. The LLM doesn't trust the reader to stay engaged without constant forward momentum, so it over-delivers plot. A human writer trusts that stillness and digression can be more powerful than escalation. **Over-Explanation of Emotion.** "The silence was heavy." "The mood shifted." "For the first time, Finn smiled." LLMs are terrified the reader won't understand what they're supposed to feel, so they label every emotional beat like a museum exhibit. A human writer knows that the most powerful emotions in fiction are the ones the reader has to *infer*—from behaviour, from what's said versus what's meant, from the gap between what a character does and what they feel. The human trusts the reader. The LLM doesn't. **Everything Serves the Plot.** In an LLM story, every detail is a Chekhov's gun. The search history, the notebook, the burner phone, the circled name—all placed in Chapter 2 like clues in a locked-room mystery. Real life is cluttered with irrelevant detail. A real teenager's laptop search history would include 200 TikTok links, three failed homework searches, and something deeply embarrassing. The LLM scrubs the mess to keep the plot machine running. The human writer knows that the irrelevant detail is often where the truth of a character lives. **Tonal Metronome.** The plan specifies "at least three moments per chapter where the reader laughs out loud." This is a quantified emotion—a recipe. It produces fiction with a metronome: serious, funny, serious, funny, like a sitcom. Real dark comedy doesn't alternate between tones; it finds the absurdity *inside* the horror. A teenager describing the worst night of their life might make a joke that isn't funny—it's a defence mechanism, and the comedy and the dread are the same beat, not alternating beats. A human writer follows the emotional logic of a scene, not a laugh quota. **The Clean Villain.** LLMs create villains who are legibly evil with specific, articulate threats. Davies saying "I'll plant search terms on your school laptop" is a movie villain line. Real abusers are sloppier, more pathetic, more manipulative in ways that are harder to name. They don't monologue—they deny, they minimise, they make you doubt your own memory. The LLM villain is a plot device. A human writer might make Davies more unsettling by making him *less* coherent—someone who might not even fully understand what he's doing, which is scarier. **Britishness as Aesthetic Checklist.** The plan lists Greggs, bus stops, the weather, and "it's fine" like ingredients in a recipe. This produces fiction that wears its setting as a costume rather than breathing it as atmosphere. Real British YA doesn't announce its Britishness—it just *is*. The rhythm of the dialogue, the specific class dynamics, the emotional repression, the way people talk around a thing rather than about it. A human writer who grew up in this world wouldn't need to checklist it; it would inflect every sentence naturally. **The Promised Resolution.** The plan states upfront that "Davies faces real consequences" and the group "presents evidence as a united front." This is the LLM's need to reassure: don't worry, this dark story has a satisfying ending. But a braver, more human story might leave consequences ambiguous. It might have the headteacher not believe them. It might have one friend betray the group. It might end with the question unanswered—did it work? Did anyone listen? A human writer is more willing to let the reader sit in discomfort without a safety net. --- ## Deep Critique of the Current Plan ### The Plot Is Too Competent Finn is presented as a panicking teenager, yet his evidence trail is improbably neat. A coded notebook under the mattress. A burner phone with organized screenshots. A search history that reads like a table of contents for the story's themes. A circled name. This is a detective show's evidence board, not a seventeen-year-old's frantic documentation. A real teenager in crisis would be messier—some evidence would be incomplete, contradictory, or accidentally deleted. Some of it might even exonerate Davies, creating genuine uncertainty for the group. The discovery scene in Chapter 2 is a particular offender. The group walks into Finn's room and finds *everything* they need in one location, in one visit. This is the LLM's efficiency problem: it clears the table in one scene so the plot can advance. A human writer might have them find *some* things but miss crucial pieces. Maybe the burner phone is missing. Maybe the notebook is in a code Leo can't crack. Maybe they find something that doesn't fit the theory—that makes them question whether Finn is as innocent as they assumed. The investigation should be frustrating and incomplete, not a tidy evidence reveal. ### The Emotional Beats Are Pre-Scripted "Callum stops eating." This is a classic LLM dramatic beat—the comic character goes serious to signal that the stakes have risen. It works in a sitcom. In fiction, it feels like a stage direction that reads: {INSERT GRAVITAS HERE}. A human writer might not have Callum stop eating at all. Maybe Callum cracks a joke that falls flat and doesn't know why. Maybe he gets angry at a minor detail—a poster on the wall—and the real emotion leaks out sideways. People don't signal their feelings in neat, legible ways. They misdirect, they deflect, they express grief as irritability or terror as boredom. The plan reads everyone's emotions as if they're displayed on a screen. A human writer would bury the feelings deeper and trust the reader to dig. Similarly, "For the first time, Finn smiles" at the end of Chapter 4 is a planted emotional payoff. It tells the writer what to aim for rather than discovering the moment organically. What if Finn doesn't smile? What if he's too far gone for that? What if the moment of connection is smaller and less cinematic—a nod, a shrug, the offer of a crisp? Small moments land harder than performed ones. ### The Structure Is Mechanical Each chapter has one clear job: - Ch1: Inciting incident - Ch2: Discovery of evidence - Ch3: Reconnaissance - Ch4: Full backstory - Ch5: Plan formation - Ch6-7: Twist and complication - Ch8: Resolution This is a gear system, not a story. Real stories do multiple things at once. A chapter that's ostensibly about reconnaissance might really be about Leo confronting his own cowardice. A chapter about the plan might derail into an argument that reveals something about the group's dynamics that has nothing to do with Davies. The human writer would let chapters have messy, multiple purposes—and might not know what a chapter is *really* about until after it's written. The "Operation Greggs" concept in Chapter 5 is particularly LLM-flavoured. It's a fun nickname for the plan, but it turns the investigation into a heist-movie structure. Real teenagers don't have operations with code names. They have chaotic, improvised, contradictory approaches that they argue about constantly. The "plan" should feel fragile and stupid, not like a briefing scene in *Ocean's Eleven*. ### The Friend Group Is Too Complementary Leo observes, Maya plans, Callum disrupts. They never step on each other's roles. But in reality, Maya might also be chaotic when she's scared. Callum might occasionally be the most perceptive person in the room. Leo might not be the reliable narrator the reader thinks he is—he might be blind to his own selfishness, or he might have his own relationship with Davies that complicates his objectivity. More importantly, the plan doesn't account for disagreement. The group seems to move in lockstep after Chapter 2. A human writer would want sustained conflict *within* the group. Maybe Maya wants to go to the police and the others refuse. Maybe Callum's approach to Poppy puts her in danger and the group fractures. Maybe Leo is tempted to just... not get involved. To forget he ever saw the text. That cowardice—really sitting with the temptation to walk away—is more human and more compelling than the plan's assumption that the group will unite and fight. ### The Villain Is Too Articulate Davies's threats are cinema-ready: "I'll plant search terms on your school laptop... destroy your GCSEs... no one will believe a difficult boy." This is a monologue crafted to sound chilling. But real abusers don't operate this way. They operate through plausible deniability, through small kindnesses that make the victims doubt themselves, through institutional power that doesn't need to articulate its threat because it's obvious to everyone. Davies's danger should come from his *ordinariness*—from the fact that he's so well-liked that accusing him feels like accusing a family member. The scariest thing Davies could do isn't threaten Finn—it's be kind to Finn in front of witnesses, so that Finn's account sounds unhinged. A human writer would make the villain harder to see clearly, even for the reader. ### The Resolution Is Too Satisfying "The group presents evidence to the headteacher as a united front. Davies faces real consequences but the story acknowledges that this kind of damage doesn't just get fixed." This is the LLM hedging: it promises consequences while promising emotional complexity. But the two impulses work against each other. A truly brave ending might have the evidence fall apart. Might have the headteacher side with Davies. Might have the police say there's not enough. Might have one of the group get cold feet and not show up. The "united front" is a fantasy—the most human version of this story would be the group *trying* to form a united front and finding it harder than they thought. And "Davies faces real consequences" is promised like a guarantee. A human writer might leave this open. Not as a cliffhanger, but as an honest reflection of how these things actually go: slowly, imperfectly, with no guarantee of justice. --- ## Brainstorming: Ways to Make It More Human **1. Let Leo be an unreliable narrator.** Maybe Leo knows more than he's letting on. Maybe he saw something with Davies and chose not to act. Maybe his "dry, observational" voice is a defence against his own guilt. A human writer would make the narrator complicit in the world they're describing, not just a camera. Leo's voice should have blind spots the reader can see but he can't. **2. Make the evidence trail messier and more uncertain.** Finn's documentation should be incomplete, contradictory, and hard to interpret. Maybe some of the recordings are unclear. Maybe the notebook entries are paranoid-sounding and could be read either way. Maybe the group isn't sure if Finn is documenting abuse or if Finn is unwell. This uncertainty is more honest and more tense than a clean evidence trail. It also forces the characters to make a *moral* choice—to believe their friend without proof—which is more interesting than simply confirming what they already know. **3. Let a scene be just people doing nothing.** A whole chapter—maybe 800 of its 1000 words—that's just the group sitting in Leo's bedroom after school, eating biscuits, not talking about Davies. Talking about nothing. About a girl in Callum's maths class, about whether a hot dog is a sandwich, about a video they saw. The Davies situation hangs over the scene like weather. Nothing "happens" but everything is loaded. This is where the reader falls in love with these characters, and it makes the dark scenes land harder because we care about these specific people. **4. Make one member of the group actively unhelpful.** Maybe Callum doesn't just provide comic relief—he actually makes things worse. He confronts Davies directly and blows their cover. He tells someone he shouldn't have. He's not a lovable chaos agent; he's a seventeen-year-old who can't keep his mouth shut and it costs them. This creates real tension within the group and avoids the "complementary ensemble" problem. **5. Let the investigation stall.** A whole chapter where they try to do something and it fails. They plan to record Davies and the recorder doesn't work. They approach Poppy and she denies everything. They sit in the garage waiting for Finn and he doesn't show. The plan has no momentum. The characters feel stupid and scared. This is more human than a machine that turns clues into progress. **6. Make the villain less legible.** Maybe Davies does something that seems genuinely kind—helps a struggling student, stays late to tutor someone—and the group sees it and thinks: what if we're wrong? What if Finn is wrong? The villain shouldn't be a villain in every scene. He should be a person in every scene, and the horror is in the duality. **7. Let the ending be small and uncertain.** No united front. No triumphant presentation. Maybe Leo goes to the headteacher alone because the others got scared. Maybe the headteacher says "thank you for telling me" and then nothing happens for two weeks and they don't know if anything is being done. Maybe the last scene is just the four of them sitting together, not talking about what comes next, eating chips in the rain. The courage is in the telling, not in the outcome. **8. Let the voice be less polished.** Leo's narration should be messier—more tangent-prone, more self-contradictory, more prone to going off on a thought and losing the thread. A human voice isn't a perfectly curated dry wit. It's someone trying to make sense of something while simultaneously trying not to feel it. Let Leo be wrong about things. Let him misread situations. Let his humour occasionally miss, or come at inappropriate moments, revealing something about him that he doesn't intend to reveal. **9. Let the emoji text haunt the story differently.** The three bloody emojis should recur in unexpected ways—not just as the inciting incident but as an image that attaches itself to other things. Leo sees a row of three red lights and thinks of them. Finn's blood on the garage floor. A smear of ketchup on a napkin. The motif should be organic and accidental-feeling, not a deliberate literary device. A human writer would notice the echo during writing and decide whether to keep it; an LLM plants it intentionally and it feels designed. **10. Let the Britishness be in the rhythm, not the references.** Instead of name-checking Greggs and bus stops, let the Britishness live in the dialogue patterns: the way teenagers say "yeah, no, no, yeah." The way they insult each other as a form of affection. The way they deflect serious conversations with sarcasm. The emotional repression that means Leo would rather bike through the rain at midnight than admit to anyone, including himself, that he's scared. The Britishness should be structural, not decorative. **11. Question whether Mr. Davies is even the real story.** A human writer might start with the villain premise and then realise, halfway through writing, that the real story is the friendship. Davies is the catalyst, not the subject. The story is about what these kids do when the world demands they be braver than they are. Maybe Davies is barely on the page. Maybe he's a presence—a shadow, a reputation, a thing that's talked about—more than a character. The human writer follows what's interesting, even if it diverges from the original plan. **12. Don't explain the blood.** The original prompt is three bloody emojis. The plan resolves this neatly: Finn drew his own blood in panic. But what if the explanation is muddier? What if Finn sent the text in a dissociative state and isn't entirely sure why he sent it? What if the blood is his but the act of sending the emojis was almost involuntary—a cry so coded even he can't fully decode it? The LLM wants the emoji to have a clean answer. The human writer might let it remain slightly ambiguous, because real cries for help often are.

# Intention **What This Story Is:** Four teenagers. One text message at midnight. Three bloody emojis and nothing else. The story is about what happens next—not as a thriller plot but as a portrait of a friendship being stress-tested by something real. The comedy comes from who these people are when they're scared. The darkness comes from a world where a teacher can hurt a student and the system is designed not to believe them. The heart comes from four kids who aren't brave or smart or qualified deciding, badly and fearfully, to try anyway. **Plot:** Finn sends 🩸🩸🩸 from a school bathroom after Mr. Davies—a well-liked assistant headteacher—physically intimidated him and threatened to fabricate evidence against him. Finn has been quietly documenting Davies's pattern of targeting vulnerable students. The group discovers fragments of this, not all of it, and has to decide what to do with incomplete knowledge and no authority. The investigation is halting, frustrating, and frequently derailed by the characters being teenagers. One member of the group makes things worse. The attempt to gather proper evidence fails. Ultimately, Leo takes what they have to the headteacher alone, because the others can't face it, and the story ends without knowing whether it was enough. The villain is not a monologuing predator. He's a man who is kind in public and dangerous in private, whose ordinariness is the mechanism of his power. We see him only in glimpses—through corridors, through other people's reactions, through a single, brief, ambiguous scene. The horror is in the gap between what he appears to be and what he is. **Voice:** Leo narrates in first person. The voice is dry, digressive, self-aware, and slightly evasive—someone who uses humour to keep the reader at a distance while inadvertently revealing more than he intends. Leo is not a reliable narrator. He has blind spots: his own fear, his own complicity in a school culture that protects adults, and possibly his own prior interactions with Davies that he's chosen to forget. The voice should feel like a real teenager trying to make sense of something while simultaneously trying not to feel it. It should meander, contradict itself, go on tangents, and occasionally land on something devastating without acknowledging it. The dialogue should sound like actual British teenagers: overlapping, profane, full of in-jokes, constantly deflecting sincerity with sarcasm. Characters insult each other as a form of affection. Emotional moments are undercut by someone saying something stupid. Nobody gives speeches. **Structure:** The chapters don't each have one clean job. They do multiple things at once—advance the plot while also being about something else entirely. One chapter that's supposedly about the investigation is really about Leo avoiding his homework. One that's about finding Finn is really about the group arguing about crisps. The Davies plot and the friendship plot are braided together, and the story knows that the friendship is the actual subject. At 1000 words per chapter, there is no room for fat. Every chapter needs to earn its place. But "earning its place" doesn't always mean advancing the plot—sometimes it means making the reader care about these people so that the later chapters hurt. **What I Aim For:** - Characters who feel like specific individuals, not role-filling archetypes. They surprise each other and the reader. - An investigation that is messy, partial, frustrating, and doesn't yield all its answers. - Comedy that comes from character and situation, not from a narrator winking at the reader. - A villain whose evil is mundane and institutional, not theatrical. - Emotional restraint: the most powerful moments are the smallest ones. - An ending that is honest rather than satisfying. The story earns its dark by not offering false light. - The emojis as a motif that accumulates meaning organically through the story. - 1000 words per chapter that feel full but not packed. Room to breathe. **What I Avoid:** - Clean, efficient plot mechanics. Real investigations stall, backfire, and produce confusing results. - Complementary ensemble casting. These friends overlap, contradict, annoy each other, and occasionally fail each other. - Explained emotions. No "the mood shifted," no "for the first time, he smiled." Let behaviour speak. - A satisfying resolution. The headteacher might not act. The police might not come. The outcome is uncertain. - Name-checking Britishness. Let it live in rhythm and register, not in brand names. - Over-articulate villains. Davies doesn't threaten—he denies, minimises, and makes people doubt themselves. - The group forming a united front. In reality, they'd argue, get scared, and only one or two would follow through. - A tidy villain defeat. This isn't a story about catching a bad guy. It's a story about the cost of speaking up. --- # Chapter Planning **Chapter 1: "🩸🩸🩸" (~1000 words)** Midnight. Leo is in bed, not sleeping, scrolling through nothing on his phone. The text arrives from Finn: three bloody emojis. No words. Leo's first reaction is annoyance—he's tired, and Finn does this sort of thing. A brief, wry catalogue of past Finn emergencies establishes the dynamic: Finn is the friend who creates crises, and Leo is the friend who sighs and deals with them. But Leo tries calling. Phone off. He waits. Nothing. He texts back. Nothing. He gets up. Something sits wrong—not drama, just a quiet wrongness. He remembers Finn at school today: quieter than usual, eating alone at lunch, not taking the piss out of Leo's jumper. Small details Leo didn't register at the time. He bikes to Finn's house in the rain. Finn's mum answers. She says he's sleeping at a friend's house. Her face is someone who's been crying but won't say why. She closes the door. Leo stands on the doorstep. The rain is cold. He looks at the emojis on his phone. He texts the group chat: "Finn's in trouble. The actual kind." Maya responds in seconds. Callum sends a thumbs-up. Leo stares at the three red droplets. The chapter ends not on dread but on Leo's irritation at himself for being scared, and his inability to articulate why. **Chapter 2: "The Bench" (~1000 words)** Morning. The three meet at the bench behind Greggs—wet, cold, their unofficial spot. The comedy of the mundane: Callum arrives eating a sausage roll he shouldn't have bought, Maya has a notebook she's clearly been up making, Leo is hungover on zero sleep. They discuss theories. The theories are mostly stupid. Callum thinks Finn's been kidnapped. Maya thinks it's medical. Leo thinks it's a girl. They argue. The argument is funny and revealing—it shows how they each process uncertainty. They decide to go to Finn's house while his mum is at work. Finn's older sister lets them in, bored, doesn't care. Finn's room is messy in the expected ways—but there are wrong notes. Not a neat evidence trail. A crumpled piece of paper in the bin with a paragraph of Finn's handwriting about "the room after school" and "he said no one would believe me." Leo's stomach drops but he reads it as possibly about a girl, possibly about anything. Maya finds a search history that's more troubling: "how to record conversations legally," "can a teacher be reported for—" (the search was abandoned). No circled name. No smoking gun. Just fragments that could mean anything. They leave the room feeling uneasy but uncertain. On the way out, Finn's sister mentions offhandedly that he's been "weird for weeks." Nobody knows what to do with this. They stand in the street and don't decide anything. Leo goes home and lies on his bed staring at the ceiling. **Chapter 3: "School" (~1000 words)** A school day. The three try to function normally while hyperaware of everything. This chapter is 60% just being at school—the bell, the corridor chaos, a teacher droning about the Treaty of Versailles—because the horror lives inside the ordinary, and the story needs the reader to feel the texture of this place. Mr. Davies appears in passing: charming, warm, asks Leo how he's doing, compliments his essay. Leo feels a flicker of doubt—this man seems fine. In the canteen at lunch, they watch Davies interact with students. He's good at it. He's everyone's favourite teacher. But they notice small things: a Year 10 girl—Poppy—who goes rigid when Davies puts a hand on her shoulder; the way he steers certain students into one-on-one conversations; Mrs. Chen, another teacher, watching from the staff table with an expression that might be concern or might be nothing. They try to talk to Poppy. She sees them coming and leaves. After school, Leo spots Davies in the car park, on the phone, not smiling. It's the first time Leo's seen him without the mask. The image is fleeting. Leo doesn't know what to make of it. The chapter ends with the group standing at the school gates, not talking about what they saw, because none of them are sure they saw anything at all. **Chapter 4: "The Lock-Up" (~1000 words)** Finn texts Leo's phone—an address, a time. A lock-up on an industrial estate. The three go. The comedy: Callum brings a cricket bat for reasons he can't articulate; Maya brings a first aid kit with the grim preparedness of a field surgeon; Leo brings his phone on record and a stomach full of anxiety. The lock-up is damp and cold. Finn is there. He looks bad—not cinematic-bad, just unwashed and jittery and thin in a way he wasn't a month ago. He's been sleeping on a camp bed. The story comes out in pieces, not a clean monologue. Finn has been documenting Davies's behaviour toward students—quiet ones, vulnerable ones, ones from difficult homes. It started when Poppy told him something. He began keeping notes, recording conversations on his phone. Some of it is damning. Some of it is ambiguous. Some recordings are just Davies being nice, which makes Finn doubt himself. Then Davies found out. The confrontation: cornered Finn in an empty classroom after school. Grabbed his arm. Told him calmly that he'd make sure Finn was expelled. That he'd tell the right people the right things. That no one would believe him. Finn showed the group his arm—bruise still visible, yellow-green. Then he held up his hand. A small cut across his palm, scabbed over. From gripping the door frame. He sent the emojis because it was the only thing he could think to send—his own blood, his own proof that something happened, even if he couldn't explain what. The group sits in the garage. Callum doesn't say anything clever. Maya's face is very still. Leo wants to leave. He doesn't say that either. The chapter ends with Leo asking what Finn wants them to do, and Finn saying he doesn't know. **Chapter 5: "Nothing" (~1000 words)** This is the chapter where nothing happens and everything happens. The group meets at Leo's house after school. His mum's at work. They sit in his bedroom and eat biscuits and argue about what to do. This chapter is mostly dialogue. The argument is real and ugly. Maya wants to take everything to the headteacher immediately. Finn says the headteacher plays golf with Davies. Callum wants to confront Davies directly—walk up to him and call him out. Leo points out that's insane. Callum says Leo's plan is to do nothing. Leo doesn't have a plan and it stings to hear it said out loud. Finn is quiet. He doesn't want to go to the police because he's scared. He says this plainly and it silences the room for a moment. They sit with it. Then Callum makes a joke and the moment passes but it hasn't. They don't decide anything. Callum leaves. Maya stays and helps Leo wash up the biscuit plates without discussing the actual problem. They talk about a girl in Maya's maths class instead. It's the most normal five minutes of the book. Then Maya leaves and Leo is alone in his kitchen and the normalcy collapses. He opens Finn's crumpled note again and reads the words he didn't want to see: "he said I was special, the same thing he said to the others." Leo puts the note down. He sits in the kitchen for a long time. **Chapter 6: "Poppy" (~1000 words)** Two days pass. The group hasn't done anything. The silence in the group chat is loud. Then Callum, impulsively, approaches Poppy in the corridor before school. He doesn't have a plan. He just says her name and asks if she's okay. Poppy panics. She tells him to leave her alone, loudly, and a teacher sees. The teacher takes Poppy aside. Callum gets a detention. The incident ripples: Poppy tells the teacher Callum was harassing her (to protect herself, because she's terrified of what Davies will do if she's seen talking to the group). The teacher reports it. Callum's mum gets a call. The group meets after school, frayed. Callum is defensive. Leo is angry. Maya is frightened. Finn is absent—he's stopped responding to messages. They go to the lock-up. It's empty. Finn's stuff is gone. They don't know where he is. Leo calls his phone. Off. They call his house. His mum says he's at a friend's. She sounds like she's lying again. Leo is scared now—not the productive kind of scared but the kind that makes you want to go home and close the door. The chapter ends with the three of them standing on the industrial estate in the rain, having achieved nothing, possibly having made things worse, with one fewer member of the group than they started with. **Chapter 7: "Alone" (~1000 words)** Leo goes to school the next day alone. Maya is staying home—she tells Leo via text that she "can't today," and Leo doesn't push it, which says something about him that he doesn't examine. Callum is suspended for two days for the Poppy incident. Leo navigates the school by himself. Everything looks the same but feels wrong. He sees Davies in the corridor. Davies smiles at him. "How's Finn doing? Heard he's been off." The casualness of it, the warmth—Leo feels something cold move through him. He realises, in this moment, that Davies knows. Davies knows they know, or suspects it, and the smile is a message: I'm still here. I'm still in charge. Leo goes to the bathroom and is sick. He texts Finn. Nothing. He texts Finn again: "Are you okay?" An hour later, one word comes back: "No." Leo looks at it for a long time. He goes to the library at lunch. He opens Finn's crumpled note on his phone—he photographed it. He reads it again. He reads the other fragments he has: the search history, the bruise, Poppy's flinch, Mrs. Chen's expression, the way Finn looked in the garage. He sits with the weight of it. He knows what he has to do. He doesn't want to do it. The chapter ends with Leo opening a new message to the headteacher's school email, and typing, and deleting, and typing again. **Chapter 8: "Three" (~1000 words)** Leo goes to the headteacher's office before morning registration. He has a USB drive with photos of Finn's notes, screenshots of the search history, and the fragment of the crumpled note. It's not enough evidence. It might not be anything. He sits in a plastic chair outside the office and his hands are shaking and he wants to throw up. The headteacher—a woman named Dr. Osei, efficient, tired—listens. She doesn't interrupt. She doesn't make a face. She asks measured questions. Leo answers badly, tripping over words, contradicting himself. At one point he almost stops, almost says "actually, it's nothing, forget it," because the urge to undo this is physical. He doesn't stop. When he's done, Dr. Osei says she'll look into it. She asks him not to discuss this with other students. He nods. He leaves the office. He doesn't know if she believed him. He doesn't know if she'll do anything. He walks back through the corridor and school is exactly the same—loud, ordinary, nothing has changed. He finds Maya at her locker. He tells her what he did. She looks at him for a moment and says, "Okay." That's all. He finds Callum on the bench behind Greggs, back from suspension, not eating. Callum asks what happened. Leo tells him. Callum nods. They sit. Finn texts the group chat for the first time in three days: "thank you." Not a big moment. Not a resolution. Just three words and three emojis and four teenagers on a wet bench behind a Greggs, not talking about what comes next, because they don't know, because it isn't over, because maybe it won't be, because they did the thing and the thing is done and the world hasn't changed but something small and permanent has, in them, and none of them can name it.

# Leo **Background & Personality:** Leo lives with his mum in a three-bed semi that's too big for two people since his dad moved to Swindon with his new partner two years ago. He's starting to fill out but still has the build of someone who forgets to eat. Brown skin, close-cropped hair, dark eyes that people describe as "intense" when they're being kind and "creepy" when they're not. He has a habit of staring at people when he's thinking, not realising he's doing it. He slouches. He walks with his hands in his pockets or fidgeting with his phone. When he's nervous, he touches the back of his neck. When he's lying, he goes very still. He dresses in the same rotation of hoodies and jeans—not out of style but out of a genuine indifference that he sometimes performs as a choice. He has a small scar on his chin from falling off his bike at age nine and he's privately vain about it because it's the most interesting thing about his face. **Motives, Allegiances & Relationships:** Leo's primary allegiance is to Finn, but it's complicated. Finn is his oldest friend—the one from primary school, the one who knew him before the divorce, the one who texts him stupid memes at 2am. Leo loves Finn in the inarticulate, clumsy way teenage boys love each other, and he would never say this out loud or even think it in those terms. What he thinks is: Finn's my mate. That's it. That's the whole thought. But the depth of it is visible in his actions—biking through the rain at midnight, photographing Finn's crumpled note, sitting in a headteacher's office with shaking hands. His relationship with Maya is one of genuine affection overlaid with a slight power struggle. They're both smart, and they both know it, and sometimes they compete for the role of "person who understands what's really going on." He admires her decisiveness and is irritated by it in equal measure. She's the person he'd call if something went wrong, and also the person he'd least want to see if something went wrong, because she'd know he'd failed to act. His relationship with Callum is simpler and more uncomplicated—genuine fondness for someone he considers an idiot, with a thread of real fear underneath. Callum's impulsiveness is everything Leo isn't, and part of Leo resents that Callum can just *do things* without spiralling into analysis paralysis. The other part of Leo knows that Callum's doing-things instinct is genuinely dangerous and that someone needs to hold the brakes, and he's volunteered himself for that role without ever being asked. Leo's relationship with authority is one of表面 compliance and internal dissent. He's the student teachers describe as "a pleasure to have in class" because he does the work, keeps his head down, and never challenges anything. He hates this about himself. Davies has always been particularly warm toward Leo, and Leo has always accepted this warmth without questioning it, and this is a thing he is going to have to reckon with. **Voice Samples:** Internal monologue: "The thing about getting a text at midnight is that your brain immediately starts negotiating. It's a prank. His cat died. He's drunk. He's bored. He's testing you. You go through every possibility that isn't the one where your friend is in actual danger, because that one requires you to do something, and doing something at midnight in the rain means being the kind of person who does things at midnight in the rain, and I have never once in my life been that person." Dialogue: Maya: "We need to compile the evidence properly." Leo: "We don't have evidence. We have a crumpled bit of paper and a search history that could also belong to someone doing a sociology coursework." Maya: "You're not helping." Leo: "I'm providing critical analysis. It's different." Maya: "It's really not." --- # Finn **Background & Personality:** Finn lives with his mum and older sister, Kayleigh, in a rented house that's been "temporarily" rented for four years. His dad is alive but absent—works on oil rigs somewhere, sends money sporadically, calls on Christmas and Finn's birthday and gets the date wrong at least once. The month before that, a voice note of him making a sound he described as "what a swan would sound like if it was British." I should have put the phone down. I should have done what any reasonable person does with a Finn emergency at midnight, which is assume it's fine and deal with it in the morning when the emergency has invariably resolved itself or been revealed as a misunderstanding involving a goat or a protein shake. I hung up. Texted back: "What?" Nothing. I called again. Phone off. Okay. I sat up. Looked at the screen again. Three red droplets, arranged in a neat triangle. I put on shoes without socks because I couldn't find socks and the urgency, if that's what it was, had passed the point of matching footwear. My bike was in the garden, leaning against the fence where I'd left it three days ago. The rain had started while I was in bed—I could hear it on the window—and by the time I got outside it was properly raining, the kind of English rain that doesn't commit to a direction but just sort of exists in the air, soaking everything equally. I pedalled. His house was dark. Not unusual—his mum works early shifts and is usually in bed by ten, and Kayleigh, his sister, is nocturnal in the way of seventeen-year-olds who've discovered staying up until 3am is technically possible. # Chapter 2: The Bench The bench behind Greggs is not a good bench. It's one of those bolted-down municipal things made from recycled plastic that's supposed to look like wood but instead looks like what wood would be if wood had given up on itself. It's always damp. There's a Greggs logo engraved on the backrest, which someone has annotated with a permanent marker to read "Greggs Deez," which has been there since Year 9 and which we have never once found not funny. This is our bench. Not in a sentimental way—we didn't choose it, it just became the place. When you're fifteen and you don't have a car and your parents don't want you in the house during daylight hours, you gravitate toward places that will let you sit without buying something, and the bench behind Greggs is the closest thing our town has to a neutral zone. We've sat on it in every weather. We've sat on it eating sausage rolls and eating nothing. We've sat on it after exams and before arguments and once, memorably, during a thunderstorm, because Callum wanted to know what it felt like and the rest of us wanted to witness the Darwinism. I got there first. This was unusual—I'm normally last, the one who arrives already apologising. But I hadn't slept. I'd lain in bed watching the rain move across my window like a living thing, and at six I'd got up and showered and eaten toast that tasted like cardboard and cycled to Greggs and sat on the bench and waited, and the waiting felt like a held breath that had been held since midnight. Maya arrived second. She was carrying a notebook. Not a school notebook—a proper one, A5, with a hard black cover and a pen clipped to the side. She'd clearly been up making it. The cover had a label on it, handwritten, that said "Finn — Situation" with the date. She sat down next to me, put the notebook on her knee, and didn't say anything for a moment, which was how I knew she was scared. Maya fills silence the way water fills a glass—completely and without effort. Silence from Maya means she's processing something she doesn't have a system for. "He look okay when you saw him?" she asked. "He wasn't there. I told you. His mum said—" "I know what his mum said. I mean last night. The text. What did it feel like?" I thought about this. "Wrong." "Wrong how?" "Just wrong. He didn't—there were no words, Maya. Finn always has words. Even when he's being an idiot he's verbose about it." She opened the notebook. Page one had a timeline—hand-drawn, in blue ink, with timestamps. "He posted on Instagram at 6:47pm. A story—a picture of a kebab with the caption 'regret.' Comments on it at 7:15 and 8:03. Then nothing. Phone's off from midnight. Text to you at 12:23am." "You tracked his Instagram story?" "I track everyone's Instagram stories. This isn't new." It was, in fact, new, but I didn't say that because she'd clearly been up all night building this thing and criticising the methodology felt like pulling the pin on a grenade. Callum arrived fifteen minutes late, which was early for Callum, carrying a paper bag from Greggs. He was eating a sausage roll. He was always eating something. I sometimes thought of Callum's mouth as a separate entity with its own agenda. "Right," he said, sitting down on the arm of the bench because the seat was occupied by Maya's notebook. "What are we thinking." "Finn's in trouble," I said. "Obviously. What kind of trouble." "We don't know." "Cult?" "No." "How do you know it's not a cult? He literally joined a cult for pizza." "That was three years ago." "Cults don't have an expiry date, Leo." Maya looked up from her notebook. "Can we focus?" Callum spread his hands. "I'm focused. My focus is: our mate sent us blood emojis at midnight, which, by the way, are not the emoji you send if you're having a good time. Those are the emergency emojis. Those are the 'ring 999 and describe the wound' emojis. So I'm thinking—" "You're thinking kidnapping," Maya said. "I'm not thinking kidnapping. I'm thinking... let's say extralegal detainment." "That's kidnapping." "It's a more specific kind of kidnapping." I put my face in my hands. The rain had stopped but the bench was still wet and my jeans were cold through and the sausage roll smell was making me hungry in a way that felt inappropriate given the circumstances. "He was weird at school yesterday," I said. "Quiet. Sat on his own at lunch. Didn't take a chip off my plate." "So it's a girl," Callum said. "It's not a girl." "How do you know?" "Because Finn would have told me about a girl. He told me about the Year 9 one. He told me about the one from the ice rink. He told me about—" "He told you about all of them because he's got no concept of privacy, which is why we love him, but also—" "It's not a girl, Callum." Maya closed her notebook. "There's only one way to find out. We go to his house." His mum would be at work by now. His sister would be home. We cycled there in a line—Maya at the front because she cycles with purpose, Callum at the back because he cycles the way he does everything, which is loudly and with unnecessary terrain negotiation—and arrived at Finn's house at twenty past nine. Kayleigh answered. She was in pyjamas with a dressing gown over the top, holding a cup of tea that looked like it had been made an hour ago and forgotten. She looked at us the way older siblings look at their younger brother's friends, which is to say with a mixture of tolerance and faint suspicion. "He's not in," she said. "Where is he?" I asked. "Out." "Out where?" "Out." She shrugged. "I don't track him. Come in if you want. I'm not his mum." We went in. The house smelled like washing-up liquid and toast. Finn's room was at the top of the stairs, door slightly ajar. Kayleigh went back to the kitchen without comment, which told us she either didn't care or was used to us turning up like stray cats. Finn's room was a disaster. Not a clean disaster—an actual disaster. Clothes on the floor, a plate with toast crusts on the desk, a blanket crumpled on the bed in a shape that suggested he'd slept in it and then left. Posters on the wall that hadn't been changed since Year 7. A copy of a book I didn't recognise on the nightstand—something about investigative journalism, which was weird because Finn didn't read. Not like that. I opened the desk drawer. Pens, broken, and a phone charger, and a crumpled piece of paper. I smoothed it out. Finn's handwriting—big and impatient, the letters leaning forward like they were trying to get somewhere. "He grabbed my arm. He said no one would believe me. I think he's done this before." I read it twice. Then I put it down on the desk and looked at Maya, who was scanning the room with the focused attention of someone cataloguing a crime scene. "Cupboard," she said, nodding at the wardrobe. I opened it. Inside, behind a pile of hoodies, was a notebook. Not Finn's usual kind of notebook—this one was small, black, with a rubber band around it. I pulled the rubber band off and opened it. The pages were dense with writing, dates, quotes. I couldn't make sense of it at a glance—it looked like fragments, half-sentences, timestamps. "Monday 3.15pm — Rm 14. Door closed." "Poppy said—" "He said the same thing." "RECORD THIS." Maya took the notebook and held it like it was something fragile. On the laptop—a battered Chromebook that the school had issued—she opened the browser. The search history was visible, recent, not cleared. "How to record conversations legally UK." "Can a teacher be reported for harassment." "What happens if you report a teacher and they deny it." The searches stopped there, as if he'd typed the last one and then closed the laptop and couldn't face anything else. We stood in the room. The four of us minus one, standing in the missing one's room, looking at fragments of something we couldn't assemble into a complete picture. It could have been anything. It could have been exactly what it looked like. Callum picked up the book on the nightstand. "Evidence and How to Find It," he read. "Finn's been reading a book about gathering evidence." "Give it here," Maya said. She took the book and flipped through it. Post-it notes stuck out from the pages, marking sections. "He's been studying this. He's been—Leo, he's been building a case." "Against who?" Callum asked. Nobody answered. Because we didn't know. Because the notebook didn't name names. Because Finn wasn't here to tell us. We left the room. In the hallway, Kayleigh was leaning against the kitchen doorframe. "He's been weird for weeks," she said, without being asked. "Not eating properly. Up all hours. Keeps going to that lock-up thing on Garland Street, I don't know what's there." She looked at us. "Is he in trouble?" "We don't know," I said. She nodded. "If you hear from him—" "Yeah." We left. Stood in the street. The rain had started again, lightly, more like an idea than an actual weather event. "So what do we do?" Callum said. Nobody answered. Maya had the notebook. She held it against her chest like a shield. I had the crumpled paper in my pocket. We had search histories and fragments and a word—"Poppy"—that meant nothing to us and everything to someone. I went home. Lay on my bed. Stared at the ceiling and felt something settle in my chest that I didn't have a name for yet, something heavy and cold that sat there while the afternoon light moved across the wall and my phone stayed silent and the world outside carried on as if nothing had happened, which was the worst part—that it was carrying on at all.

# Chapter 3: School School is a place that runs on bells. This is the first thing you need to understand about it, because everything else—the learning, the friendships, the slow erosion of your will to live—is secondary to the bells. They tell you when to move, when to stop, when to eat, when to think, when to stop thinking. They are the architecture of the day. Without them, we'd just be people in a building, and that's not allowed. The morning bell went at 8:40 and I was at my locker, which is three along from the water fountain that doesn't work, and the hallway was doing its thing, which is to say it was a war zone of bodies and noise and someone's blazer catching on someone else's bag strap and a Year 7 crying near the stairwell for reasons that would never be explained. I'd slept maybe two hours. The world had that unreal, slightly-too-bright quality it gets when you've been awake since 6am and your body is running on adrenaline and the ghost of the toast you ate. I hadn't told anyone about the night. About standing on Finn's doorstep. About his mum's face. The crumpled note was in my pocket, folded into a square so small it had become a hard little brick against my thigh. I could feel it every time I moved. I kept my hand in my pocket, pressing it flat, as if flattening the paper would flatten whatever was sitting in my chest. Maya found me at my locker. She had her notebook under her arm—the black one, not the school one—and she leaned against the locker next to mine and said, "History first. Treaty of Versailles. Try to look normal." "I always look normal." "You look like you haven't slept." "I haven't slept." "Then look like you haven't slept in a normal way." Callum appeared from the direction of the vending machine, which he had been attempting to extract a packet of Skittles from for approximately ninety seconds. He'd succeeded. He tore the packet open and offered me some. I shook my head. "Heard anything?" he asked, quieter than usual. "No." "Finn still not answering?" "No." Callum nodded. Chewed a Skittle. Looked down the corridor. "Right. Normal day, then." Normal day. History was Mr. Hargreaves, who was sixty-three and had been teaching the Treaty of Versailles for what appeared to be his entire life. He showed us a PowerPoint that hadn't been updated since 2011 and talked about Article 231 with the weary enthusiasm of a man describing his commute. I sat in the third row and looked at the words on the screen—WAR GUILT, REPARATIONS, TERRITORY—and thought about Finn's notebook. The fragments. "He grabbed my arm." "Poppy said—" "RECORD THIS." The words sat behind the lesson like wallpaper behind furniture, visible only when you looked past the thing you were supposed to be seeing. Maya sat two rows ahead. She was taking notes, because Maya takes notes, but her pen wasn't moving in the way it usually moved—fluid, continuous, certain. It was stopping. Starting. Stopping. She was present but not here. Callum was in the row behind me. I could hear him tapping his pen on the desk in a rhythm that meant he was thinking, which meant he was not thinking about the Treaty of Versailles. The bell went. We spilled into the corridor. I had double maths after that, which meant forty minutes of quadratic equations that I could do in my sleep, which meant forty minutes of my brain being free to go wherever it wanted, which meant forty minutes of staring at Mr. Patterson's whiteboard while my mind ran through Finn's notebook like a searchlight. After maths, in the corridor, Davies found me. He was coming from the staff room, coffee in hand, blazer slung over one shoulder because he was that kind of teacher—the ones who make the blazer look like a choice rather than a uniform. He was smiling. He was always smiling. It was his default setting, the way other people have brown eyes or a birthmark. He was maybe forty, slightly tall, with the kind of face that looks like it was designed for school photos. And when he saw me, his face did the thing it does, which is light up, specifically and warmly, in a way that made you feel like you were the only person in the corridor. "Leo! How's it going?" "Fine, sir." "That essay you handed in last week—on *An Inspector Calls*—genuinely one of the best I've read from a Year 10. The bit about Birling's responsibility? Really sharp." "Thanks, sir." "You should think about English A-level. Seriously. You've got the mind for it." He clapped me on the shoulder. His hand was warm and firm and it sat there for a second longer than it needed to. "How's Finn doing? He's been quiet lately." There it was. Casual. The question you'd ask any student about any friend. The concern of a good teacher. "I haven't seen much of him," I said. "Well, tell him I said hello. Tell him my door's always open. He knows that." He smiled again. Moved on. The corridor swallowed him, the way corridors swallow people—into the crowd, into the noise, into the ordinary. I stood there. His hand was still warm on my shoulder. And I thought: this man is fine. This man is a good teacher who reads essays and remembers names and keeps his door open. This man asked about Finn because that's what teachers do. And then I thought: but Finn's notebook didn't have a name in it, and I'm looking for one, and I'm standing in a corridor inventing a villain out of a man who complimented my essay. The doubt was so enormous it was physical. It filled the space between my ribs and pushed everything else out. Lunch. Canteen. The noise was extraordinary—every conversation in the building compressed into a single room, layered over the clatter of trays and the squeak of chairs on linoleum. We sat at our usual table, near the window that didn't open. Callum had chips. Maya had a salad she'd made at home and would deny making at home. I had my meal deal—the same one I always had, chicken and stuffing wrap, salt and vinegar crisps, water—and I ate it without tasting it. Davies was at the staff table across the canteen. He was eating lunch and talking to Mrs. Chen, who taught Biology and had the permanently frazzled air of someone who'd been asked to explain photosynthesis four thousand times. Davies was leaning back in his chair, relaxed, one arm draped over the back. He looked like a man with nothing to hide. I watched him. We all were, though we were pretending not to. Maya was "reading" her notebook. Callum was "eating" his chips. I was looking at Davies and trying to see what Finn had seen, and I couldn't, and the couldn't was the worst part—because either I was wrong and Davies was exactly what he appeared to be, or I was right and Davies was so good at being what he appeared to be that even knowing what I knew, I couldn't see through it. Then Poppy walked past the staff table. Year 10. Small, dark hair, the kind of quiet that isn't shy but is protective. Davies turned and said something to her—her name, probably, some pleasantry—and put his hand on her shoulder. Light. Casual. A teacher acknowledging a student. Poppy went rigid. Not dramatically. Not in a way anyone else would notice. But I was watching, and I saw it—a full-body freeze, a contraction, like a small animal encountering something it instinctively recognises as a predator. It lasted half a second. Then she smiled, said something back, and kept walking. Davies turned back to his lunch. I looked at Maya. She was looking at Poppy's retreating back with an expression I couldn't read. I looked at Callum. He was looking at Davies with his chip halfway to his mouth, not eating, just holding it. Mrs. Chen was watching too. From the staff table, she'd seen the interaction, and her face did something—a tightening, a slight pull at the corner of her mouth—before she looked down at her tray. It could have meant anything. It could have meant nothing. We didn't talk about it. Not then. We finished lunch and went to our separate classes and the afternoon ground on—Science, then PE, then tutor time—and the day did what school days do, which is fill every empty space with noise and motion until there's no room left for thought. After school. The gates. The rain had started again—light, persistent, the kind that doesn't justify an umbrella but punishes you for not having one. I was unlocking my bike when I looked up and saw Davies in the car park. He was by his car—a silver Golf, the car of a man who makes sensible financial decisions—and he was on his phone. Not smiling. His face was completely different from the face in the corridor, the face in the canteen, the face that lit up when he saw me. This face was hard. Focused. He was talking quietly, quickly, and his free hand was gripping the roof of the car in a way that made his knuckles white. It lasted maybe five seconds. Then he saw me looking. The mask returned—smile, wave, a casual "See you tomorrow, Leo"—and he got in his car and drove away. I stood by my bike. The rain was on my neck. Maya was beside me. She'd seen it too. I knew she had because she was doing the thing she does when she's processing, which is go very still and look at a fixed point in the middle distance like she's reading something invisible. "Did you see that?" I said. "He was on the phone," she said. "He wasn't smiling." "No." We looked at each other. The car park was emptying. A seagull was screaming at nothing on the roof of the gym block. Callum caught up, out of breath, bag bouncing. "What are we doing? Standing in the rain like two Victorian ghosts?" "Did you see Davies?" I said. "In the car park?" "He was on the phone. Looked properly angry." "Yeah." Silence. The rain. The seagull. The school behind us, fluorescent lights flickering off one by one through the windows, shutting down for the evening like a machine powering off. "So what does that mean?" Callum asked. None of us answered. Because it didn't mean anything. A teacher on the phone looking annoyed is not evidence of anything except that teachers have bad phone calls, which is not a revelation. We had a crumpled note and a partial notebook and a search history and a girl who flinched and a man on a phone. We had nothing. We had everything. We couldn't tell the difference. We went our separate ways. I cycled home in the rain and the note in my pocket was wet at the edges, the ink starting to bleed, the words blurring into each other, and I thought: I am not the kind of person who sees things and does something about them. I am the kind of person who sees things and goes home and lies in the dark. And then I thought: but I saw. I saw his face. I saw his face, and I can't unsee it, and I don't know what it means, and that not-knowing is going to eat me alive.

I didn't ask about the cricket bat. I'd learned long ago that asking Callum about the cricket bat only produced more cricket bat. I asked, looking at the bat. "In case of something." "That's not an answer." "It's the only answer I've got." We cycled. The lock-up was between the tyre place and a fencing company that looked like it was also closed. Four metal doors in a row, two grey, two rust-coloured. Finn's text said number three.
