Maya tried the handle. Locked. I knocked. Nothing. I knocked again. "It said 6pm," Maya said. "It's 5:52." "So we wait." We waited. Callum leaned against the wall and held the cricket bat like a walking stick. Maya checked her phone. I checked the burner phone. No new messages. The wind picked up and blew a crisp packet across the estate and it made a sound like something breathing. At 6:01, the door opened. Not from outside—from inside. It swung inward with a groan of metal on metal, and Finn was standing there. He looked—wrong. Not injured, not bleeding, not anything that would make a good film scene. Just wrong in the way that a person looks when they've been sleeping badly and eating nothing and carrying something too heavy for too long. Thinner. His face was narrower than I remembered, the bones more visible. His hair hadn't been washed. His eyes had a quality I can only describe as displaced, like he was seeing the lock-up from somewhere further away than the room he was standing in. The lock-up was small. A plastic bag from Tesco with something inside—food, maybe, or just the idea of food. It smelled like damp and metal and something else underneath that I didn't want to identify. "Come in," Finn said. His voice was normal. That was the worst part—the normalness of it, the way it clashed with everything else. "Close the door." We went in. Callum brought the cricket bat. Maya brought the first aid kit. I brought the torch I hadn't needed. We stood in a damp garage on an industrial estate and looked at our friend, who was standing in front of a camp bed in a room he'd been sleeping in instead of his own house, and none of us said anything for a moment too long. "Right," Finn said. "So." He sat on the camp bed. Crossed his legs. Started picking at the scab on his palm—the one we hadn't seen yet, the one he'd shown no one—and talked. It wasn't a monologue. It wasn't clean. He started and stopped and went back and added things and forgot to say things and then remembered them ten minutes later and said "oh, also" as if he was adding a footnote to an essay rather than describing the worst period of his life. He talked fast, the words tripping over each other, and sometimes he looked at the wall and sometimes he looked at his hands and sometimes he looked at me, specifically me, with an expression I couldn't bear. It started with Poppy. Weeks ago—maybe a month, maybe more, Finn wasn't sure. Poppy had pulled him aside after school, in the corridor near the science labs, and told him something. She didn't tell him everything. She told him enough. She told him about a conversation with Davies in his classroom after school, behind a closed door, that had made her feel wrong in a way she couldn't name. She told him Davies had said things to her that a teacher shouldn't say. She told him Davies had touched her arm, her shoulder, her hair. She told him she'd tried to tell another teacher and the other teacher had said Davies was "just friendly" and to not "read into it." "She was crying," Finn said. "Not properly. The quiet kind. The kind where you can see the person is trying very hard not to." Finn had listened. That was all. He'd listened and he'd said "that's shit" and she'd said "yeah" and that was the end of it. Except it wasn't the end of it, because Finn had started paying attention. To Davies. To how Davies moved through the school. To which students Davies touched, and where, and how they reacted after. "Once you see it," Finn said, "you can't not see it." He started a notebook. Dates, times, observations. Not evidence—not at first. Just notes. Things he noticed. The way Davies steered quiet students into one-on-one conversations. The way certain students came out of Davies's classroom looking like something had been taken from them. The way Davies's hand lingered. The way he selected. Quiet ones. Vulnerable ones. Ones from difficult homes, the ones who wouldn't be believed, the ones who didn't have adults who'd fight for them. Some of the students told him things. Not all of them. Not clearly. Fragments—whispered in corridors, hinted at in texts. Two of them confirmed what Poppy had described. One of them said "he does this to everyone" and then didn't speak to Finn again. Finn started recording. His phone, in his pocket, during conversations he initiated with Davies—asking about grades, asking for help with coursework, engineering excuses to be in Davies's classroom with the door closed. Some of the recordings were nothing. Davies being charming. Davies being helpful. Davies asking after his family with what sounded like genuine concern. These were the worst ones, because they made Finn doubt everything—made him think he was wrong, paranoid, seeing patterns in noise. And then there were the other recordings. The ones where Davies said things that shouldn't be said. The ones where the warmth in his voice curdled into something else, something possessive, something that understood exactly how much power it held and found the weight of it pleasurable. Finn didn't play them for us. He didn't need to. His face was enough. "Then someone talked," he said. "I don't know who. One of them, maybe. Or maybe he just—" He stopped. Started again. "He called me in after school. Last week. Said he wanted to talk about my grades. I went. I knew—I knew it might be—I went anyway." The room was very quiet. The bare bulb made a faint buzzing sound. "He closed the door. He was nice about it at first. He's always nice about it first." Finn's voice was steady. Too steady—the kind of steady that means you've rehearsed this, that you've told this story to yourself so many times in the dark that the words have worn smooth. "He asked me how I was doing. He said he was worried about me. He said he'd noticed I'd been spending time in his classroom and he appreciated that, he appreciated a student who took an interest. And then he—" He stopped. Picked at the scab. "He grabbed my arm. Here." He pushed up his sleeve. The bruise was yellow-green now, fading but still there, a thumbprint on the inside of his forearm. "He pulled me toward him. Close. And he said—" Finn swallowed. "He said I was special. He said I was the same as all the others. He said he'd planted search terms on my school laptop that would look—I can't—" He stopped again. "He said no one would believe me. He said he'd been teaching for twenty years and I was a difficult student with behavioural issues and a father who isn't around and he would—his words—he would 'manage the narrative.' He said I'd be expelled. He said he'd make sure I never went to university. He said it calmly, Leo. He said it like he was reading from a script he'd written before." The garage was silent. The bare bulb buzzed. Somewhere outside, a lorry started up on the estate, the engine turning over with a sound like coughing. "He let go of my arm. I walked to the door. I grabbed the door frame—I don't know why, I just grabbed it, and my hand—" He held up his palm. The cut was there, scabbed over, a thin red line across the skin. "It bled. Not a lot. It just bled. And I looked at it and I thought—" He looked at me. "I thought: I need to show someone something. I need to prove something happened. I need—" His voice cracked. Just slightly. A hairline fracture in the composure. "I couldn't type. I couldn't—I opened my phone and those were the only things I could send." 🩸🩸🩸 His own blood. His own proof. Three drops on a screen because words weren't enough and he didn't have words and the only thing he could think to send was the thing that was on his hand, the thing that proved that something had happened, even if he couldn't explain what. We sat there. Callum hadn't moved. Hadn't spoken. The cricket bat was resting against his leg and his hands were in his lap and his face was—open. Not performing. Not joking. Not filling the silence with anything. Just open, in a way I'd never seen from him, and the openness was so total it was almost unbearable, because it meant he understood, fully and without deflection, what had been done to their friend. Maya's face was very still. She was holding the notebook—the black one, Finn's notebook—and her knuckles were white around it. She wasn't going to cry. Maya doesn't cry. But something behind her face was moving, something tectonic, and I knew that when it surfaced it wouldn't be tears. It would be action. It would be the most precise, most controlled, most devastating action Maya was capable of. I wanted to leave. I wanted to stand up, walk out of the garage, get on my bike, and go home, and lie on my bed, and not be here, in this damp room, with this story, with this responsibility. I wanted to be the person who didn't know. I wanted to go back to midnight and put the phone face-down on the table and go to sleep and wake up in a world where Finn was just Finn, the friend who sends weird texts, the boy who bought a goat. I didn't leave. I sat there and I felt the wanting-to-leave move through me like a wave, and I let it pass, and I stayed. "So what do you want us to do?" I said. Finn looked at me. Looked at the floor. Looked at the door, the concrete, the sleeping bag, the crate of water—the architecture of his hiding place. "I don't know," he said. [Analysis] This is a genuinely accomplished piece of creative writing that largely delivers on its ambitious plan. Let me work through its strengths and weaknesses carefully. **Voice and Narration** Leo's first-person voice is consistently rendered throughout. The dry, self-aware, slightly evasive quality described in the character profile is present and functional: "Wednesday at 4:47 is when people are on buses, thinking about dinner. It's the beige of time." This is good - it's specific, it's character-revealing, and it doesn't strain. The voice maintains its register without becoming precious. The observation about wanting to leave - "I wanted to be the person who didn't know. I wanted to go back to midnight and put the phone face-down on the table and go to sleep" - is genuinely effective because it's honest about Leo's passivity without editorialising it. The narrator's unreliability is present but subtle. Leo notices things and doesn't fully process them. He describes Callum's face as "open" and calls it "almost unbearable" - this is the narrator inadvertently revealing more than he intends, which is exactly what the plan called for. **Dialogue and Character** The opening section with the cricket bat is the chapter's most successful comedy. It's earned, it's character-specific, and it doesn't overstay its welcome. Callum's "In case of something / That's not an answer / It's the only answer I've got" is exactly the kind of deflection-as-character that the plan describes. The first aid kit exchange between Leo and Maya is similarly efficient. Finn's testimony is handled with real skill. The plan called for it to come "in pieces, not a clean monologue" and the chapter delivers: "He started and stopped and went back and added things and forgot to say things and then remembered them ten minutes later and said 'oh, also' as if he was adding a footnote to an essay." This is told rather than shown, which is a weakness - we're told the testimony was fragmented rather than experiencing the fragmentation in the actual dialogue. The testimony itself, when rendered in direct speech, is actually fairly coherent and well-organised, which undercuts the claim of fragmentation. This is the chapter's most significant flaw. **The Reveal and Emotional Mechanics** The chapter plan specified that the story should come out "in pieces, not a clean monologue" and that "some recordings are just Davies being nice, which makes Finn doubt himself." The chapter does include the self-doubt element, but the actual revelation is more linear than the plan intended. Finn's account, despite the narrator's framing, reads as a fairly complete and coherent testimony. The plan's instruction that "some of it is ambiguous" is somewhat honoured (the recordings being described rather than played), but the overall effect is cleaner than intended. The bruise reveal and the cut-on-the-palm callback to the emojis is well-executed. The return of 🩸🩸🩸 as a structural beat - "His own blood. His own proof." - earns its place. This is the motif accumulating meaning organically, as the plan specified. **Davies** The plan called for Davies to be seen "only in glimpses" and to be "a man who is kind in public and dangerous in private." Finn's description of Davies in the confrontation scene - "He said it calmly, Leo. He said it like he was reading from a script he'd written before" - is effective precisely because it's mundane. The horror is in the administrative quality of the threat. This is the plan's vision of the villain executed well. **Prose Quality** There are some genuinely strong sentences: "the words have worn smooth" (about Finn's rehearsed testimony) is excellent. "Something tectonic" for Maya's suppressed emotion is slightly overworked but functional. The description of Finn as having eyes with "a quality I can only describe as displaced" is good. However, there are moments where the prose reaches for effect and doesn't quite land. "The rust on the door was the colour of dried blood, and I looked at it and then looked away because my brain was doing the thing it does, which is make connections that aren't there and present them as evidence" - this is self-aware about the forced metaphor, which partially redeems it, but it's still a bit laboured. The ending - "inside the world had stopped, and we were the only four people in it" - is the chapter's weakest moment, a reach for profundity that tips into the kind of closing-line grandiosity the plan explicitly warned against. **Structural Fidelity** The chapter follows its plan closely. The cricket bat, the first aid kit, the lock-up, the camp bed, the testimony in pieces, the bruise, the cut, the emojis explained, Callum's silence, Maya's stillness, Leo's wanting-to-leave, the final "I don't know" - all present. The chapter earns its darkness through accumulation rather than melodrama, which is the plan's central ambition. **Weaknesses** The primary weakness is the tell-don't-show problem with Finn's testimony. We're told it was fragmented; it isn't, really. The narrator describes the quality of the speech rather than rendering it. A braver choice would have been to actually write the fragmented testimony in dialogue, with interruptions, repetitions, and dead ends. Instead, we get a fairly clean narrative delivered in Finn's voice, framed by Leo's description of its messiness. The ending paragraph is slightly overwrought - "the world had stopped, and we were the only four people in it" is the kind of closing that the plan's author would have flagged as too neat, too cinematic. It's not terrible, but it's the chapter's most conventional moment. The "crisp packet like something breathing" simile is the kind of forced atmospheric detail that doesn't quite earn its place. Overall, this is strong work - significantly above average, with a consistent voice, well-drawn characters, and genuine emotional intelligence. Its flaws are real but not fatal. # Chapter 5: Nothing My mum's house smells like washing powder and the candle she lights in the kitchen when she's trying to make the house feel like something it isn't. The candle is called "Autumn Woodland" and it costs £14 from Next and it doesn't smell like autumn or woodland. It smells like a factory that makes the idea of autumn. She'd lit it before she left for her shift at the hospital and the smell was still there, hanging in the kitchen like a guest who'd overstayed. We were in my bedroom. Not because it was the right place but because it was the only place. Maya was on the floor, cross-legged, with her notebook open. Callum was on my desk chair, spinning it back and forth, one foot on the seat, the other pushing off the wall. Finn wasn't there. Finn had stopped responding to messages after the garage. He was somewhere—home, maybe, or the lock-up—and he was not here, and his absence was a shape in the room that nobody mentioned because mentioning it would make it worse. Maya had biscuits. She'd brought them from her house—digestives, the good ones, not the cheap ones that taste like compressed sand. She'd put them on a plate, a proper plate, not a napkin, because Maya doesn't eat biscuits off napkins, she eats biscuits off plates, and the plate was sitting on my carpet between us like evidence at a trial. "We need to decide," she said. "We've been deciding for three days," I said. "We've been deciding since Tuesday and it's now Thursday and we haven't decided anything." "That's exactly why we need to decide now. The longer we wait—" "The longer we wait, what? Davies gets worse? He's already—" I stopped. The note was in my pocket. I could feel it. "He's already done it. The thing is done. We're just—sitting here." "So let's stop sitting. We have the notebook. We have the search history. We have Finn's account. We go to Dr. Osei. We lay it out. We let her handle it." "The headteacher plays golf with Davies." This was Finn. Not in the room. In the garage, yesterday, when we'd talked about who to go to. The headteacher, Dr. Osei, the woman who ran the school, who gave assemblies about "community" and "respect" and who had a photo on her office wall of herself at a charity fundraiser with Davies standing next to her, both of them smiling, both of them holding plastic cups of wine. Maya knew this. She'd looked it up. She'd looked up everything. "Golf isn't a conspiracy," she said. "People play golf with people they don't suspect of things." "People also protect people they play golf with." "That's an assumption." "So is everything else." Callum pushed off the wall with his foot. The chair spun. "I've got a plan." "No," I said, immediately. "You don't even know what it is." "I know you, Callum. Your plan involves walking up to Davies and saying something you'll regret." "I wouldn't regret it." "You'd regret it in about four seconds." "Regret is for people who lose." "You'd lose. You'd absolutely lose. He's a teacher. You're a student. He'd say you threatened him. You'd get excluded. Then we'd have one less person and he'd have a complaint against us and everything would be worse." Callum stopped spinning. He sat in the chair with his feet flat on the floor and his hands on his knees and he looked at me with an expression that was more serious than I'd seen from him in a long time. "What's your plan, then?" "I don't have a plan." "So your plan is nothing." "My plan is to think about it." "You've been thinking about it since Tuesday. You think about everything. That's your whole thing, Leo. You think and you think and you think and then you don't do anything and then the thing happens anyway and you say 'well, I could see that coming' like you've won something. But you haven't won anything. You've just watched." The room went still. Not dramatically. Not the way it goes still in films, with a musical cue and a close-up. Just still, the way a room goes still when something true has been said and nobody knows how to respond to it because the truth is inconvenient and ugly and it belongs to the person who said it and the person it was said about, and everyone else is just there, witness to something they didn't ask to witness. I didn't say anything. Because he was right. That was the thing. He was right, and the rightness of it sat in my chest like a stone, and I didn't have a rebuttal because there wasn't one. I think and I think and I don't do anything. It's what I do. It's what I've always done. It's why Finn sent the text to me at midnight—because I'm the one who notices, the one who sees, the one who understands—and it's also why the text changed nothing, because seeing and understanding are not the same as acting, and I am good at the first two and useless at the third. Maya broke the silence. "We're not helping." "We're not doing anything," Callum said. "That's what I mean. We're not helping each other. We're just—" She stopped. Looked at her notebook. Closed it. "Finn needs to go to the police." The room went still again, differently this time. "He won't," I said. "We don't know that." "He won't, Maya. He told us in the garage. He's scared." "Scared isn't—" "Scared is exactly the thing. It's the whole thing. Davies told him no one would believe him and Finn believed him because—because he's a fifteen-year-old boy and Davies is a teacher with twenty years of experience and the entire institution of the school behind him, and Finn—Finn doesn't have—" I stopped. The note in my pocket. The words on the paper. "He doesn't have anything except us, and we're sitting in my bedroom eating biscuits." Maya looked at me. She had crumbs on her knee from the digestives. She brushed them off, a small, precise gesture. "Then what do we do?" "I don't know." "You keep saying that." "Because I keep not knowing." "That's not good enough." "I know." She opened her notebook again. Closed it. Opened it. "I could build the document. Properly. Timestamped. Organised. Everything Finn has—the notebook, the recordings, the search history. Format it so it's—so it looks like—" "Like what?" "Like something a headteacher has to take seriously." "And then what? You walk into her office with a dossier on a senior teacher and she reads it and calls Davies in and Davies says it's all lies and she believes him because he's Davies and she plays golf with him and—" "Then at least we've tried." "Trying and failing is worse than not trying." "Is it?" I didn't answer. Because I didn't know. Because the answer was yes and also the answer was no and also the answer was that I was terrified and that my terror was dressed up as philosophy and that Callum had seen through it and Maya was trying to build a ladder out of it and neither of them could help me because the thing that was wrong with me was mine. Callum stood up. "I'm going." "Where?" "Home. Tyson needs feeding." Tyson was his dog. The Staffordshire bull terrier. The one he talked to when he was alone. I knew this because I'd been to his house once and heard him through his bedroom door, having a full conversation with the dog about whether crisps counted as a meal. "I'll be on my phone. If anything happens." "Nothing's happening," I said. "Yeah." He picked up the cricket bat, which he'd leaned against my wardrobe. "That's the problem." He left. I heard him go down the stairs, heard the front door open and close. The house was quiet. Maya was still on the floor. The biscuits were half-eaten. The plate was on the carpet between us like a border neither of us wanted to cross. She stood up. "I'll help you wash up." "I didn't—there's nothing to wash up." "The mug your mum left. And the plate." She picked up the plate with the digestives. Walked to the kitchen. I followed. The kitchen was clean in the way my mum's kitchen is always clean—not sterile, just maintained, the dishes done, the counters wiped, everything in its place. The Autumn Woodland candle was on the windowsill, unlit, a reminder of something that had been attempted and abandoned. Maya turned on the tap. Hot water. She put the plate under it and started washing, and I stood next to her and picked up the mug my mum had left by the sink—tea, cold, the milk curdled at the bottom—and washed it without being asked. We didn't talk about Davies. We didn't talk about Finn or the police or the notebook or the headteacher. We talked about a girl in Maya's maths class named Jess who'd worn the same earrings as Maya three days in a row and Maya didn't know whether to be flattered or annoyed and she'd decided on both. "Is it copying if it's earrings?" she said, drying the plate with a tea towel. "I think it's only copying if it's everything." "It's earrings and a top. The top was from Primark so that's less personal." "Earrings are personal." "Earrings are accessories." "Earrings are the most personal thing you can wear." She looked at me. "That's weird, Leo." "It's not weird. Earrings go through your body. That's intimate." "You've never worn earrings." "No." "Then you don't know what you're talking about." "Probably not." She put the plate in the rack. Dried her hands. Leaned against the counter. The kitchen was quiet except for the tap dripping and the hum of the fridge and the faint sound of traffic outside, which was so ordinary it made me want to cry. "Okay," she said. "I'll build the document." "Maya—" "I'll build it and I'll show it to you and we'll decide together. Okay? We'll decide together. You and me. And Callum. And Finn. We'll decide." She picked up her bag. The black notebook was inside. She slung it over her shoulder and walked to the front door and opened it and stood on the step and looked back at me. "You're not useless," she said. "You know that, right?" I didn't say anything. She closed the door. I stood in the kitchen. The tap dripped. The fridge hummed. The house was empty and it was mine and it was not enough. I sat down at the kitchen table. I took the crumpled note out of my pocket. Unfolded it. The ink had bled in the rain—some words were blurred, others sharp. I read the parts that were still legible. The part I'd read before, the part about being grabbed, about no one believing him. And then, below it, in handwriting that got smaller toward the bottom of the page, as if Finn was running out of courage the way he was running out of paper: "He said I was special. Same thing he said to the others." I put the note down. I sat in the kitchen. The candle on the windowsill. The dripping tap. The quiet. Outside, someone was walking past the house and their footsteps faded and the quiet returned, and I sat in it, in the silence that was mine, in the knowledge that a man had said those words to a boy—had said them before, to others, had used the word "special" like a key, like a lock, like a thing designed to open a person up and get inside—and I was sitting in my kitchen with clean plates and a dying candle and a crumpled note and no plan, no action, no courage, just the knowledge, just the seeing, just the useless, inadequate, terrible gift of understanding what was happening and being unable to stop it. I sat there for a long time.

VOICE AND NARRATION Leo's voice is consistently rendered throughout. The internal narration has the quality of someone using wit as a buffer while inadvertently revealing more than intended. The digressive quality is present but controlled—the earring conversation is a genuine tonal achievement, landing as both comic relief and emotional respite before the devastating final section. The voice doesn't wink at the reader; the comedy emerges from character. The narrator's unreliability is subtly present. Leo frames Callum's accusation as "right" but then immediately retreats into philosophical abstraction ("Trying and failing is worse than not trying"), which is exactly the evasion the character profile describes. He knows he's doing it and can't stop. This is sophisticated characterisation. DIALOGUE The dialogue is the chapter's strongest element. The exchange about plans is genuinely funny and revealing simultaneously: "What's your plan, then?" / "I don't have a plan." / "So your plan is nothing." This is economical and character-specific. Callum's voice is distinct from Maya's is distinct from Leo's. The earring conversation is particularly well-executed—it sounds like actual teenagers, it deflects sincerity with mundane specificity, and it earns its place by being the most normal five minutes in the story. The dialogue doesn't explain itself or over-articulate. One minor weakness: Callum's speech about Leo watching rather than acting ("You think and you think and you think and then you don't do anything") is slightly more articulate than his character profile suggests he'd be. It's not egregiously so—it's a moment of genuine anger producing clarity—but it edges toward the "nobody gives speeches" rule the plan set for itself. EMOTIONAL ENGAGEMENT The chapter's emotional architecture is well-constructed. The plan called for "nothing happens and everything happens," and this is largely achieved. The biscuit plate as a "border neither of us wanted to cross" is a good image—grounded, not overwrought. The washing-up scene is the chapter's emotional heart and it works precisely because nothing is said about the actual problem. The final section—Leo alone with the note—is where the chapter risks and mostly succeeds. The revelation of "He said I was special. Same thing he said to the others" lands with genuine weight because it's been withheld and because the chapter has earned the silence around it. The prose here becomes more expansive, which is appropriate to the emotional register. POTENTIAL WEAKNESSES The final paragraph is the chapter's most vulnerable moment. It's a long, accumulating sentence that risks tipping into purple prose: "had used the word 'special' like a key, like a lock, like a thing designed to open a person up and get inside." The triple metaphor (key, lock, thing) is slightly overworked—"key" and "lock" are redundant with each other, and "get inside" is doing the same work a third time. The sentence is reaching for devastation and mostly gets there, but it's the one moment where the restraint the plan calls for wavers. The candle motif (Autumn Woodland, £14 from Next, smells like a factory that makes the idea of autumn) is excellent—specific, class-conscious, quietly sad without announcing itself. It recurs naturally at the end. This is the kind of detail the plan called for. The chapter follows its plan closely: the argument is real and ugly, Maya wants to go to the headteacher, Finn's absence is a shape in the room, Callum leaves, Maya stays to wash up, Leo reads the note. The plan's instruction that "the normalcy collapses" after Maya leaves is executed well. ADHERENCE TO PLAN The chapter hits every beat: the ugly argument, Callum's accusation, the biscuit-eating, the washing-up scene as the most normal five minutes, Leo alone with the note, the devastating final line. The plan specified that Leo reads the note and sees "he said I was special, the same thing he said to the others"—this is delivered exactly as planned, and the chapter earns it. MINOR ISSUES The opening paragraph about the candle is good but slightly over-extended. "A guest who'd overstayed" is a fine image but the paragraph could be tighter. The chapter is slightly long in its setup before the argument begins. The phrase "the knowledge that a man had said those words to a boy" in the final paragraph is slightly clunky—"a man" and "a boy" feel like deliberate distancing that calls attention to itself. Overall, this is accomplished work. It achieves its tonal goals, the characters are specific and consistent, the dialogue is strong, and the emotional restraint holds for most of the chapter. The final paragraph slightly overreaches but doesn't collapse. The chapter earns its darkness. # Chapter 6: Poppy Two days passed. The group chat went silent, which was worse than arguments, worse than bad news. Our group chat had been active every single day for four years—through holidays, through exams, through the time Callum's phone was confiscated for a week and he used his brother's to send messages that were recognizably his only because of the volume. Silence in the group chat was not normal. Silence in the group chat was a symptom. I checked it seventeen times on Thursday. Twenty-three on Friday. On Saturday I stopped counting but I didn't stop checking, and each time the screen showed the same last message—Maya's "I'll build the document," sent Thursday evening—and below it, nothing. Finn's phone was off. I called it four times on Thursday, twice on Friday, once on Saturday. Each time the automated voice said the number was unavailable, which was different from switched off, which meant the SIM had been removed or the phone was destroyed or Finn had done something I didn't want to think about. I called it anyway because the alternative was not calling it and that felt like giving up and I wasn't ready to give up yet even though I didn't know what not-giving-up looked like. Monday morning. School. The corridor was doing its thing—noise, bodies, the faint smell of floor cleaner that never quite cleaned anything. I was at my locker when I saw Callum. He was walking down the corridor from the direction of the science labs, and he was walking fast, which meant he'd seen something or was going to do something, because Callum only walked fast when he was in motion toward an objective. Then I saw Poppy. She was ahead of him, maybe twenty metres, walking toward the canteen. She had her bag over one shoulder and she was looking at her phone and she didn't see Callum. Callum saw her and stopped, and I watched his face do the thing it does, which is process a decision in real time—the flicker of recognition, the calculation, the calculation failing, the body already moving. He was going to talk to her. I should have shouted. I should have said his name. I should have done any of the things that a person does when they see their friend about to walk into a wall. I didn't. I stood by my locker with my hand on the combination dial and I watched him go. "Callum." It was Maya, behind me. She'd seen it too. "Callum, don't." He didn't hear her. Or he heard her and kept walking. The corridor was too loud and he was too far ahead and Maya's voice was not the kind of voice that carries over noise. It was the kind of voice that works in rooms, at tables, in silence. It was not built for corridors. He caught up to Poppy near the water fountain. The one that didn't work. She was filling a bottle from the tap next to it, the one that dispensed water at a temperature best described as "technically liquid," and she turned when she heard him and her face— I can't describe her face. I can only describe what it did, which was collapse inward, every muscle tightening at once, the way a small animal folds in on itself when it hears a sound it recognises as danger. She didn't scream. She didn't run. She went very still and her hand tightened on her water bottle and her eyes went wide and fixed on Callum like he was something that had come through a wall. "Poppy," Callum said. "Are you okay? I just wanted to—" "Leave me alone." Her voice was steady but wrong—the steadiness of someone holding something together by force. "Please just leave me alone." "I'm not—I just want to talk. About Finn. And Davies." "Leave me alone." Louder now. People were turning. The corridor was doing what corridors do, which is notice everything. "Stop following me. Please stop following me." "I'm not following you. I—" "Miss!" Poppy turned, and a teacher was there—I didn't see which one, the corridor was too thick with bodies—but a teacher was there, a hand on Poppy's shoulder, and Poppy was saying something fast and low, and the teacher was looking at Callum with the expression teachers wear when they've identified a problem and are already composing the email in their heads. Callum stood there. His hands were at his sides. He hadn't touched her. He hadn't done anything except say her name in a corridor, and now a teacher was walking Poppy away and another teacher was walking toward him, and the corridor was watching, and I was watching from twenty metres away, and I could see the exact moment Callum understood what was happening. He didn't run. He didn't argue. He stood there and let the teacher take his arm and lead him toward the behaviour office, and as he passed me, he looked at me, and his face was—confused. Not scared. Confused. The face of someone who'd reached out to help and couldn't understand why the hand had been slapped. Maya was beside me. She'd moved without my seeing her, the way she moves—quiet, purposeful, already three steps ahead. "He talked to her," she said. "I know." "In the corridor." "I know." "She's going to say he harassed her." "She won't." "She will. She has to. If Davies—" Maya stopped. Looked at the corridor. The corridor looked back. "She has to protect herself. The only way to protect herself from Davies is to be as far from us as possible. Callum just made her a target." The bell went. We went to class. I sat through Registration and double English and didn't hear a word. At break, I saw Callum coming out of the behaviour office. His face was red. He had a detention. Two days. His mum had been called. He found us at the bench. Not the Greggs bench—the other one, the one near the tennis courts that nobody uses because the net has been down since 2019. He sat down and didn't say anything for a moment. Then: "She told them I was harassing her." "I know," Maya said. "I didn't—I just said her name." "I know." "She was scared. I could see she was scared and I was just—I was trying to—" "I know, Callum." He looked at his hands. They were shaking. Callum's hands never shook. Callum's hands threw cricket bats and tore open crisp packets and punched walls when he was angry and they never, ever shook. They were shaking now. "She was trying to protect herself," I said. I said it gently, or I tried to. "She's scared of Davies. If she's seen talking to us—" "I know that. I know. I just—" He looked at me. "I thought if I just talked to her. If someone just said her name and asked if she was okay. I thought that was enough." It wasn't enough. None of it was enough. The notebook wasn't enough. The search history wasn't enough. Finn's blood on a screen wasn't enough. A fifteen-year-old boy had documented a pattern of abuse by a teacher and the evidence sat in a folder on Maya's phone and a black notebook in her bag and it wasn't enough, it was never going to be enough, because enough requires power and we didn't have any and the man who'd done this had all of it. After school. I texted Finn. Nothing. Texted again. Nothing. Called. Off. "Let's go to the lock-up," I said. We went. The three of us, minus one. Maya had her bag with the notebook. Callum had his hands in his pockets, hunched, the bravado gone. I had my phone and the burner phone and the crumpled note, which had been in my pocket for so long it had softened into something that barely held its shape. Garland Street. The industrial estate. The fencing company, the tyre place, the shuttered dry cleaner. Number three. The door was unlocked. I pushed it open. Empty. Not Finn-empty—the garage before Finn arrived, the space where a person had been. Not that. The space after a person has left and taken everything with them. The camp bed was gone. The sleeping bag was gone. The crate of water was gone. The Tesco bag was gone. The bare bulb hung from its wire, swaying slightly in the draught from the open door, casting shadows that moved across concrete that was clean in the way a space is clean when someone has wiped it down. Finn was gone. His things were gone. The lock-up was a garage again—nothing inside it, nothing to show that anyone had been sleeping here, eating here, hiding here. Whatever Finn had brought, he'd taken. Whatever he'd been, he wasn't anymore. "He moved," Maya said. She was standing in the doorway, not going in. "He's somewhere else." "Or he's gone," I said. "Gone where?" "I don't know." "He wouldn't just—" "He stopped answering his phone. He stopped responding to messages. He moved out of the one place we knew where to find him. What do you think that means?" Maya didn't answer. Callum walked into the garage and stood in the centre of it, looking at the concrete floor where the camp bed had been. There were marks—four small indentations where the legs had rested. He crouched down and touched one of them with his finger, pressing into the faint depression in the concrete, as if he could feel the weight of Finn through the mark left behind. "His mum lied again," I said. "I called. She said he was at a friend's." Maya looked at me. "Which friend?" "She didn't say. I didn't ask. I knew she'd lie." "So we don't know where he is." "No." We stood in the garage. The light was going—the sky through the open door was the colour of old pewter, the kind of grey that means rain, that means this country, that means Tuesday, that means every day. The bulb swung. The shadows moved. Callum stood up. He didn't look at either of us. He looked at the door, at the rain that was starting to fall, at the industrial estate stretching out in both directions, grey and empty and offering nothing. "We made it worse," he said. Nobody contradicted him. Because we had. Callum had talked to Poppy and Poppy had panicked and the school knew now—knew that students were asking questions, knew that Callum had "harassed" a Year 10 girl, knew that there was a shape forming in the margins that Davies would see, would recognise, would already be moving to contain. And Finn—who Davies had threatened, who Davies had grabbed, who had drawn his own blood and sent it in three red drops to the one person he trusted—was gone. We walked back to our bikes. The rain was proper now, committed, falling in sheets that soaked through my hoodie in thirty seconds. Maya was walking fast, ahead of us, her bag clutched against her chest. Callum was walking slow, head down, the cricket bat still in his hand from—why did he have the cricket bat? When had he brought the cricket bat? I didn't ask. We stood by our bikes. The rain. The estate. The noise of traffic on the ring road beyond the fencing company, ordinary traffic, people going places, people with destinations. "I'm going home," Maya said. "Maya—" "I'm going home. I need to—I'll work on the document tonight. I'll—I need to go." She got on her bike and rode away. I watched her go. She didn't look back. Callum was beside me. He was looking at the rain, at the puddles forming in the potholes on Garland Street, at the rust on the garage door and the shuttered dry cleaner and the sky that offered nothing. "I'm sorry," he said. "I know." "I thought I was helping." "I know." He got on his bike. Rode away. The rain swallowed him. I stood alone on Garland Street. The garage was behind me, empty, wiped clean. My phone was in my pocket. The burner phone was dead. The crumpled note was in my jeans, damp, the ink almost entirely gone now, Finn's words dissolving into the fabric like they'd never been there at all. The rain was cold and I was wet and I was alone and I had nothing—no evidence, no friend, no plan, no courage, nothing except the memory of a face on a phone screen and the knowledge that I'd seen it and I'd done nothing and now the person who'd trusted me enough to send three bloody emojis at midnight was somewhere I couldn't find, in a situation I couldn't fix, and the only thing I'd contributed to the entire affair was standing on doorsteps and watching. I got on my bike. The rain was in my eyes. I rode home. The garage disappeared behind me, getting smaller in the mirror I didn't have, swallowed by the estate and the grey and the ordinary, relentless, unforgiving weather of this country, which doesn't stop, which never stops, which falls and falls and falls and falls and doesn't care who's standing in it.

Judge Response:
[Analysis] This chapter is a strong piece of YA fiction that largely delivers on its ambitious plan. Let me work through its qualities and weaknesses systematically. **Voice and Narration** Leo's first-person voice is consistently rendered throughout. The dry, self-aware quality from the character profile is present: "the corridor was doing its thing," "the automated voice said the number was unavailable, which was different from switched off." The voice is restrained without being cold, and the self-indictment at the chapter's end ("the only thing I'd contributed to the entire affair was standing on doorsteps and watching") lands with genuine weight because it's been earned by the chapter's action rather than announced. The digressive quality from the plan is present but controlled. The parenthetical about the water fountain temperature ("technically liquid") is a good example of Leo's humour functioning as character rather than authorial winking. The voice doesn't meander excessively; it stays purposeful. **Dialogue** The dialogue is the chapter's strongest element. The exchange after Callum's detention is particularly good: "She told them I was harassing her." "I know." "I didn't—I just said her name." "I know." "She was scared. I could see she was scared and I was just—I was trying to—" "I know, Callum." This is exactly the kind of dialogue the plan called for: deflecting sincerity, nobody giving speeches, emotional moments undercut by the inadequacy of language. The repetition of "I know" is doing real work—it's Maya's pragmatism, her inability to offer comfort, her own paralysis. The dialogue never over-explains. When Callum says "I thought if I just talked to her. If someone just said her name and asked if she was okay. I thought that was enough," it's devastating precisely because it's so simple. **Character Consistency** All four characters behave consistently with their profiles. Callum's impulsive approach to Poppy is exactly what the profile predicts—right instinct, catastrophic execution. His shaking hands are a well-deployed detail; the profile notes that "when he's scared, he goes quiet, and the quiet on Callum is the most alarming thing." The shaking hands serve the same function. Maya's retreat ("I'm going home. I need to—I'll work on the document tonight") is her flaw made visible: mistaking preparation for action, retreating to structure when structure fails. Leo's passivity—watching Callum walk toward Poppy and doing nothing—is his central flaw in action, and the chapter doesn't excuse it. Poppy's reaction is handled with real care. The description of her face collapsing inward "the way a small animal folds in on itself when it hears a sound it recognises as danger" is one of the chapter's best moments—it communicates her terror without sentimentalising it, and it makes her subsequent accusation against Callum comprehensible rather than villainous. **Plot Execution** The chapter follows its plan closely. Callum approaches Poppy, the incident ripples, Callum gets detention, the group goes to the lock-up, Finn is gone. The plan is executed with fidelity and the chapter earns its darkness honestly. The empty lock-up is a strong scene—the detail of Callum touching the indentations left by the camp bed legs is the kind of small, specific gesture that the plan called for ("the most powerful moments are the smallest ones"). **Weaknesses** The chapter's main weakness is in its final paragraphs, where the prose tips into something slightly overwrought. The ending—"which falls and falls and falls and falls and doesn't care who's standing in it"—is the chapter's most strained moment. The rain-as-indifferent-universe metaphor is not wrong, but the quadruple repetition of "falls" is a self-conscious flourish that the rest of the chapter's restraint doesn't support. The "mirror I didn't have" is a slightly awkward construction. The final paragraph accumulates clauses in a way that feels like it's reaching for profundity rather than earning it. Similarly, the passage "the sky through the open door was the colour of old pewter, the kind of grey that means rain, that means this country, that means Tuesday, that means every day" is the chapter's most purple moment. The anaphora ("that means... that means... that means") is a technique that can work but here feels like it's trying too hard to be literary. "That means Tuesday" is a nice specific detail that gets buried under the accumulation. The paragraph beginning "It wasn't enough. None of it was enough" is also slightly over-explained. The sentiment is correct but the chapter has already shown us this; the explicit statement of it is slightly redundant and tips toward telling rather than showing. **Forced Poetry Assessment** The forced poetry is present but not pervasive. Most of the chapter's figurative language lands—the small animal simile, the camp bed indentations, the "softened into something that barely held its shape" description of the crumpled note. The failures are concentrated in the final third, particularly the ending. This is a meaningful flaw but not a fatal one. **Darkness and Lightness** The chapter earns its darkness. There's no false comfort, no easy resolution. The comedy is minimal in this chapter—appropriately so, given the stakes—but the brief moments of it (the water fountain temperature, the cricket bat appearing without explanation) feel organic rather than forced. The chapter knows when to be funny and when not to be. **Overall Assessment** This is a genuinely accomplished piece of YA fiction. It executes its plan faithfully, maintains consistent characterisation, and delivers emotionally without sentimentality. Its weaknesses are real but concentrated: the ending overreaches, and there are two or three moments where the prose becomes self-consciously literary in ways that undercut the chapter's prevailing restraint. These are the flaws of a writer who knows what they're doing but occasionally tries too hard to prove it. # Chapter 7: Alone Maya texted at 7:14am, which was thirteen minutes before I was going to text her. "Can't today. Sorry." No explanation. No follow-up. Just the two words and the small, inadequate "sorry" that meant something I didn't want to examine. I typed "that's fine" and deleted it and typed "are you okay" and deleted it and typed "no worries" and sent that, which was the most nothing response I could produce and which was, I suspected, exactly what she needed. I thought about calling. I thought about cycling to her house. I thought about standing on her doorstep the way I'd stood on Finn's, in the rain, looking at a closed door. I didn't do any of these things. I got dressed. I ate toast. I went to school. Callum was suspended. Two days. The email had gone to his mum on Friday and she'd kept him home over the weekend as punishment and he wasn't coming back until Wednesday. I knew this because he'd texted me at 11pm on Saturday with a single message: "mum took my phone so using Ryan's. tell Finn I'm sorry. tell him I didn't mean it." I hadn't replied because I didn't know what to say and because the word "sorry" in this context was doing a kind of work that sorry wasn't built for. So I went to school alone. The first thing you notice about school when you're alone in it is the noise. School is always loud, but when you're with people—the right people, your people—the loud becomes a texture, something you move through without registering. When you're alone, the loud is just loud. It presses against you. Every conversation in the corridor is happening to someone else. Every laugh is directed at a joke you didn't hear. You're in the river but you're not in it. You're watching it flow past and you're standing on the bank and the bank is a place where nobody stands because standing on the bank is not what the river is for. I went to Registration. Mr. Hargreaves took it because our tutor was off, and Mr. Hargreaves did the register in the same flat voice he used for everything, and when he said "Finn Gallagher" and there was no answer, he looked up from the list and said "absent" and moved on. He didn't say "again." He didn't look at me. He didn't know to look at me. He moved on to the next name, and the next, and the silence where Finn's name had been was filled by the next silence, and the next, because registers are designed to move forward and not to stop and dwell on the names that don't answer. I went to History. The Treaty of Versailles again—this time the aftermath, the reparations, the collapse. Hargreaves talked about Germany's economic crisis and I thought about the word "reparations" and what it meant, which was the idea that you could make someone pay for what they'd done, that there was a system, a structure, a way of quantifying harm and extracting payment. It sounded clean. It sounded like something that worked. It sounded like nothing that had ever happened to a fifteen-year-old boy in a classroom with the door closed. Double English. Mrs. Adebayo. We were studying *An Inspector Calls*—ironic, given that Davies had complimented my essay on it, had told me I had "the mind for it," had put his hand on my shoulder and said I should study English at A-level, and I had stood there and felt warm and seen and special, and the word "special" was a word Finn had heard too, in a different room, behind a different door, with a different intention behind it. I sat in English and I looked at the text and I thought about Birling and his responsibility and I thought about how Priestley had written a play about a man who couldn't see what was in front of him because seeing it would require him to change, and I was sitting in a classroom learning about a fictional man's blindness while being blind myself, and the irony was not lost on me, and it was also not useful. At break, I saw Davies. He was in the corridor outside the staff room, talking to another teacher—Mr. Okafor, who taught PE and had the build of someone who'd once been a rugby player and now just remembered being one. They were laughing about something. Davies had his coffee. He had his blazer over his shoulder. He looked exactly the way he always looked: warm, relaxed, present. A man who liked his job. A man who was good at it. I walked past. I didn't mean to walk past—I was going to the canteen to get water—but my body changed direction without consulting me, the way bodies do when they're avoiding something, and I was past him before I'd decided to be. "Leo." I stopped. Davies turned from Mr. Okafor. Smiled. The smile was perfect—the kind of smile that reaches the eyes, that crinkles at the corners, that says I see you, I know you, you matter. "How's Finn doing? I've noticed he's been off." The casualness of it. The warmth. The teacher-concern that was indistinguishable from the real thing. "He's ill," I said. "I think." "Well, tell him we miss him. Tell him the door's always open." He held my gaze for a moment. The smile didn't change. Nothing about his face changed. But something in his eyes—something behind the smile, something I couldn't name—moved. A flicker. A recognition. The look a cat gives a bird through a window. It lasted a quarter of a second. Then it was gone and Davies was smiling again and clapping Mr. Okafor on the shoulder and saying something about the staff football match and I was walking away, toward the canteen, toward the water fountain that didn't work, toward the bathroom. I made it to the bathroom. I got there and I locked the cubicle door and I was sick. Not a lot. Just enough. Toast and stomach acid and the taste of something sour that might have been fear. I sat on the floor of the cubicle with my back against the wall and my phone in my hand and I thought: he knows. He knows we know. Or he suspects. Or he's watching. Or he's always been watching and I'm only just now seeing the watching because I wasn't looking before and now I'm looking and the looking is— the looking is— I put my head between my knees. The floor was cold. The bathroom smelled like bleach and something else. Someone came in and used a urinal and washed their hands and left. I stayed on the floor. I texted Finn. The real phone, the one that had been off for three days. "Are you okay?" I expected nothing. I got nothing. I put the phone in my pocket and unlocked the cubicle and washed my hands and looked at myself in the mirror. I looked tired. I looked like a person who hadn't slept properly in a week. I looked like a person who was doing something and also not doing anything, which is the most accurate description of me I've ever produced. An hour later, during Chemistry, my phone buzzed. One message. From Finn. "No." One word. No capitalisation. No punctuation. Just the two letters, sitting in the message bubble like something dropped from a height, like something that had fallen a long way and landed with a sound you couldn't hear. I looked at it for the rest of the lesson. Mr. Singh talked about exothermic reactions and the release of energy and I sat at my desk and looked at the word "no" and I thought: that's the most honest thing anyone has said to me in a week. Not "I'm fine" or "it's complicated" or "I'm at a friend's." Just: no. No, I'm not okay. No, I'm not safe. No, I'm not where you can find me. No, the thing that was done to me has not stopped being done to me and I am somewhere and I am not okay and that is the whole truth and I'm giving it to you in two letters because two letters is all I have left. I put the phone away. I sat through Chemistry. I watched the experiment—Mr. Singh pouring one liquid into another and the heat rising off the beaker in visible waves, the temperature climbing on the thermometer stuck to the side. The energy had to go somewhere. It always does. You can contain it for a while—in a beaker, in a room, in a body—but the energy doesn't disappear just because you've put a lid on it. It's still there. It's always still there. After school, I didn't go home. I went to the library. Our school library is a room at the back of the building that nobody uses because it has no windows and the fluorescent lights have a hum that makes your teeth itch, and it's staffed by Mrs. Pereira, who is seventy and reads romance novels behind the circulation desk and pretends she isn't. I sat at a computer. I opened the photos on my phone. I'd photographed Finn's crumpled note before the ink dissolved—the photos were blurry, the words warped by rain and time, but some of them were legible. I zoomed in. "He grabbed my arm." "He said no one would believe me." "I think he's done this before." I opened the folder Maya had described building—she'd sent me a screenshot of it, a folder on her phone labelled "Finn - Urgent," with the notebook pages, the search history, the timestamps. It existed. She'd done it. She'd built the document and it was sitting on her phone and it was something—fragile and incomplete and possibly useless, but something. I thought about the headteacher. Dr. Osei. The woman with the charity fundraiser photo on her wall. The woman who played golf with Davies. The woman whose job it was—literally, contractually, institutionally—to protect students. The woman I would have to walk up to, sit across from, and tell everything I knew, which wasn't enough, which was fragments and photographs and the word of a friend who was missing and the bruise on an arm I'd seen in a garage and the cut on a palm and the search history and the note and the look in Davies's eyes in the corridor today, that flicker, that quarter-second recognition that said: I see you seeing me. I closed the photos. I opened a new tab. I typed the school's email address into the browser and stared at the blank compose window for a long time. The cursor blinked. It blinked and blinked and blinked, patient, waiting, offering nothing except the implication that if I typed, something would happen. If I pressed send, something would change. The cursor didn't know what I knew, which was that pressing send might change nothing, might make things worse, might put a target on my back the way Callum had put one on Poppy's. The cursor just blinked. Mrs. Pereira looked up from her romance novel. She looked at me, sitting at the computer, staring at a blank screen, and she didn't say anything, because Mrs. Pereira understood the particular silence of a person trying to decide whether to do something brave or something safe and not yet knowing which was which. I sat there. The fluorescent lights hummed. The cursor blinked. Outside the windowless library, the school was emptying—the sounds of the day folding up, chairs scraping, doors closing, the building settling into the silence it kept between 4pm and 8am. Soon the cleaners would come. Soon the lights would go off. Soon this room would be dark and empty and I would have to have decided. I didn't decide. Not yet. I sat there and I looked at the cursor and I let it blink and I thought about Finn saying "No" and I thought about Davies smiling in the corridor and I thought about Callum saying "your whole thing is you think and you think and you don't do anything" and I thought about Maya's text this morning, "can't today," and I thought about the way the world outside this room was carrying on as if nothing was happening, as if nothing had happened, as if the normalness of a Tuesday was the truest thing and everything else—the emojis, the garage, the bruise, the cut, the note, the look—was just a story I was telling myself. The cursor blinked. I didn't type. I didn't send. I closed the laptop and put my head in my hands and sat in the silence of the empty library and felt the full weight of the day settle on me—every word I hadn't said, every call I hadn't made, every door I hadn't walked through—and I knew that tomorrow I would either do the thing or I wouldn't, and I didn't know which, and the not-knowing was the worst feeling I'd ever had, because it wasn't uncertainty, it was cowardice, and cowardice dressed as uncertainty is the most dishonest thing a person can do, and I was doing it, and I knew I was doing it, and I sat there and I did it anyway.

Judge Response:
[Analysis] Chapter 7 is a sustained, largely successful piece of interior fiction that follows Leo through a day of isolation, fear, and paralysis. The chapter's central achievement is its fidelity to the character plan: Leo is passive, self-aware about his passivity, and unable to bridge the gap between knowing and doing. The chapter earns this portrait honestly rather than simply asserting it. The opening is clean and precise. The detail of Maya texting at 7:14am, "thirteen minutes before I was going to text her," is a small, excellent stroke—it tells us about Leo's relationship to action (he was going to do something, but someone else did it first) without announcing itself as characterisation. The response he sends—"no worries"—is perfectly chosen: the most nothing response, as he himself notes, and the chapter trusts the reader to understand why without over-explaining. The school-as-river metaphor ("You're in the river but you're not in it") is one of the chapter's more extended metaphorical passages. It works reasonably well—the image of standing on the bank while the river flows past captures Leo's alienation—but it runs slightly long and tips toward the self-conscious. The metaphor is not quite forced, but it's the chapter's most vulnerable moment stylistically. The Davies corridor encounter is the chapter's centrepiece and it's handled with real skill. The description of Davies's smile—"the kind of smile that reaches the eyes, that crinkles at the corners, that says I see you, I know you, you matter"—is effective precisely because it's the language of warmth being used to describe something cold. The "look a cat gives a bird through a window" is the chapter's one genuinely sharp metaphorical landing: brief, specific, and immediately retracted ("It lasted a quarter of a second. Then it was gone"). The retraction is important—it preserves the ambiguity the plan calls for. We can't be certain Leo saw what he thinks he saw, and the chapter doesn't resolve this. The bathroom scene is handled with appropriate restraint. Being sick is not dramatised; it's reported flatly. The floor is cold. Someone comes in and leaves. Leo stays on the floor. This is exactly the right register—no swelling emotion, just the physical fact of a body responding to fear. The An Inspector Calls passage is the chapter's most overtly thematic moment and its most risky. The irony Leo identifies—studying a play about blindness while being blind himself—is a little too neat, a little too articulated. The plan specifically warns against "explained emotions" and "no 'the mood shifted.'" Here, Leo is essentially explaining his own thematic position to the reader. It's not egregious—the voice is self-aware enough that Leo noticing the irony feels in-character—but it's the chapter's most tell-don't-show failure. The Treaty of Versailles passage has a similar problem: "reparations" as a concept is used to gesture at the Davies situation in a way that's slightly too tidy. The "No" from Finn is the chapter's emotional peak, and the extended meditation on it is where the chapter most risks purple prose. "Like something dropped from a height, like something that had fallen a long way and landed with a sound you couldn't hear" is the kind of doubled simile that can feel like reaching. It's not quite purple—the restraint of "a sound you couldn't hear" saves it—but it's close. The subsequent paragraph, where Leo unpacks what "No" means, is more successful: the list of possible meanings ("No, I'm not okay. No, I'm not safe...") has a cumulative rhythm that earns its length. The exothermic reaction passage is the chapter's most forced metaphor. "The energy had to go somewhere. It always does. You can contain it for a while—in a beaker, in a room, in a body—but the energy doesn't disappear just because you've put a lid on it." This is the chapter's clearest instance of the narrator winking at the reader—using a classroom observation to make a thematic point about suppressed emotion. The plan explicitly warns against this. It's not terrible, but it's the kind of thing a good editor would cut. The library ending is strong. The cursor blinking is a cliché, but the chapter is aware enough of it to not over-invest in it—it's used functionally rather than poetically. The final paragraph, where Leo names his cowardice directly ("cowardice dressed as uncertainty is the most dishonest thing a person can do"), is the chapter's most honest moment and also its most on-the-nose. The plan calls for "explained emotions" to be avoided, and here Leo is explicitly explaining his emotional state and moral failure. However, the self-awareness is so complete—he knows he's doing it, he names it, and he does it anyway—that it functions as character revelation rather than authorial intrusion. It's a borderline call, and the chapter mostly earns it. Dialogue is minimal in this chapter by design—Leo is alone for most of it. The Davies exchange is brief and effective. The absence of Callum and Maya is felt as a structural choice rather than a failure. The chapter follows its plan closely: Leo alone, Davies in the corridor, the "No" from Finn, the library, the email he doesn't send. The plan's note that this chapter is "really about Leo avoiding his homework" is not quite realised—the chapter is more straightforwardly about Leo's paralysis than the plan's slightly more oblique framing suggested—but this is a minor deviation. Overall, this is a chapter of genuine quality: controlled, character-faithful, emotionally honest, and largely free of the worst tendencies (purple prose, forced metaphor, clean resolution). Its failures are real but minor: the exothermic reaction passage, the Inspector Calls irony, the occasional tendency to over-articulate what should be left implicit. The chapter does what it needs to do and does it with more craft than most.
