Output in this format: # Intention <State your formulated intentions for the piece, synthesised from the the parts of the brainstorming session that worked, and avoiding the parts that didn't. Be explicit about the choices you have made about plot, voice, stylistic choices, things you intend to aim for & avoid.> # Chapter Planning <Write a brief chapter plan for all {n_chapters} chapters.>
Model Output:
# Intention **Core Concept:** A repressed insurance fraud investigator is assigned a case that leads him to a charismatic, morally compromised private investigator. The case is the frame; the real story is two men learning to be honest — with each other and themselves — in a world that punishes honesty. **Characters:** - **Declan Hale (POV / narrator):** Early 30s. Insurance fraud investigator for a large firm. Methodical, guarded, emotionally buttoned-up. Came out late and quietly — he's not closeted, but he's not *lived* in his queerness either. His life is spreadsheets, case files, and silence. He tells himself he likes it that way. He doesn't. First-person narrator. - **Ezra Vane ("the bad ideas man"):** Mid 30s. Disbarred lawyer turned unlicensed private investigator. Smokes hand-rolled cigarettes, quotes half-remembered poetry, operates in moral gray zones. Lost his law license after a case where he did the right thing the wrong way — defended a queer client so aggressively he crossed ethical lines and got burned. Charismatic, reckless, genuinely kind underneath the performance. He's not a liar, exactly — he's someone who stopped believing the truth was enough. **Setting:** A fictional coastal city called **Harbor City**, present day but with a retro, analog texture. Rain-soaked, neon-lit, full of waterfront bars and old buildings with bad plumbing. Think a blend of San Francisco's fog and New Orleans' decay. **Voice & Style:** First-person narration from Declan. Hard-boiled but self-aware — he knows he's performing toughness, and occasionally lets the reader see the cracks. Witty, dry, sensory-rich prose. The tone balances noir atmosphere with genuine emotional vulnerability. Think Chandler's rhythm but with the emotional honesty of a man who's slowly letting himself feel things. **Romantic Arc:** The romance develops through proximity, danger, and reluctant trust. It is not instant — there's attraction in Chapter 1, but it's layered with suspicion and resistance. The physical and emotional intimacy builds gradually and is always entangled with the stakes of the case. The sex scene (Chapter 6) is emotionally loaded and earned. **Plot:** Declan's firm assigns him to investigate a suspicious insurance claim tied to a waterfront warehouse fire. The claim was filed by a client represented by a PI named Ezra Vane, who has a reputation for bending the truth. As Declan investigates, he realizes the case is more complex — the fire was deliberate, someone is in danger, and Ezra is protecting them. Declan is forced to choose between his job and doing the right thing. The noir "turn" is Declan committing a professional betrayal — falsifying his findings — to protect the person Ezra is shielding. **What I'm Aiming For:** - Atmosphere that does real work — rain, smoke, and neon aren't just decoration, they reflect the characters' internal states. - Dialogue that crackles — banter as foreplay, silence as intimacy. - A queer noir that queers the *genre*, not just the casting. Declan's repression isn't just about sexuality; it's about emotional honesty in a world that rewards detachment. - A bittersweet but hopeful ending — they choose each other, knowing it's complicated, knowing the world is still broken. - Pacing that alternates between tension and tenderness. **What I'm Avoiding:** - Making Ezra a pure fantasy — he needs real flaws, real consequences, real unglamorous moments. - Making the case more interesting than the romance — the plot serves the love story, not the other way around. - Gimmicky structure — staying linear with a brief in-media-res opening. - Gratuitous darkness — the noir elements should feel purposeful, not edgy for edgy's sake. - A tidy resolution — loose ends remain, because noir demands it. --- # Chapter Planning ## Chapter 1: "The Claim" **Word count target:** ~1000 words **Opens with a brief in-media-res flash-forward** — a single paragraph of Declan in the rain, knowing this is going to end badly, unable to stop. Then we flash back to his ordinary world. Declan is introduced through his work: meticulous, controlled, good at his job in a way that's made him boring. He lives alone in a sparse apartment. He's assigned a new case — an insurance claim tied to a warehouse fire on the waterfront. The claim is suspicious, and the client's representative is a PI with a disciplinary record: Ezra Vane. Declan's boss warns him that Vane is "all cigarette smoke and bad ideas." We see Declan's professional competence and emotional sterility. He goes to the waterfront to begin his investigation, and the chapter ends with him spotting Ezra for the first time — leaning against a lamppost in the rain, smoking, watching the burned-out warehouse like he's mourning something. **Key beats:** Establish Declan's world, introduce the case, first glimpse of Ezra, set the noir tone. --- ## Chapter 2: "The PI" **Word count target:** ~1000 words Declan formally meets Ezra when he visits Ezra's office — a cluttered, second-floor walk-up above a laundromat. Their first conversation is a duel: Declan asks direct questions, Ezra answers with charm and misdirection. The attraction is immediate and unwelcome to Declan. Ezra reveals just enough to be helpful but clearly knows more than he's saying. He's representing the claimant — a woman named **Maren Voss**, who owns the warehouse and lost everything in the fire. Ezra implies the fire wasn't random, that Maren is in danger, but won't say more. After the meeting, Declan does background research and learns Ezra was disbarred after aggressively defending a queer asylum seeker — he fabricated evidence to prevent deportation, got caught, lost everything. Declan is disturbed by how much this information affects him. The chapter ends with Declan unable to sleep, thinking about Ezra's hands, his voice, the way smoke curled from his lips like he was breathing out secrets. **Key beats:** First real interaction, establish chemistry and tension, reveal Ezra's backstory, Declan begins to be drawn in against his better judgment. --- ## Chapter 3: "The Claimant" **Word count target:** ~1000 words Declan tracks down Maren Voss, the woman who filed the claim. She's a trans woman in her 40s, tough and frightened, running a small art restoration business out of the warehouse. The fire destroyed her life's work. She's evasive when Declan asks questions, clearly coached by Ezra. But in a moment of vulnerability, she tells Declan she's been receiving threats — someone wants her out of the waterfront district, and the fire was a message. Declan realizes this is bigger than an insurance claim. Someone is systematically pressuring waterfront property owners to sell. Maren won't name names. She trusts Ezra, and only Ezra. Declan feels a complicated mix of professional frustration and something softer — he sees a woman in genuine danger, and he sees Ezra's loyalty to her, which doesn't fit the "bad ideas" narrative he's been told. That night, Declan goes to a waterfront bar and finds Ezra there. They drink together. The conversation is half-investigation, half something else. Ezra tells Declan, quietly, that Maren is like family to him — she was the first person who treated him with kindness after he was disbarred. The chapter ends with them standing outside in the rain, close enough to touch, and Ezra saying: "You seem like the kind of man who always does the right thing. That must be exhausting." **Key beats:** Introduce Maren and the larger conspiracy, deepen Ezra's characterization, first moment of genuine vulnerability between the two men, the attraction becomes undeniable. --- ## Chapter 4: "The Evidence" **Word count target:** ~1000 words Declan digs into the property pressure angle and discovers a connection to a development company called **Tidewater Holdings** — a shell company buying up waterfront land. The company is connected to a city councilman. Declan brings this to his boss, who tells him to stay focused on the insurance claim and not chase conspiracies. Declan feels the first crack in his loyalty to the institution. Meanwhile, Ezra contacts Declan — he has evidence that the fire was arson, proof that could help Maren's claim but would also expose the development scheme. Ezra can't go to the police because of his disbarment and lack of credibility. He needs Declan. They meet at Ezra's office late at night. Ezra lays out the evidence — photos, recordings, a pattern of fires. The tension between them is acute. Declan sees that Ezra has been building this case alone, obsessively, burning through his own resources to protect Maren and the other waterfront residents. A quiet moment: Ezra, exhausted, falls asleep at his desk. Declan watches him sleep and realizes he's in trouble — not professional trouble (though that too), but the kind of trouble where you care about someone you shouldn't. **Key beats:** Plot escalates, institutional pressure on Declan, Ezra's vulnerability and dedication revealed, Declan's emotional walls begin to crack. --- ## Chapter 5: "The Threat" **Word count target:** ~1000 words Things go wrong. Maren's studio is broken into — not to steal, but to leave a message. A dead bird on her workbench. She calls Ezra, who calls Declan. Declan goes to Maren's place and finds Ezra already there, furious and frightened. For the first time, Declan sees Ezra lose his composure — the charm drops, and what's underneath is raw, protective rage. Declan makes a decision: he goes to the police with the evidence. The detective he speaks to, **Detective Lusk**, is sympathetic but clearly under pressure from above to keep the waterfront development smooth. Lusk warns Declan to be careful — "These aren't people who send warnings twice." That night, Ezra shows up at Declan's apartment. He's rattled. They drink whiskey. The conversation turns personal — Ezra asks Declan why he's helping, why he's risking his job. Declan can't articulate it. Ezra presses: "Is it because you want to do the right thing, or because you don't want anything to happen to me?" Declan doesn't answer. The silence is its own answer. They almost kiss. They don't. Ezra leaves. **Key beats:** Stakes escalate, violence enters the picture, Declan takes a side, the emotional tension reaches a critical point, the almost-kiss. --- ## Chapter 6: "The Fire" **Word count target:** ~1000 words Declan's boss calls him in — Tidewater Holdings has contacted the firm directly, pressuring them to deny Maren's claim and drop the investigation. Declan's boss tells him to comply. Declan refuses. His boss warns him he'll be fired. Declan walks out. He goes to Ezra's office. Ezra is there, surrounded by evidence, looking like he hasn't slept in days. Declan tells him what happened — he's burned his career. Ezra stares at him, something breaking open behind his eyes. "Why?" he asks again. This time Declan answers: "Because I'm tired of being the kind of man who does nothing." They sleep together. It's not gentle — it's desperate, the kind of sex that happens when two people have been holding themselves apart for too long and finally stop. It's tangled up with grief and relief and the knowledge that they've crossed a line they can't uncross. Afterward, they lie in the dark, and Ezra tells Declan the full story — how he lost his law license, how Maren saved him from self-destruction, how he's been running on bad ideas and cigarette smoke ever since because the good ideas didn't save anyone. **Key beats:** Declan's professional crisis, the consummation of the romance, Ezra's full backstory revealed in intimacy, the emotional climax of their relationship. --- ## Chapter 7: "The Report" **Word count target:** ~1000 words The consequences arrive. Declan writes his insurance report — and falsifies it. He structures the evidence to support Maren's claim and obscure the arson connection, protecting her and the case Ezra is building. It's the first time Declan has ever broken the rules, and it feels both terrible and right. He files the report. But Tidewater Holdings isn't finished. They send someone to intimidate Maren directly — not a threat this time, but a buyout offer with a veiled menace. Maren, shaken, tells Ezra she's considering taking it. Ezra is devastated. He argues with Maren — a real argument, ugly and painful, between two people who love each other. Declan witnesses it and sees Ezra's desperation fully. Meanwhile, Detective Lusk contacts Declan — quietly, off the record. He's been building his own case against Tidewater but needs the insurance investigation to stay open as cover. He asks Declan to keep playing the role of the investigator, even though he's already falsified the report. Declan realizes he's now committed fraud and obstruction — crimes that could end more than his career. The chapter ends with Declan and Ezra on a rooftop, looking at the waterfront. Ezra says: "I never wanted to drag you into this." Declan says: "You didn't. I walked in. That's the difference." They stand in silence, and Declan knows that whatever happens, he won't regret it. **Key beats:** The noir "turn" — Declan crosses the legal line, consequences mount, the institutional pressure intensifies, the bond between Declan and Ezra solidifies through shared risk. --- ## Chapter 8: "Smoke Signals" **Word count target:** ~1000 words Resolution. Detective Lusk moves against Tidewater Holdings — quietly, through a federal connection. The development scheme unravels. Maren's claim is approved. The waterfront residents are safe — for now. It's not a clean victory; the councilman will likely avoid prosecution, and the system that enabled the corruption remains intact. Declan is fired from his firm. He doesn't fight it. He sits in his empty office, packs a box, and realizes he feels lighter than he has in years. The final scene: Declan finds Ezra at the waterfront bar from Chapter 3. Ezra is smoking outside, in the rain, watching the harbor lights. Declan stands next to him. They don't touch. They don't need to. Ezra says: "So what now? I'm a disbarred lawyer, you're a fired insurance investigator. Between us, we have approximately zero credibility and a shared talent for bad decisions." Declan says: "Sounds like the beginning of something." Ezra smiles — a real one, not the performance. "That's what I'm afraid of." The story ends with them standing together in the rain, not solving anything, not fixing the world, but choosing each other — a bad idea, the best one either of them has ever had. The final line echoes the opening: *He was all cigarette smoke and bad ideas. And for the first time in my life, I didn't walk away.* **Key beats:** Plot resolution (partial, noir-appropriate), Declan's professional reckoning, the final scene — emotionally honest, bittersweet, hopeful, and a closing line that circles back to the opening image.
With a view to making the writing more human, discuss how a human might approach this particular piece (given the original prompt). Discuss telltale LLM approaches to writing (generally) and ways they might not serve this particular piece. For example, common LLM failings are to write safely, or to always wrap things up with a bow, or trying to write impressively at the expense of readability. Then do a deep dive on the intention & plan, critiquing ways it might be falling into typical LLM tropes & pitfalls. Brainstorm ideas to make it more human. Be comprehensive. We aren't doing any rewriting of the plan yet, just critique & brainstorming.
Model Output:
# How a Human Writer Might Approach This Piece A human writer receiving the prompt "He was all cigarette smoke and bad ideas" would likely start from a **personal, emotional place** rather than a structural one. They might think: *Who do I know like this? Who have I loved like this? What does cigarette smoke smell like in a way that's specific to my memory?* The prompt is atmospheric and character-driven — it's about a *feeling*, not a plot. A human would probably sit with that feeling first. A human might also have a specific relationship to noir — maybe they grew up reading Chandler, maybe they watched *Brick* in college and it rewired their brain, maybe they had a partner who smoked and the smell still does something to them. That personal texture — the uneven, sometimes contradictory, sometimes embarrassing specificity of real emotional experience — is what makes fiction feel alive. A human doesn't write from a database of tropes. They write from a body that has been in a room with someone dangerous and found themselves leaning closer instead of pulling away. A human would also likely be **messier** in their process. They might write the sex scene first, or the ending first, or a single line of dialogue that won't leave them alone and build outward. They might not know the plot when they start. They might discover what the story is about halfway through writing it. Our plan is neat. Human plans are neat too, sometimes — but the *writing* is where the mess lives, and that mess is where the humanity is. # Common LLM Writing Failures **1. Safety and sanitization.** LLMs tend to sand down anything that might be uncomfortable. Violence gets softened. Sex gets either skipped or rendered in vague, euphemistic language. Moral complexity gets flattened into "both sides." Characters who should be messy and sometimes unlikeable get smoothed into sympathetic archetypes. Real noir is *uncomfortable*. The reader should feel implicated, should feel the pull of the bad idea, should understand on a visceral level why Declan makes the choices he makes — even the self-destructive ones. **2. Over-explanation.** LLMs tend to tell you what a character is feeling instead of trusting the reader to feel it. "He felt a complicated mix of frustration and attraction." A human writer would *show* that through action, dialogue, or a single precise physical detail — Declan's hand tightening on his glass, or the way he reads the same sentence three times without absorbing it. The plan currently has some of this over-explanation baked in ("Declan feels a complicated mix of professional frustration and something softer"). **3. Impressive-at-the-expense-of-readable prose.** LLMs default to purple prose when trying to write "literary" fiction. Every sentence becomes a metaphor. Every description is lyrical. This is exhausting to read. Real noir prose is often **spare**. Chandler was lyrical, yes, but he was also blunt. "It was a blonde. A blonde to make a bishop kick a hole in a stained-glass window." That's not purple. That's precise and funny and human. The plan's intention section says "Chandler's rhythm" but I should be careful not to just mean "fancy sentences." **4. Thematic tidiness.** LLMs wrap things up. They resolve tensions. They make sure every thread is addressed. Real noir resists this. Real life resists this. The plan's Chapter 8 currently resolves almost everything — the case unravels, Maren is safe, the claim is approved, the villain is caught (sort of). That's a lot of resolution for a noir story. A human might leave more broken. Might let the reader sit with discomfort. **5. Dialogue that sounds like dialogue.** LLM dialogue tends to be too clean, too quippy, too perfectly timed. Real people interrupt each other. They trail off. They say "I don't know" too often. They repeat themselves. They say the wrong thing. Noir dialogue can be stylized — that's part of the genre — but it still needs to feel *spoken*, not *written*. **6. Uniform emotional register.** LLMs tend to maintain a consistent tone throughout — everything is atmospheric, everything is moody, everything is Significant. Real stories breathe. They have scenes that are mundane, or funny, or awkward, or boring, before the next wave of intensity. The plan doesn't have much room for levity or mundanity, which risks the story feeling like a tone poem rather than a lived experience. **7. Characters as functions.** LLM characters tend to serve the plot. They do what the story needs them to do. Real characters have lives that exist off-page — they have habits, opinions about food, a song they can't get out of their head, a knee that hurts when it rains. The plan's secondary characters (Maren, Detective Lusk, Declan's boss) are currently functional. They serve the plot. They don't yet feel like people. **8. Symbolism that's too neat.** LLMs love symbolism, and they tend to make it obvious. Rain = cleansing. Cigarettes = self-destruction. Fire = transformation. A human writer would use these symbols but complicate them — maybe the rain is just rain, sometimes, and the cigarettes are just a habit, and the reader is the one who brings the meaning. --- # Deep Critique of the Current Plan **The plan is structurally sound but emotionally safe.** Here's what I mean: **The romance arc is too smooth.** Declan and Ezra meet, are attracted, face obstacles, deepen their bond, consummate, and end up together. This is a perfectly competent romance arc. It's also the *expected* arc. A human writer might make the attraction uglier — maybe Declan is attracted to Ezra partly *because* Ezra is a mess, and that attraction feels shameful and self-destructive, not just inconvenient. Maybe the sex scene in Chapter 6 isn't just "desperate" in a romantic way but is actually a bad decision that they both know is a bad decision even as they make it, and the morning after is uncomfortable, not tender. The plan treats their coming together as the emotional climax. A human might treat it as another complication. **Declan is too sympathetic too early.** He's repressed, he's buttoned-up, but the plan presents him as fundamentally good — he's just been following the rules. A more human approach might make his repression *active*, not passive. Maybe he's the kind of person who has reported colleagues for minor infractions. Maybe he chose insurance fraud investigation specifically because it lets him judge other people's dishonesty from a safe distance. Maybe his ex left him because he was controlling, not just distant. We need to understand why Ezra — chaos, risk, moral flexibility — is both exactly what Declan needs and exactly what he should stay away from. Right now, Declan is too easy to root for. **Ezra is too cool.** He's described as charismatic, reckless, kind underneath the performance. That's a trope — the secretly-sweet bad boy. A human writer might make Ezra's "bad ideas" less charming and more genuinely concerning. Maybe he's burned bridges not because he's noble but because he's self-destructive. Maybe his loyalty to Maren is partly about his own guilt and need for redemption, not just pure kindness. Maybe he sometimes takes cases that are actually shady, not just gray. We need to see the *real* cost of being Ezra Vane — the loneliness, the financial precariousness, the mornings when the charm doesn't work and he's just a broke man in a bad apartment. **The plan resolves too neatly.** Chapter 8 has Tidewater Holdings unraveled, Maren safe, the claim approved, the waterfront preserved. The only loose end is "the system remains intact," which is a thematic statement, not a felt consequence. A human noir would leave more damage. Maybe Maren takes the buyout anyway, and Ezra has to live with that. Maybe Declan's fraud is discovered, and he faces actual legal consequences. Maybe the councilman gets away with it entirely, and the waterfront is developed anyway, and all Declan and Ezra have is each other — which is enough, but also isn't. The current ending is hopeful. Noir endings should be *complicated*. **The case is too legible.** Tidewater Holdings, the shell company, the corrupt councilman — it's all very clean, very Scooby-Doo. Real corruption is diffuse, boring, bureaucratic. It's not a villain you can point at; it's a system. A human writer might make the antagonists less visible, less nameable. The threat isn't a person; it's a process. That's scarier, and it's more true. **The plan doesn't account for boredom, awkwardness, or humor.** Every scene is loaded with significance. Where are the moments where nothing happens? Where Declan eats a bad sandwich at his desk? Where Ezra's car won't start? Where they have a conversation about nothing — about whether hot dogs are sandwiches, about a terrible movie they both saw, about the weird noise Ezra's radiator makes? These mundane moments are where readers fall in love with characters. The plan is all highlights. It needs valleys. **The POV choice needs more consideration.** First-person from Declan is the right call for noir, but the plan doesn't reckon with what it means for Declan to be an *unreliable* narrator — not because he lies to the reader, but because he doesn't understand his own motivations. A human writer would lean into this. Declan *thinks* he's helping Maren because it's the right thing to do. The reader should be able to see that he's also doing it because of Ezra, because of what Ezra represents, because Ezra is the person Declan has spent his whole life being afraid to become. The gap between what Declan says and what the reader understands is where the real story lives. **The sensory world is generic.** "Rain-soaked, neon-lit, waterfront." These are noir defaults. A human writer would find the *specific* sensory details that belong to *this* world, *these* characters. What brand of cigarettes does Ezra smoke? What does Declan's office smell like? What song is playing on the jukebox in the waterfront bar? What does Ezra's handwriting look like? Specificity is what separates a world that feels real from a world that feels like a set. --- # Brainstorming: Ideas to Make It More Human **1. Give Declan a specific, unglamorous flaw.** Not just "repressed" — something concrete and unattractive. Maybe he snoops. He reads Ezra's mail when Ezra leaves the room. He checks Ezra's phone. Not because he's jealous (yet) but because investigating people is the only way he knows how to relate to them. It's creepy. It's human. And it mirrors the noir detective's compulsion to uncover truth, reframed as an intimacy disorder. **2. Give Ezra a genuinely bad quality that isn't secretly good.** Maybe he's unreliable about time. He shows up late, forgets plans, breaks small promises. Not because he's free-spirited but because he's disorganized and depressed and self-medicating with nicotine and alcohol. It's not charming. It's frustrating. And Declan, who is pathologically punctual, finds it maddening — and also finds himself caring about it, which is worse. **3. Let the sex scene be awkward.** Not bad — awkward. They're both nervous. Something goes slightly wrong — a knee, a miscommunication, a moment of "wait, what are we doing?" And then it works, but not smoothly, and afterward they don't know what to say to each other. This is how real sex between two guarded people actually works, especially when there's a power dynamic and professional stakes involved. The plan describes it as "desperate" and "tangled up with grief and relief." That's too literary. Sometimes sex is just sex, and the meaning comes after, in the silence. **4. Give Maren a moment of selfishness or pettiness.** She's currently a sympathetic victim. Let her be a person — maybe she's sharp with Declan in a way that has nothing to do with fear, just her personality. Maybe she and Ezra have a history that includes a real falling-out, not just mutual loyalty. Maybe she makes a decision in Chapter 7 that is understandable but also self-serving — she takes the buyout not because she's scared but because the money is good and she's tired. This is more interesting and more human than a woman who just needs saving. **5. Let the case be partly Declan's fault.** What if the reason Tidewater Holdings is pressuring the firm is because Declan's firm has a pre-existing relationship with them? What if Declan has unknowingly been part of the machine that's now threatening Maren? This makes his "break from the institution" less heroic and more about complicity and guilt. He's not just choosing to do the right thing; he's trying to undo something he was part of. **6. Include a scene where Declan and Ezra disagree about something real.** Not about the case — about a value, a belief, a way of being in the world. Maybe Ezra thinks the system is fundamentally corrupt and can't be reformed. Maybe Declan still believes in institutions. Maybe they argue about it, and the argument doesn't resolve, and they go to bed angry, and it's uncomfortable, and the reader has to sit with the fact that these two people might be fundamentally incompatible even though they're drawn to each other. **7. Let the ending be less triumphant.** Instead of Lusk moving against Tidewater and the scheme unraveling, what if the resolution is murkier? What if the best they can do is slow the development down, not stop it? What if Maren gets her insurance money but loses the warehouse anyway? What if Declan's fraud is discovered and he's under investigation, and the last image is him and Ezra together but with a real, unresolved threat hanging over them? The current ending is: "They choose each other, and it's enough." A more human ending might be: "They choose each other, and it's not enough, but it's what they have." **8. Give Declan a physical tic or habit that reveals his interior state.** Not just "his hand tightened on his glass" — something specific and recurring. Maybe he straightens things. Aligns objects on tables. Folds napkins into precise squares. And as the story progresses and he loosens, the habit loosens too — by the end, he's leaving things messy, and it's its own kind of freedom. **9. Let Ezra be wrong about something.** His read on the situation, his evidence, his plan — let one of his "bad ideas" actually be a bad idea. Maybe the evidence he's gathered is inadmissible or leads them in the wrong direction. Maybe his plan to protect Maren backfires. This prevents him from being the noir archetype of the brilliant-but-tortured PI and makes him a real person who makes real mistakes. **10. Include a moment of queer joy.** The plan is relentlessly heavy — danger, repression, corruption, risk. Where is the moment where these two men are just happy? Where they laugh? Where they exist in a queer space — a bar, a party, a moment of recognition — that isn't defined by threat? Noir doesn't have to be joyless. The darkness is more bearable, and more true, if there's light in it too. **11. Rethink the opening flash-forward.** The plan opens with a flash-forward to "Declan in the rain, knowing this is going to end badly." This is a very common LLM move — the dramatic hook, the promise of excitement. A human might open more quietly. Maybe the opening is just Declan at his desk, doing his job, and the cigarette smoke line comes from a memory or a passing thought. The flash-forward might be unnecessary. Trust the reader to stay without the teaser. **12. Find the specific emotional wound.** Every noir protagonist has a wound. The plan says Declan is "repressed" but doesn't specify *why*. "Came out late and quietly" is a start, but it's not a wound — it's a circumstance. A human writer would know the exact moment that made Declan the way he is. Maybe it was a specific rejection. Maybe it was a specific relationship that taught him that desire leads to loss. Maybe it was growing up in a household where emotions were treated as inconveniences. We don't need to spell this out in the story — but the writer needs to *know* it, the way you know the sore tooth you keep touching with your tongue. It has to inform every scene, even if it's never named. **13. Give the story a specific, non-generic relationship to place.** Harbor City is currently a noir composite. A human writer would anchor it in something real — even if it's fictional, it should feel like a specific place with specific weather and specific smells and specific politics. What's the local cuisine? What's the dominant industry? What's the demographic makeup? What does the gentrification look like on the ground — the coffee shop that used to be a hardware store, the condo development where the cannery used to be? These details aren't atmosphere — they're the *world* these characters live in, and they matter. **14. Let the prose style vary.** The plan calls for "hard-boiled but self-aware" prose throughout. But real voice isn't uniform. In moments of high emotion, the prose might get shorter, more fragmented. In moments of quiet observation, it might get more lyrical. In moments of humor, it might get dry and deadpan. The plan should acknowledge that the prose style is a tool, not a constant. **15. Consider what's at stake *emotionally*, not just plot-wise.** The plan tracks plot stakes well — career, safety, legal consequences. But what about the emotional stakes? Declan risking his career is a plot stake. Declan risking the carefully constructed self that has kept him safe for thirty-some years — *that's* an emotional stake. The plan gestures at this but doesn't fully commit. Every chapter should have both a plot beat and an emotional beat, and they shouldn't always align. --- This critique is comprehensive but it's important to say: the plan is a strong foundation. The bones are good. What I'm identifying is the difference between a competent piece and one that feels *alive*. The adjustments needed are not structural — they're about specificity, mess, discomfort, and trust. Trust the reader. Trust the characters to be worse and more lovable than the plan currently allows. Trust the silence. Trust the mess.
Ok now with these considerations in mind, formulate the final plan for the a humanlike, compelling short piece in {n_chapters} chapters. Bear in mind the constraints of the piece (each chapter is just 1000 words). Above all things, the plan must serve the original prompt. We will use the same format as before: # Intention <State your formulated intentions for the piece, synthesised from the the parts of the brainstorming session that worked, and avoiding the parts that didn't. Be explicit about the choices you have made about plot, voice, stylistic choices, things you intend to aim for & avoid.> # Chapter Planning <Write a brief chapter plan for all {n_chapters} chapters.>
Model Output:
# Intention **The prompt is:** *He was all cigarette smoke and bad ideas.* That sentence is a feeling before it's a story — the feeling of being drawn to someone you know will hurt you, or change you, or burn something down. The piece must serve that feeling above all else. Everything else — the plot, the noir framework, the setting — exists to deliver that emotional truth with specificity and weight. **Core Characters:** **Declan Hale (POV / narrator, early 30s):** Insurance fraud investigator. Not repressed in a romantic, brooding way — repressed in an *ugly* way. He's the kind of person who checks his neighbors' recycling bins. He chose fraud investigation because judging other people's dishonesty from a safe distance is easier than being honest himself. He came out at 26, not because he was ready, but because his mother found a text message and he couldn't lie anymore. He didn't feel brave. He felt caught. He has a habit of straightening objects on tables — coasters, salt shakers, the edges of books — and he doesn't know he does it. He is not easy to like at the start. The reader should understand him before they root for him. **Ezra Vane (mid 30s):** Disbarred lawyer, now unlicensed PI. Smokes Drum tobacco, hand-rolled, because he can't afford tailor-mades and tells himself it's aesthetic. Lost his license after fabricating evidence to protect a queer asylum seeker — but the real story is messier: he was also drinking heavily at the time, and the fabricated evidence wasn't just noble, it was sloppy, and it almost got the client deported anyway. He saved the person and ruined himself, but he wasn't purely heroic. He's late to everything. He forgets to eat. He has a gap in his knowledge about wine that he covers with bluffing. His apartment has a radiator that makes a sound like a small animal dying. He is genuinely funny — not quippy, not performatively clever, but funny the way tired people are funny, where the humor comes from honesty. He is not secretly good. He is a person who has done good and bad things and is trying, inconsistently, to do fewer bad ones. **Maren Voss (40s):** Trans woman. Runs a small art restoration business out of a waterfront warehouse. She is not a victim — she is a person to whom a bad thing has happened, and there is a difference. She has a sharp tongue, a low tolerance for self-pity, and a complicated relationship with Ezra that includes a real falling-out two years ago (over a case where Ezra's recklessness cost her a client). They reconciled, but the scar is there. In Chapter 7, she makes a decision that is understandable, self-serving, and painful to Ezra: she takes a buyout from Tidewater Holdings. Not because she's scared, but because the money is good and she's tired and she doesn't owe the waterfront anything. This is the most human thing she does. **Setting:** Harbor City. Present day. A mid-sized coastal city that's being developed — the waterfront is the contested ground. Not a noir composite; a *specific* place. The cannery that closed in 2011 and is now a condo site. The coffee shop that used to be a hardware store. The Vietnamese restaurant on Third Street that Declan orders from three times a week because it's the only place that gets the broth right. Weather is a constant: rain, fog, the smell of salt and rust. **Voice:** First-person, Declan's POV. Hard-boiled in rhythm but not in affect — he's not performing toughness for the reader, he's performing it for himself, and occasionally the mask slips. The prose should vary: short and blunt in tense moments, more observational and even funny in quieter ones, lyrical only when Declan is overwhelmed and his defenses are down. The opening line of the whole piece should be the prompt itself — not as a flash-forward, but as a present-tense observation. Let the reader sit with it before they know what it means. **What the story is about (emotionally):** Two men who have spent their lives controlling the narrative — Declan through order, Ezra through performance — and what happens when they meet someone who makes control impossible. It's about the terror and relief of being seen by someone who doesn't need you to be anything other than what you are. It's about choosing a person over a principle, and not knowing if that's brave or stupid. **What the story is about (structurally):** An insurance investigation that uncovers a property development scheme targeting the waterfront. Declan is supposed to be investigating Ezra's client; instead, he finds himself allied with Ezra against his own firm. The case is the engine, but the romance is the story. **What I'm aiming for:** - Specificity over generality. Every detail should feel chosen, not defaulted to. - Discomfort. The reader should sometimes feel uneasy about Declan's choices, Ezra's reliability, the relationship's power dynamics. - Silence and space. Not every moment needs to be narrated. Let scenes breathe. Let conversations trail off. - Humor. Not constant, but present — dry, tired, human. - A sex scene that feels like two real people in a room, not like a set piece. - An ending that is emotionally honest but not wrapped in a bow. Loose threads. Uncertainty. Hope that costs something. - Prose that trusts the reader. Don't explain what the reader can figure out. Don't describe what the reader can infer. **What I'm avoiding:** - Tidy resolution. The villain doesn't get caught. The system doesn't reform. The best outcome is imperfect. - Characters as functions. Every named character should feel like they have a life beyond the page. - Impressive prose. Aim for *precise* prose. The difference matters. - Uniform tone. Let the story be funny, then sad, then tense, then boring, then electric. - Over-explaining emotion. If Declan is attracted to Ezra, show it through what he notices — his hands, his voice, the way smoke moves — not through internal monologue about attraction. - Flash-forwards or structural gimmicks. The story is linear. Trust the reader to stay. --- # Chapter Planning ## Chapter 1: "Drum" **Target:** ~1000 words Opens with the prompt line, in present tense: *He was all cigarette smoke and bad ideas.* But this isn't a flash-forward — it's Declan thinking about Ezra after the fact, a single beat of reflection before we're pulled into the present. Then we're in Declan's world: his office, his desk, his routine. We see him at work — methodical, precise, good at a job that rewards suspicion. He's assigned a new case: an insurance claim tied to a warehouse fire on the waterfront. The claimant's representative is an unlicensed PI named Ezra Vane with a disciplinary history. His boss says the line: "He's all cigarette smoke and bad ideas." Declan takes the file. That evening, Declan drives to the waterfront to see the burned warehouse. It's raining. The neighborhood is in flux — half-gentrified, half-falling apart. He stands outside the warehouse, looking at the damage, and notices a man across the street, leaning against a lamppost, smoking hand-rolled cigarettes. Watching the same building. Their eyes meet. The man doesn't look away. Declan gets back in his car. He can smell the tobacco through the rain. **Key beats:** Establish Declan's world and voice (controlled, observant, subtly self-deprecating), introduce the case, first sight of Ezra — atmospheric but brief, no interaction yet. The cigarette smoke enters Declan's sensory world and won't leave. --- ## Chapter 2: "The Walk-Up" **Target:** ~1000 words Declan visits Ezra's office to ask questions — a second-floor walk-up above a laundromat. The stairs smell like detergent and mold. Ezra's office is cluttered, covered in pinned notes and maps. There's a French press with yesterday's coffee still in it. Ezra is late to his own office; Declan waits. When Ezra arrives, he's flustered, charming, and immediately disarming. They talk. It's a duel — Declan asks direct questions, Ezra answers with stories, digressions, half-truths. Declan is frustrated but also — and this is the part he won't examine — *interested*. Not just in the case. In the way Ezra talks with his hands. In the gap between his front teeth. In the fact that he offers Declan coffee from a dirty French press without embarrassment. Ezra reveals that the claimant, Maren Voss, lost everything in the fire — her art restoration business, years of work. He implies the fire was deliberate but won't say more until he trusts Declan. The meeting ends without resolution. Afterward, Declan does background research. He reads the disciplinary record: Ezra fabricated evidence in an asylum case. The file is clinical, but Declan reads between the lines — a queer lawyer fighting for a queer client and losing everything. He closes the file. He straightens the edges of the papers. **Key beats:** First real interaction. Chemistry through dialogue and observation. Ezra's world contrasted with Declan's. The background research humanizes Ezra without making him a saint. Declan's attraction is shown through *what he notices*, not what he feels. --- ## Chapter 3: "Third Street" **Target:** ~1000 words Declan tracks down Maren Voss. She's working out of a temporary space — a friend's studio, cramped, full of other people's damaged paintings. She's guarded but not helpless. She answers Declan's questions with clipped efficiency and a few pointed remarks that make it clear she thinks insurance investigators are parasites. In a moment of candor — not vulnerability, candor — she tells him the fire wasn't the first threat. Someone has been pressuring waterfront property owners to sell. She won't name who. That evening, Declan orders takeout from the Vietnamese place on Third Street. He eats at his desk, alone, reading case files. Then he goes to a waterfront bar — not to find Ezra, he tells himself. Ezra is there anyway. They drink together. The conversation is half-investigation, half something else. Ezra talks about Maren — how she gave him work when no one else would, how they had a falling-out two years ago over a case he mishandled, how he sometimes wonders if she keeps him around out of pity. It's not a performance. It's just a man talking. They step outside. It's raining. Ezra smokes. Declan watches his hands — the practiced roll, the match strike. Ezra says: "You seem like the kind of person who always knows what the right thing is. That must be tiring." Declan doesn't answer. They stand close enough that Declan can smell the tobacco and something underneath it — laundry detergent from the laundromat, maybe, or just Ezra. He goes home. He doesn't straighten anything on his desk that night. **Key beats:** Maren as a real person (sharp, not a victim), the first moment of genuine connection between Declan and Ezra, the bar scene as a space where their guards drop slightly, the sensory detail of Ezra (smell, hands) as the language of attraction. --- ## Chapter 4: "The Radiator" **Target:** ~1000 words Declan digs into the property angle and finds Tidewater Holdings — a shell company buying waterfront land. He brings it to his boss, who tells him to focus on the claim. His boss doesn't say "drop it" — he says "that's not what we're paying you for," which is worse, because it's true. Declan feels the first crack: not moral outrage, but the uncomfortable realization that his job exists to protect institutions, not people. Ezra contacts Declan — he has evidence of a pattern: fires, break-ins, pressure. But he can't use it himself. He's unlicensed, disbarred, uncredible. He needs Declan. They meet at Ezra's apartment. The radiator is making its horrible noise. Ezra makes coffee — bad coffee, from a jar of instant. He lays out the evidence on his kitchen table: photos, dates, a map of the waterfront with pins in it. It's obsessive, meticulous, and clearly the work of months. Declan sees the gap between the charming performance and the reality: Ezra has been doing this alone, burning himself out, because no one else would. At one point, Ezra steps out to take a phone call. Declan is alone in the apartment. He looks at the evidence, the maps, the mess. He notices a photograph of Maren and Ezra, years younger, laughing. He notices a stack of unpaid bills. He notices a book of poetry — Lorca, dog-eared — left open on the arm of a chair. He doesn't snoop further. He wants to. He doesn't. That restraint is its own kind of progress. Ezra comes back, distracted. The phone call was bad news — another waterfront owner caved and sold. They talk about next steps. Ezra is tired, and the tired makes him honest: "I don't know if any of this works. I just know I can't stop." Declan stays until the radiator stops making noise, which takes a long time. **Key beats:** The case deepens, institutional pressure on Declan, Ezra's apartment as a window into his real life (messy, broke, human), Declan's snooping impulse checked, the evidence scene as a turning point — Declan sees that Ezra's "bad ideas" are actually desperate, lonely, and brave. --- ## Chapter 5: "The Message" **Target:** ~1000 words Maren's temporary studio is broken into. Nothing stolen — just a dead bird left on her workbench. She calls Ezra, who calls Declan. Declan arrives to find Ezra already there, pacing, furious. For the first time, Declan sees Ezra without the charm — what's underneath is fear and rage, and it's not elegant. Ezra is snapping at Maren, who is snapping back. They argue — not about the break-in but about Ezra's methods, his recklessness, whether he's making things worse. It's an old argument with new fuel. Declan witnesses it and feels like he's intruding on something private. Afterward, Ezra and Declan sit in Ezra's car. Ezra smokes. His hands are shaking. He says: "I keep thinking if I just work harder, find the right angle, I can fix this. But I can't. I'm not a lawyer anymore. I'm not anything." It's not a line. It's not charming. It's a man at the end of something. Declan doesn't comfort him — he doesn't know how. Instead, he says: "You're a PI. You're just not licensed." It's a stupid thing to say. Ezra laughs. It's a broken laugh, but it's real. That night, Ezra shows up at Declan's apartment. He doesn't say why he's come. Declan lets him in. They drink whiskey. The conversation is halting — about nothing, about everything. At one point, Ezra touches Declan's hand, briefly, and Declan doesn't pull away. They don't kiss. Ezra leaves at 2 a.m. Declan stands at the window and watches him walk to his car in the rain, and he thinks: *This is the bad idea. This is the one I can't investigate my way out of.* **Key beats:** The threat becomes physical, Ezra's facade fully drops, the argument between Ezra and Maren shows their complicated relationship, the car scene as emotional rawness, the apartment visit as tenderness without consummation — restraint that makes the reader *want*. --- ## Chapter 6: "The Report" **Target:** ~1000 words Declan's boss calls him in. Tidewater Holdings has contacted the firm. The message is clear: deny the claim, close the investigation, or there will be professional consequences. His boss doesn't threaten — he *explains*, patiently, the way you explain to a child. The firm's relationship with Tidewater is worth more than one claim. Declan listens. He nods. He goes back to his desk. He sits there for an hour. He doesn't straighten anything. Then he goes to Ezra's office. Ezra is there, looking worse than usual — unwashed, unshaven, surrounded by paper. Declan tells him what happened. Ezra says: "So you're out." Declan says: "I didn't say that." He sits down. He takes one of Ezra's hand-rolled cigarettes and lights it. He's never smoked before. It's terrible. He coughs. Ezra watches him with an expression Declan can't read. Declan says: "I'm going to file the report. I'm going to structure it to support Maren's claim. The arson evidence won't appear." Ezra is quiet for a long time. Then: "That's fraud." Declan: "I know." Ezra: "Why?" And here — here is where the story earns its weight. Declan doesn't say something noble. He says: "Because I'm tired of being the person who checks the recycling bins." Ezra doesn't understand the reference. That's fine. Declan does. They sit in the cluttered office, and the light comes through the window in a way that makes the dust motes visible, and they look at each other, and something passes between them that isn't desire exactly, or isn't only desire — it's recognition. Two people who have each been alone in a specific way, seeing each other clearly for the first time. What happens next is not described as a set piece. It's two nervous people in a room. There's a moment of "are we doing this?" There's a knee that bumps a desk. There's a kiss that starts uncertain and becomes sure. There's an article of clothing that gets caught. It's not smooth. It's real. Afterward, they lie on the floor because Ezra's couch is covered in files, and Ezra smokes, and Declan stares at the ceiling, and neither of them says "this changes everything" because they both already know. **Key beats:** Declan's professional crisis and moral choice, the smoking as a physical metaphor (Declan entering Ezra's world, doing something that's bad for him and knows it), the first kiss and sex scene — awkward, human, earned, not described in explicit detail but in *specific* detail, the aftermath on the floor as a moment of fragile, uncertain intimacy. --- ## Chapter 7: "The Buyout" **Target:** ~1000 words Declan files the fraudulent report. It's the best work he's ever done — meticulously structured, legally airtight, completely false. He feels sick and proud in equal measure. Then Maren calls Ezra. She's taking the buyout from Tidewater. Not because of the dead bird, not because she's scared — because the money is good, and she's forty-four, and she's tired of fighting, and she doesn't owe the waterfront or Ezra or anyone her life. Ezra argues. It's an ugly argument — he accuses her of giving up, she accuses him of using her cause to avoid dealing with his own life. They're both right. They're both cruel. Declan listens and knows he shouldn't be there, and stays anyway. After the argument, Ezra sits on the steps outside Maren's temporary studio and smokes. Declan sits next to him. Ezra says: "She's not wrong. About me." Declan says: "No." It's the most honest thing he's said. Ezra looks at him — not angry, not hurt, just looking. "You're not what I expected," he says. Declan: "What did you expect?" Ezra: "Someone easier." A beat. Then Ezra says: "There's a detective. Lusk. He's been building something on Tidewater — I've been feeding him information for months. Off the books. If your fraudulent report holds, it gives him cover to keep the investigation open." The plot threads connect: Declan's fraud isn't just protective, it's strategic. But it also means Declan is now complicit in an ongoing obstruction. Lusk calls Declan that evening — a quiet conversation, off the record. Lusk doesn't moralize. He just says: "Keep your head down. This might take a while." The chapter ends with Declan in his apartment. He looks at his desk — the neat stacks, the aligned edges. For the first time, he leaves a coffee ring on the surface without wiping it away. It's a small thing. It's everything. **Key beats:** Maren's decision as a wrench in the works — not a villain's move, a human's, the argument between Maren and Ezra as the story's most emotionally honest scene, the plot revelation about Lusk giving the fraud a purpose beyond personal sacrifice, the coffee ring as Declan's smallest and most significant act of letting go. --- ## Chapter 8: "Smoke Signals" **Target:** ~1000 words Time passes — weeks, maybe a month. Declan's firm hasn't discovered the fraud yet, but it's a matter of time. He's been let go — not fired, "restructured" — and is doing freelance consulting work that bores him. Ezra is still Ezra — still broke, still late, still smoking on the waterfront in the rain. Maren has taken the buyout and moved inland. The warehouse is slated for demolition. The waterfront is changing, and the small victory of keeping the investigation alive feels small. One afternoon, Declan meets Detective Lusk for coffee. Lusk says the federal investigation is progressing but slowly. The councilman is insulated. Tidewater is careful. It could take years. "You should know," Lusk says, "that if this comes out, your report will be evidence. Against you." Declan nods. He knew this. That evening, he finds Ezra at the waterfront bar. Ezra is at the bar, talking to the bartender about something mundane — a plumbing issue, maybe, or the weather. Declan sits next to him. They don't touch. They order drinks. They talk about nothing — about a bad movie on TV, about the Vietnamese place on Third Street, about whether Ezra's radiator has finally died or is just biding its time. Outside, it's raining. They stand under the awning. Ezra smokes. Declan watches the smoke — how it curls, how the rain almost catches it, how it disappears. Ezra says: "I've been thinking about what happens next. With us. I don't have a plan. I usually don't." Declan says: "I know." Ezra: "Is that a problem?" Declan considers this. He thinks about the report, the risk, the way his life has become something he doesn't recognize. He thinks about the smell of Drum tobacco and bad coffee and the sound of a dying radiator. "I don't know," Declan says. It's the most honest thing he can offer. Ezra nods. They stand together, not solving anything, not fixing the world, just two people in the rain who have chosen each other without any guarantee that it will work. The last line isn't a declaration. It's an observation — quiet, specific, and true: *He was all cigarette smoke and bad ideas. And I was standing in the rain with him, which was another one.* **Key beats:** Resolution that isn't resolution — the case is ongoing, the threat is real, the future is uncertain. Maren is gone but not forgotten. The fraud hangs over Declan like a held breath. The final scene is quiet — two people choosing each other with open eyes. The last line echoes the prompt, completing the circuit, but with a shift: now Declan is part of the bad idea, and he knows it, and he's staying.

# Declan Hale ## Background & Personality Declan grew up in a mid-sized town in the Midwest — the kind of place with a Dairy Queen and a VFW hall and a general understanding that you don't talk about certain things. His father was a claims adjuster for an insurance company, which is how Declan learned that the world is divided into people who file claims and people who investigate them, and that the second group sleeps better. His mother managed a dentist's office and organized the church bake sale every year. Neither of them was cruel. Neither of them was particularly warm. When Declan came out at 26 — not by choice, but because his mother saw a text from a man named Paul on his phone — his mother said, "We still love you," in a voice that made it sound like a medical diagnosis. His father didn't say anything for three weeks. Then he called to ask about a football score, and they never discussed it again. Paul was the only man Declan has been with in any serious way. They dated for eleven months. Paul was warm, social, uncomplicated — the kind of person who made friends in grocery store checkout lines. Declan loved him and also found him exhausting, and he never learned to reconcile those two things. Paul left because he said being with Declan felt like "trying to hug a filing cabinet." Declan didn't argue. He went home and reorganized his spice rack alphabetically, which had previously been organized by frequency of use, and that reorganization felt like grief. He's been alone since. Not unhappily, most of the time. He has his work, which he's good at. He has routines. He goes to the Vietnamese place on Third Street — Pho 88 — three times a week. He always orders the same thing: pho with rare beef and extra cilantro, no bean sprouts. The woman who runs the restaurant, Mrs. Nguyen, once tried to suggest he try the bun bo hue, and he said "No thank you" with such polite finality that she never suggested anything again. He's been going there for two years. She knows his order. They have a relationship built on consistency and mutual non-interference, and Declan finds it deeply comforting in a way he would never articulate. He's not cold. That's the thing people get wrong. He's *careful*. He learned early that emotions are expensive and that most people can't afford them, and he organized his life accordingly. The straightening-the-coasters thing — he does it at restaurants, at other people's houses, at his own desk. He does it without thinking. It's a way of making the world line up when it doesn't want to. He knows it's a compulsion. He doesn't examine it. If he examined it, he'd have to look at what it's compensating for, and he's not ready for that. He is good at his job not because he loves catching liars but because he understands systems. Insurance is a system. Fraud is what happens when people try to break the system. Declan's job is to find the break, document it, and restore the system to order. He finds this satisfying in a way that is not exciting but is deeply reliable. He has never once in his career falsified a report. He has never once bent a rule. This is not because he's moral. It's because rules are the only thing that have never left him. **Specific, trivial details:** - He keeps a small notebook in his jacket pocket — not for work, just for observations. He writes down things he notices: license plates, addresses, the color of someone's shoes. He's done this since college. He doesn't know why. - He can't cook anything except scrambled eggs, which he makes well — low heat, constant stirring, a splash of cream at the end. - He owns one piece of art: a small oil painting of a harbor at dusk, bought at a street fair five years ago. It hangs above his desk at home. He's never thought about why he bought it. - He drinks his coffee black. He owns a French press but has never once left yesterday's coffee in it. The idea of doing so mildly repulses him. - He bites the inside of his cheek when he's thinking. He has a permanent small sore on the left side from years of this. - He runs three mornings a week — the same route, along the harbor, 4.2 miles. He doesn't vary it. He doesn't listen to music. He counts his steps in sets of eight. - He is mildly lactose intolerant and ignores this when eating macaroni and cheese, which he does about once a month, and always regrets. - His apartment has one plant — a pothos on the windowsill that he has managed to keep alive for three years through a watering schedule taped to the refrigerator. ## Physicality Declan is 5'10", lean but not athletic — the kind of thin that comes from forgetting to eat, not from working out. Brown hair, cut short and practical, the kind of haircut you get at a chain salon and don't think about again. He wears glasses — wire-rimmed, slightly too small for his face, which gives him a look of permanent concentration. His features are unremarkable in a way that works for him: he blends in. He dresses in layers — button-down shirts, always tucked in, often with the sleeves rolled to the elbow when he's working. His shoes are clean. His nails are trimmed. He carries himself with a stillness that reads as composure but is actually vigilance — he's always watching, always cataloging, always aware of exits. When he moves, he's deliberate. He doesn't fidget. He doesn't gesture much when he talks. His hands are usually still — on a table, in his pockets, holding a pen. When he's uncomfortable, he adjusts his glasses. When he's angry, he goes quieter, not louder. People who don't know him think he's calm. People who do know him — which is almost no one — know that the quiet is the danger. He has a habit of looking at people slightly too long. Not in an aggressive way — in a *studying* way. He's collecting information. Most people don't notice. Ezra notices. ## Motives, Allegiances & Relationships **What Declan wants (at the start):** To do his job, go home, maintain the system that keeps his life in order. He wants to be left alone. He wants the world to make sense. He wants to eat his pho without anyone asking him to try something different. **What Declan wants (by the end):** To be known. Not understood — he's not sure that's possible — but *known*, by one person, in the specific and uncomfortable way that requires him to stop straightening the edges and let things be messy. **Allegiances:** At the start, to his firm and to the principle of rules. By the middle, to Ezra, reluctantly. By the end, to something he doesn't have a name for yet — something between justice and love, between doing the right thing and doing the necessary thing. **Relationships:** - *His mother:* They talk once a month. The conversations are brief and full of things not said. She sends him birthday cards with money in them — $50, every year, even though he's 32. He puts the money in a drawer. He has never spent it. - *His father:* They don't talk. Not out of animosity — out of a mutual agreement that they have nothing to say. - *Paul (ex):* Declan doesn't think about Paul often. When he does, it's not with longing — it's with the faint embarrassment of remembering a version of himself that tried to be someone he wasn't. Paul wanted warmth. Declan had spreadsheets. - *His boss, Gerald:* A professional relationship. Gerald is corporate, pragmatic, not unkind but not an ally. He sees Declan as reliable and unremarkable, which is exactly how Declan wants to be seen. Until he doesn't. - *Mrs. Nguyen:* The most stable relationship in his life. He would never call it that. - *Ezra:* The person who makes all of Declan's systems fail. ## Voice Samples **Internal monologue — early (guarded, controlled):** > The file said Ezra Vane had been disbarred in 2019. The details were in the usual bureaucratic language — "ethical violations," "misrepresentation of evidence," "conduct unbecoming." I'd read enough disciplinary records to know what they sound like when they're covering for something messier. This one smelled like a man who'd done the wrong thing for the right reason and gotten caught by people who only cared about the first half. **Internal monologue — mid (attraction leaking through the cracks):** > He rolled his own cigarettes. I watched him do it once — the paper between his fingers, the tobacco pinched and distributed, the lick-and-seal. It was practiced and imprecise, the opposite of everything I did with my hands. I thought about that for longer than I should have. **Internal monologue — late (defenses down):** > I stood in his kitchen and watched him make coffee with instant granules and cold tap water, and I thought: this is the kind of man my mother warned me about. Not because he was dangerous. Because he was the kind of person who would make you forget to be afraid. **Dialogue — professional:** > "Mr. Vane. I'm Declan Hale, with Aegis Insurance. I have some questions about the Voss claim." > He looked at me like I'd said something funny. "You always introduce yourself like you're reading from a card?" > "It's efficient." > "So's a root canal." **Dialogue — vulnerable (late in the story):** > "I don't know what this is," I said. I meant all of it — the case, the fraud, him, the fact that I was standing in his kitchen at midnight eating toast he'd made for me without asking. > "That's okay," he said. "I don't either." --- # Ezra Vane ## Background & Personality Ezra grew up in Harbor City. His mother, Irene, was a public defender who worked sixty-hour weeks and kept a bottle of gin in her desk drawer, not because she was an alcoholic but because the job required it. His father left when Ezra was seven — not dramatically, just gradually, until one day he was a man Ezra's mother used to know. Ezra doesn't have feelings about this. He says. He has a recurring dream about a red suitcase that he's never unpacked, which a therapist once told him was "probably about something," and which Ezra has since decided is about suitcases. He went to law school because his mother did. He was good at it — not brilliant, but sharp, quick on his feet, capable of the kind of lateral thinking that wins arguments and loses friends. He passed the bar. He worked at a small firm that handled immigration cases, mostly pro bono, mostly impossible. He was happy in the way that people are happy when they're doing work that matters and haven't yet learned what it costs. The asylum case — the one that ended his career — involved a queer man from El Salvador named Carlos who was facing deportation to a country where his life was effectively over. Ezra believed in the case. He believed in Carlos. He also believed that the legal system was a machine designed to process people into outcomes, and that sometimes the only way to beat the machine was to put something in it that didn't belong there. He fabricated a piece of evidence — a medical report documenting injuries consistent with persecution. It was convincing. It was also a lie, and when it was discovered, Carlos's case was set back by months, and Ezra was disbarred. What the disciplinary record doesn't say: Ezra was drinking heavily at the time. Not a little — a lot. The fabrication wasn't a calculated strategy. It was a 2 a.m. decision made by a man who was drunk and desperate and couldn't stand the idea of losing. Carlos was eventually granted asylum through other channels — his lawyer found legitimate evidence that did the job. But Ezra never forgave himself for the risk he took with someone else's life. The disbarment was almost a relief. At least the punishment was concrete. At least it matched the size of what he'd done. After the disbarment, he drifted. Worked as a bartender. Worked as a paralegal under a fake name for six months. Got sober-ish — he drinks now, but not like before, not the bottle-in-the-desk way, more like the two-beers-on-a-Friday way that he tells himself is normal. He started doing PI work because someone asked him to find a missing person and he was good at it, and one case turned into another, and now he's a person who finds things for people who can't afford to have things found through legitimate channels. He's unlicensed, which means he operates in a legal gray zone, which means he's careful about who he works for. Maren Voss was the first person to hire him after the disbarment. She needed someone to track down a supplier who had sold her counterfeit restoration materials. Ezra found the guy in three days. Maren paid him and then invited him to dinner, and they became something like friends — the kind of friends who argue and don't always like each other but show up when it matters. Two years ago, Ezra took a case that went sideways — he was working for a small business owner who was being pressured by a developer, and Ezra's investigation methods drew attention to the business owner instead of away from him. The man lost his lease. Maren blamed Ezra. She was right to. They didn't speak for four months. Then Maren called because she needed help moving a heavy table, and Ezra came, and they didn't talk about it, and that was how they reconciled — not with an apology, but with a table. Ezra is funny. Not in a performing way — in a *deflecting* way. Humor is how he survives discomfort, confusion, intimacy, fear, and boredom. He's the kind of person who makes a joke at his own expense before anyone else can. He's also capable of being completely serious, which is more disarming because it's rare. When Ezra is serious, you know he means it. He is chronically late. Not fashionably — genuinely. He loses track of time. He misjudges how long things take. He has set alarms and ignored them. He has a theory that time is "a suggestion," which he knows is insufferable and says anyway. Declan, who arrives everywhere four minutes early, finds this maddening. It becomes one of the small, real frictions between them — not a charming quirk, but a genuine source of irritation. He smokes Drum tobacco, hand-rolled. He started in law school, quit during his first year of practice, started again after the disbarment. He knows it's killing him. He has a cough in the mornings that he ignores. He rolls his cigarettes with a practiced imprecision — too much tobacco, a slightly crooked roll, a match instead of a lighter because he likes the smell of sulfur. He smokes when he's thinking, when he's nervous, when he's waiting, and when he doesn't know what else to do with his hands. Which is often. **Specific, trivial details:** - He owns three books of poetry: Lorca's *Poet in New York*, Cavafy's collected poems, and a slim volume of Wisława Szymborska that someone left on a bus and he never returned. He's read all three multiple times. He quotes them inaccurately and with confidence. - He can cook exactly two things: pasta with garlic and oil, and a passable omelet. He eats both more often than he should. - He has a scar on his left palm from a broken bottle — the night he got sober-ish, not the night he was disbarred. He sometimes traces it with his thumb when he's thinking. - He owns a 2004 Honda Civic with a cracked windshield and a driver's side window that doesn't go all the way up. The radio only gets AM stations. He listens to talk radio and argues with the hosts. - He bites his nails. His fingernails are ragged and uneven. He's aware of this and doesn't care. - He sleeps in a t-shirt and boxers, on top of his sheets, with one arm hanging off the bed. He has never once in his adult life made his bed before noon. - He has a recurring fantasy about opening a bookshop. Not a rare bookshop — a regular one, with used paperbacks and a cat. He's never told anyone this. - His handwriting is terrible — slanted, rushed, full of abbreviations. His case notes are legible only to him. ## Physicality Ezra is 6'1", with the kind of loose, angular build that suggests he was once in better shape and has been slowly losing ground. Dark hair, a little too long, often pushed back from his face with his hand rather than a comb. His face is interesting rather than handsome — sharp cheekbones, a slightly crooked nose (broken in a bar fight in his twenties, set badly), dark eyes that look like they're always half-laughing at something. He has a gap between his front teeth that shows when he smiles, which is often. He has the kind of stubble that suggests he meant to shave and then didn't. He dresses like a man who owns seven versions of the same outfit: dark jeans, a button-down shirt (usually wrinkled, sometimes missing a button), and a jacket that's seen better days — olive green, canvas, with too many pockets, all of them full of things he's forgotten about. His shoes are scuffed boots that he's had for years. He smells like cigarette smoke, laundry detergent (the cheap kind), and sometimes — when he's been in his office all day — like old coffee and paper. He moves loosely, like his body is a suggestion rather than a commitment. He gestures when he talks — big, expressive hand movements that sometimes knock things over. He leans on things: doorframes, counters, lampposts. He stands with his weight shifted to one hip, which gives him a perpetual air of casual appraisal. He sits in chairs like he's trying to take up as much of them as possible — legs spread, arms draped, head tilted. He is physically comfortable in a way that Declan finds both attractive and mildly offensive. When he's angry, he gets still — the opposite of his usual energy. When he's frightened, he talks more, faster, filling the space. When he's sad, he goes quiet, and the quiet is so unusual that it's alarming. ## Motives, Allegiances & Relationships **What Ezra wants (at the start):** To protect Maren. To prove — to her, to himself, to the ghost of the person he used to be — that he can still do something right. He wants redemption, though he'd never use the word. He'd say he just wants to "fix this one thing." **What Ezra wants (by the end):** To stop performing. To be known by someone without the charm, the deflection, the cigarette-smoke curtain. To be loved not for the idea of himself but for the actual, messy, frequently-late reality. **Allegiances:** To Maren, first and always, even when they're fighting. To the waterfront community, in a general way. To the principle that the system is broken and that broken systems require broken solutions. By the end, to Declan — reluctantly, fearfully, completely. **Relationships:** - *His mother, Irene:* Still practicing law, still drinking gin, still working too hard. They talk every two weeks. She knows about the disbarment and has never once said "I told you so," which is worse. She sends him socks. Always black. Always in pairs. He has more socks than any person needs. - *His father:* Gone. Ezra doesn't think about him. (He dreams about a red suitcase.) - *Carlos (the asylum client):* They don't speak. Carlos is in San Jose now, working at a nonprofit. Ezra knows this because he checks. He will never contact Carlos. He doesn't have the right. - *Maren:* The most important person in his life. Their relationship is built on mutual honesty, which means it's built on mutual bruising. She sees through him. He needs that. She also needs him — for his skills, his persistence, his willingness to do the thing no one else will do. When she takes the buyout in Chapter 7, it's not a betrayal. It's her choosing herself. And Ezra has to learn that people choosing themselves isn't the same as people leaving. - *Declan:* The person who makes Ezra want to be honest without the performance. Which is terrifying. Because the performance is all Ezra thinks he has. ## Voice Samples **Internal monologue (rendered through Declan's narration, but capturing Ezra's speech patterns):** > He talked the way some people swim — continuously, changing direction mid-stroke, trusting that he'd eventually reach some kind of shore. Half the time he did. The other half, you were left treading water in a conversation about Lorca or the price of eggs or the best way to get a stain out of canvas, and you weren't sure how you got there, but you weren't unhappy about it. **Dialogue — deflecting:** > "You're late," I said. > "I'm *here*. 'Late' is a relative concept." > "It's been forty minutes." > "Time is a suggestion." > "It's a measurement." > "Agree to disagree." > He sat down across from me and smiled, and I hated that it worked. **Dialogue — serious (rare, significant):** > "I keep thinking there's a version of this where I get it right. Where I find the evidence, and it's clean, and it works, and Maren is safe, and I can stop." He was looking at his hands. "But there isn't. There's just this — the mess, and the trying, and the cigarettes, and hoping I don't fuck it up worse than I already have." > He looked up at me.
