# Chapter 1: The Last Tin The last tin was beans. Of course it was beans. I'd been saving them for three days, moving them from shelf to shelf like a chess piece I wasn't ready to play. Every morning I'd pick it up, feel the weight, calculate the calories, and put it back. Three days of pretending we had options. Three days of Kael watching me do it and saying nothing, which was worse than if he'd said something. "There's a Co-op in Amble," he said, from his spot by the window. He wasn't looking at me. He was looking out at the gray line of the coast, where the Growths clustered along the rocks like barnacles. "If we went early, before the wind picks up—" "Amble's gone." I didn't look up from the tin. "You know it's gone." "I don't know that. I haven't been." "You've been close enough." He didn't argue. That was the thing about Kael—he never argued. He just waited, like he thought if he was quiet long enough, reality would rearrange itself to suit him. I turned the tin over in my hands. Heinz Baked Beans. 400g. The label was half-peeled, the red faded to a dull brown. There was a dent on one side from when I'd dropped it two weeks ago—I'd actually gasped, like I'd dropped a child, and Kael had looked at me with something that wasn't quite pity but was close. "I'll split it three ways," I said. "Four hundred grams," he said. "That's a hundred and thirty-three each." "I know how to divide, Kael." "I know you do." In the corner, under the mildewed blanket, Finn coughed. It was the wet kind, the kind that starts deep and takes a while to shake off. I watched him until the coughing stopped, until he settled back against the wall with his book—the marine biology one, the one with the ruined pictures. He hadn't turned a page in twenty minutes. "Finn," I said. "You hungry?" He looked up. His eyes were too big for his face—they'd always been big, but now, with the weight gone, they looked like they belonged to someone else. A bird, maybe. Something watchful and hollow-boned. "I'm okay," he said. "You're not okay. Don't say you're okay." "Then don't ask." I opened the tin. The smell hit me—salt, sweetness, the ghost of a meal I barely remembered. My stomach clenched so hard I had to put my hand on the counter. Behind me, I heard Kael shift his weight. He didn't say anything. He didn't have to. The sound of his breathing had changed. I heated them on the stove. The stove was temperamental—it had been temperamental before the Bloom, and now it was practically feral. Half the time the left burner wouldn't catch, and the right one shot up like a blowtorch if you weren't careful. I'd learned to cook by ear, listening for the click-click-click of the ignition, the hiss of the gas, the specific sizzle that meant the heat was right. I'd learned a lot of things by ear, lately. Listening was easier than looking. The beans bubbled. I stirred them with the wooden spoon—the one with the burn mark on the handle, the one I'd brought from the flat because it was the only thing of mine Kael had never touched. It was a petty reason to bring a spoon. I brought it anyway. "Smells good," Finn said, from the corner. "It's beans," I said. "It smells like beans." "Yeah. Good." I divided them into three bowls. I was precise about it—I'd found a rhythm in precision, a kind of comfort. One spoonful for Finn's bowl, one for mine, one for Kael's. One for Finn. One for mine. One for Kael's. The tin emptied faster than I wanted. I scraped the last of the sauce with the spoon and divided it by eye, then went back and took a half-spoonful from Kael's bowl and added it to Finn's. Kael saw me do it. He always saw me do it. He never said anything. We ate in the living room, which was also the bedroom, which was also the only room that wasn't the kitchen. The cottage was small—two rooms and a bathroom that no longer worked. The walls were stone, the kind that sweated in summer and froze in winter. Now, in the gray light of a November that didn't feel like November, they just felt damp. Everything felt damp. The blanket, the cushions, the air itself. The beans were lukewarm. They were perfect. I ate slowly, trying to make it last, but my body had other ideas. The first mouthful hit my stomach and something primal took over—I was chewing faster, swallowing before I'd tasted, my hand moving the spoon like it belonged to someone else. I caught myself, forced a pause. Looked at the others. Finn was eating the way he did everything: carefully, with small bites, as if the food might disappear if he rushed. Kael was eating with his eyes closed. He did that sometimes—not to savour, I think, but to shut something out. The sound of his own need, maybe. The indignity of being a body that required things. When it was done—when the bowls were empty, when the spoons were licked clean, when there was nothing left to delay the silence—Kael stacked the bowls and took them to the kitchen. I heard the tap run, which meant he was rinsing them with one of the last bottles of water. I should have stopped him. I didn't. Some comforts are worth the cost. "How's the book?" I asked Finn. He held it up. The pages were wavy with water damage, the photographs reduced to abstract swirls of blue and black. You could just make out the shape of a jellyfish on one page, its tentacles blurred into the background. "The pictures are gone," he said. "But I remember them." "What's your favourite?" He thought about it. "The anglerfish. The one with the light." "The one that lives in the dark." "Yeah. It makes its own light. So things come to it." "That's not a nice story, Finn." "No," he said. "But it's a good one." I took the book from him, closed it gently, and set it on the floor beside his makeshift bed. The floor was cold—I could feel it through my socks. Everything was cold. The only warmth in the cottage came from the stove, and even that was rationed, burning through their last canisters of gas like a countdown. "We need to talk about tomorrow," Kael said, from the kitchen doorway. "Tomorrow is the same as today," I said. "Tomorrow we have no food." "We have no food today either. We had beans. That's not food, that's a gesture." He looked at me. In the low light, his face was all angles—sharp jaw, deep-set eyes, the shadow of stubble he'd stopped bothering to manage. He looked older than thirty-three. He looked like the kind of person you'd see in a photograph from a hundred years ago, the kind with no smile and too much knowledge in their eyes. "I'll go to Amble," he said. "You'll go nowhere. It's dark." "First light, then." "Kael—" "What's the alternative, El?" His voice was quiet. Not angry. Just tired. "What's the plan, if I don't go?" I didn't have a plan. I'd run out of plans three days ago, when I'd moved the tin of beans from the back of the shelf to the front. I'd been running on momentum since then, on the fumes of routine. Make the soup. Divide the portions. Check the locks. Count the water. Routine was the only thing between us and the edge, and I could feel it fraying, thread by thread, every time Kael looked at me with those patient, waiting eyes. "First light," I said. He nodded. Went back to the window. The Growths pulsed in the darkness outside, their stalks swaying in a wind I couldn't feel. One-two-three. One-two-three. Like breathing. Like something waiting. I pulled the blanket tighter around Finn's shoulders. He was already asleep, or pretending to be. His breathing was shallow, but steady. I put my hand on his forehead—cool. That was good. That was something. From outside, from the base of the wall, came a sound. A wet, fibrous scraping, like something dragging itself along stone. I'd heard it before. We all had. We never talked about it. I sat there in the dark, listening, until the scraping stopped. And then I sat there a while longer, just in case.

I watched him from the door—his shape dissolving into the mist, the line of his back straight and purposeful, the knife on his belt catching no light. He didn't look back. He never looked back when he left. I used to think that was confidence. Now I think it's the opposite: he doesn't look back because he's not sure he'll find us when he returns. It was the one trait he'd got from Mum, not the illness or the watchfulness, but the quiet, private amusement at the absurdity of being alive. I closed the door. Checked the lock. Checked the windows. Checked the boards Kael had nailed over the west-facing wall where the wind came through worst. The cottage was a sieve, honestly—every fix we made revealed two more problems. But the routine of checking was the point. It gave my hands something to do while my brain worked on the real problem, which was the sound my stomach was making, which was the fact that Finn's cough was back, which was the creeping, certain knowledge that Kael would come back empty-handed because there was nothing left to find. "El," Finn said. "Sit down. You're making me nervous." "I'm not making you nervous. You don't get nervous." "I do. I just hide it well." I sat. The chair creaked. It was the kind of cough that had texture—not just air, but something underneath, something with weight. I'd stopped asking him to describe it. I knew what it meant. Without antibiotics, without rest, without *food*, his body was just... wearing away. The cough was the sound of the edges going first. "Read me something," I said. He looked at me. "You don't like the book." "I like when you read it." "You fall asleep." "That's because your voice is boring. Read anyway." He smiled again, that private little smile, and opened the book to a random page. The paper was wavy, the ink blurred, but he knew it by heart—he'd read it so many times the words had imprinted themselves on something deeper than memory. "The hydrothermal vents of the Mid-Atlantic Ridge," he began, in the voice he used for reading aloud, which was different from his talking voice—slower, more deliberate, as if the words needed care, "are home to some of the most extreme life forms on Earth. Giant tube worms, up to two metres in length, thrive in water that would scald human skin. They have no mouths. No stomachs. They survive through a symbiotic relationship with bacteria that live inside them, converting the toxic chemicals from the vents into energy." "Symbiotic," I repeated. "It means they help each other." "I know what it means." "The worms provide the bacteria with a home. The bacteria provide the worms with food. Neither can survive without the other." I looked at him. He was watching me with those too-big eyes, and there was something in his expression I couldn't name—not amusement this time, but something older. Something that didn't belong in the face of a fourteen-year-old. "Why are you reading me that part?" I asked. He shrugged. "It was the page it opened to." "Pick a different page." "You told me to read." "Finn." "Elara." We stared at each other. Then he laughed—a real laugh, short and surprised, like he'd startled it out of himself. I wanted to be angry, but the sound of his laughter was so rare these days that I just sat there, letting it fill the room, letting it push back the silence for a moment. "Tell me about the anglerfish again," I said. "The one with the light." "The one that lives in the dark." He settled back against the wall. The blanket made its whispering sound. Outside, the wind picked up, and with it came the low, almost sub-audible hum of the Growths—their stalks vibrating in the current, releasing clouds of spores that caught the light like dust motes in a cathedral. "The anglerfish lives in the deep ocean," Finn said. "Miles down, where no sunlight reaches. Most creatures down there are blind. There's no need for eyes. But the anglerfish has a light—a little glowing lure, dangling from its head. It moves through the dark, swinging that light, and things come to it. Fish, shrimp, smaller creatures. They see the light and they swim toward it, and the anglerfish eats them." "That's horrible," I said. "That's survival." "They're the same thing, sometimes." He looked at me. I looked at him. The cottage creaked around us, and the wind moaned through the cracks in the walls, and somewhere outside, a Growth pulsed in the gray. --- Kael was gone for two days. The first day was bearable. I cleaned the cottage—not because it needed it, but because cleaning was a kind of prayer. I wiped surfaces that didn't need wiping. I folded the blanket. I sorted the few remaining items in the pantry: three bottles of water, a tin of sweetcorn I'd forgotten about (a small, stupid miracle), a packet of salt with maybe a tablespoon left. I inventoried everything, twice. I made lists in my head. I made plans. I made plans for the plans. The second day was worse. Finn's fever came back around noon—his forehead hot and dry, his eyes glassy. I gave him water. I put a damp cloth on his head. I sat beside him and read to him from the book, stumbling over the scientific names, and he corrected me without opening his eyes. "Riftia," he murmured. "Not Rift-ee-a. Rift-ee-uh." "Riftia," I repeated. "The tube worm." "Lives in boiling water. Has no mouth. Symbiotic." "Symbiotic," I said. "I remember." He slept. I sat. The cottage breathed around us—creaking, whispering, the walls expanding and contracting with the temperature like a living thing. I watched the door. I watched the window. I watched the Growths sway in the wind, their pale stalks bending and straightening like something doing tai chi, slow and deliberate and utterly without hurry. They were closer than yesterday. I was sure of it. The nearest cluster had been twenty metres from the door; now it was fifteen, maybe twelve. They didn't move when you watched them—nothing so obvious. They just... were closer, the next time you looked. Like they grew in the spaces between glances. The sound came back that night. The scraping at the wall. I sat up in the dark, listening—not afraid, exactly, but alert, the way you're alert when you hear a strange noise in a house you know. The scraping was rhythmic, patient. I heard his boots on the path—the specific sound of his walk, heavy and slightly uneven, favoring his left leg, which he'd hurt years ago on a boat and never properly rested. I was at the door before he reached it. He was empty-handed. Of course he was. His face was gray, his lips cracked, and there was a look in his eyes I hadn't seen before—not exhaustion, but something beyond it. A kind of blankness, like a window with the curtains drawn. "Amble's gone," he said. "It's all gone. The whole coast." "The buildings?" "Still there. Everything inside them is... it's all gray. Covered. Like mold, but thicker. He stood in the middle of the room and didn't move, and I saw it then—the sleeve of his jacket was torn, and underneath, on his left forearm, there was a wound. Not deep. A scrape, maybe, or a graze. I brushed against one. It was dark, I didn't see it." "Let me see." "It's nothing, El." "Let me *see.*" He held out his arm. I peeled back the torn fabric. The wound was maybe three inches long, a shallow furrow in the skin, already closing. But the scab—God, the scab. It was the same color as the Growths outside, that pale, fleshy gray, and it had texture, tiny ridges like the surface of a mushroom cap. I touched it, gently. It was warm. "Does it hurt?" I asked. "No." "Does it itch?" "No. I can't feel it at all." I looked at him. He looked at me. His eyes were steady, but I could see it—the thing he wasn't saying. The fear he'd folded up and put away, the way he folded everything, neat and square and out of sight. "I'll clean it," I said. "There's no water to spare." "There's enough." I cleaned it. I wrapped it with a strip of cloth from an old shirt. He watched me do it, his face blank, and when I was done, he sat in his chair by the window and looked out at the Growths with an expression I couldn't read. Finn was asleep in the corner. His breathing was shallow, his face flushed. The tin of sweetcorn sat on the shelf like a small, golden taunt. "El," Kael said, without turning. "There's nothing out there. I walked for two days. There's nothing." "I know." "So what do we do?" I looked at the tin. I looked at Finn. I looked at the window, where the Growths pulsed in the gray, their stalks swaying, their spores drifting in the air like the first suggestion of snow. "I don't know," I said. # Chapter 3: First Bite The sweetcorn bought us a day. Maybe less. I divided it three ways—four spoonfuls each, cold, straight from the tin. Finn ate his without complaint but left a single kernel in the bottom of the bowl. I ate it before he could change his mind. That night, I couldn't sleep. Not the ordinary kind of insomnia where your brain won't turn off, but the other kind—the physical kind, where your body is so hungry it's forgotten how to rest. And underneath it all, the hum. The Growths. Always the Growths. I'd been trying not to look at them for weeks. They were just *there*, part of the landscape, like the rocks and the sea and the gray sky. But that night, in the dark, with my stomach folding in on itself, I couldn't stop seeing them. Not with my eyes—with my brain. The way they pulsed. The way their stalks bent and straightened. The texture of them, up close—I'd seen it once, when one had grown over the windowsill before Kael tore it away. The flesh had been pale, almost white, with thin lines running through it like the grain in wood. Or like the grain in meat. I sat up. The thought was there before I could stop it. Not as words, but as a feeling—a pull, low in my gut, like a hook. I looked at the window. The Growths were right there. They were *right there*, and they were made of something that had structure, that had fiber, that had— No. No. That was insane. That was— Finn coughed. A long one, deep and wet, the kind that sounds like something tearing. He curled in on himself, his thin shoulders shaking, and I went to him, put my hand on his back, felt the bones like bird wings under my palm. "Water," he whispered. I gave him water. He drank, and the cough subsided, and he settled back against the wall with his eyes closed, his face gray in the gray light. I put my hand on his forehead. Still hot. Hotter, maybe. I sat there for a long time, listening to him breathe. Then I got up and went to Kael. --- "Kael." I shook his shoulder. He woke the way he always did—suddenly, completely, like a light switching on. His hand went to the knife on his belt before his eyes were fully open. "What is it?" "I need you to bring me one." He stared at me. "One what." "You know what." The silence that followed was the loudest sound I'd ever heard. He sat up, his back against the wall, and looked at me with an expression that was not surprise, not horror, but something worse: recognition. Like he'd been waiting for me to say it. Like he'd known I would, eventually. "El," he said. "No." "Look at him." I didn't point at Finn. I didn't need to. "Look at him, Kael. He's dying." "I know." "We're all dying." "I know that too." "So bring me one." He shook his head. But the shake was slow, uncertain, like his body was arguing with itself. I pressed. "Small," I said. "Just a small piece. From the stalk. Not the outer rind—the inner part, where it's pale. I've seen the texture. I know what it looks like." "You're talking about this like it's a recipe." "I'm talking about this like it's the only option we have." He stood up. Paced the length of the cottage—three steps, turn, three steps. His hands were clenched at his sides, and I could see the tendons in his neck, tight as ropes. I knew that posture. He was fighting himself, and I was winning, and he hated me for it. "If it kills us," he said. "Then we die full." He looked at me. Something in his face changed—not softened, but broke. A fracture, small and precise, like a hairline crack in a plate. He picked up his knife. He went to the door. He paused with his hand on the latch. "If I don't come back," he said. "You'll come back." "El." "You'll come back, Kael. You always come back." He opened the door. The cold hit us both. Outside, the Growths pulsed in the darkness, their stalks swaying, their spores drifting like a mist that had forgotten how to settle. He was gone for ten minutes. When he returned, he was carrying a piece of Growth in his left hand, held away from his body like something radioactive. It was about the size of a fist, pale and glistening, and it looked— It looked like a scallop. That was the thought that arrived, uninvited and unwelcome. The color, the texture, the faint, pearlescent sheen. Like a scallop, if a scallop had been grown in a grave. "It was easy to cut," Kael said. His voice was strange. "It didn't... there was no resistance." "Put it on the counter." He put it on the counter. We both stared at it. It sat there, pale and wet, and it pulsed faintly—I wasn't imagining it. There was a rhythm, slow and steady, like a heartbeat winding down. "I'll need the knife," I said. He handed it over. His hand was shaking. I washed the blade with the last of the bottled water—a waste, but I couldn't do this with a dirty knife. Then I cut into the piece. The flesh gave way with almost no pressure, parting like soft cheese, and the inside was— Different. The outer layer was dense, almost rubbery, but the inside was lighter, more delicate. It had the texture of a raw mushroom crossed with something silkier. The smell was faint: earthy, briny, with a sharp note underneath that I couldn't place. Not rotten. Not chemical. Just... alien. I sliced a piece no bigger than my thumbnail. Then I heated the pan—the last of the gas, the burner clicking and catching on the third try. The slice hit the hot metal and sizzled, and the smell— God, the smell. It was like every good smell I'd ever known, compressed into a single note. Bread baking. Onions caramelizing. The sea on a warm day. It filled the cottage in seconds, and I heard Kael make a sound behind me—not a word, just a sound, low in his throat. I cooked it for thirty seconds on each side. No seasoning—there was nothing left. Just the heat and the flesh and the smell that was making my hands shake so hard I nearly dropped the pan. I put it on a plate. Looked at it. Looked at Kael. "Together," I said. He came to stand beside me. We looked down at the piece of flesh, golden-brown at the edges, pale in the center, still faintly pulsing even though it was cooked. "If this is the last thing I ever eat—" he began. "It won't be," I said. "Eat." We ate. The taste was— There are no words. I'm a cook. I've spent my life trying to describe how things taste, and I have no words for this. It wasn't delicious. It was *satisfying*, in a way that bypassed the tongue entirely and went straight to something deeper—to the blood, to the bones, to the hollow place in the center of me that had been empty for so long I'd forgotten it existed. It tasted like being full. It tasted like the memory of being full, made real. It tasted like— "More," Finn said. I turned. He was sitting up in the corner, his eyes wide, his face flushed, and he was looking at the pan with an expression I'd never seen on him before. Not hunger. *Need.* "There's more," I said. "I'll cook more." I sliced the rest. I cooked it in batches—thin pieces, quick sear, barely thirty seconds a side. The smell filled the cottage, and the taste filled us, and for ten minutes, there was no sound but the sizzle of the pan and the quiet, desperate sounds of three people eating something they should not have been eating, something that should not have been food, something that tasted like the opposite of everything we'd been feeling for months. When it was done, we sat in silence. The pan was empty. The plate was clean. My stomach was full—not the aching, temporary fullness of scraps, but a deep, settled warmth that spread through my limbs like slow water. Finn's color was better. I could see it even in the low light—the gray in his cheeks replaced by something closer to pink. His eyes were clearer. He was sitting up straight, and his breathing was steady, and when he looked at me, he was smiling. "That was good," he said. I went to the sink. I washed the pan. I washed the knife. I scrubbed my hands until the water ran clear, and then I scrubbed them again, and then I looked up and saw my reflection in the dark water in the basin. I was smiling. I stopped. Pressed my lips together. Tried to make my face do something else—anything else. But the smile kept coming back, pulling at the corners of my mouth, and in the dark water, my reflection looked calm and satisfied and utterly, completely wrong. Kael was standing by the door, looking out. He hadn't spoken since the meal. His left hand was pressed against the glass, and I could see the gray scab on his arm, the cloth wrapping fallen away, and in the light from the window, it looked like it had grown. "Kael," I said. He didn't turn. "Don't," he said. "Don't say it was good." "I wasn't going to." "Yes, you were." I closed my eyes. The warmth was still there, spreading through me, and under it, something else—something smaller, quieter, like a second heartbeat, just beginning.

PURPLE PROSE: The prose is restrained. There are moments of heightened language, but they're earned and specific rather than decorative. The "hook, low in my gut" for the pull toward eating the Growth is appropriate given the fishing context and the character's situation. The "fracture, small and precise, like a hairline crack in a plate" for Kael's expression is well-chosen given Elara's domestic frame of reference. No metaphors feel egregiously forced. WELL-EARNED LIGHTNESS OR DARKNESS: The darkness is well-earned. The chapter doesn't rush to horror—it builds through the mundane (the insomnia, the negotiation, the cooking) to the quietly devastating (the smile, the scab, the second heartbeat). The "cozy" elements—the warmth spreading through limbs, the full stomach, Finn's improved color—are genuinely comforting before the horror reasserts itself. This tonal balance is the hardest thing to achieve in cozy-horror, and the chapter manages it. CHARACTERS CONSISTENT WITH PROFILE: Elara's control, her precision, her willingness to use Kael, her mean streak ("You'll come back, Kael. You always come back"—this is slightly cruel in its certainty), all track. Kael's terror-that-does-it-anyway, his silent resentment, his refusal to speak after the meal, all track. Finn's morbid curiosity becoming "need" tracks with his profile as the most adaptable and the first to change. FOLLOWED CHAPTER PLAN: The chapter follows the plan closely and faithfully. The chapter delivers on its plan. FAITHFUL TO WRITING PROMPT: The chapter is faithful to the cozy-horror post-apocalypse survival prompt. The domestic and the monstrous share the same breath throughout. The kitchen is the site of horror. The cooking is simultaneously survival, violence, love, and corruption. MINOR CRITICISMS: "The silence that followed was the loudest sound I'd ever heard" is a cliché that a writer of this caliber should have avoided. The opening paragraph (the sweetcorn) is slightly abrupt as a transition—it assumes the reader knows about the sweetcorn from context that isn't in this chapter. # Chapter 4: The New Routine Kael brought the first one to the step and knocked twice. That was how it started. Not a conversation. Not a negotiation. Just two knocks on the door, the sound of boots on stone retreating, and when I opened the door, there it was: a piece of Growth, severed cleanly, pale and glistening on the step like an offering. He'd wrapped it in a piece of cloth so it wouldn't touch the stone. I picked it up. It was warm. That first morning, I didn't know what to do with it. The impulse in the dark—grab it, cook it, eat it—was one thing. Facing it in the gray daylight, with the pan clean and the gas low and the memory of the taste already fading into something I wasn't sure I'd imagined, was another. I brought it inside. Set it on the counter. Stood there looking at it. It was a different piece than the first. The outer rind was thicker, more textured, with faint lines running through it like the rings of a tree. When I cut into it, the inside was denser, almost meaty. The smell was the same—earthy, briny, that sharp note underneath—but fainter. Older, somehow. Like the difference between fresh bread and day-old. I sliced it thin. Heated the pan. Cooked it. It was good. Not as transcendent as the first time—nothing could be that first bite again, that bypassing of the tongue and going straight to the blood—but good. Deeply, solidly good. The kind of good that makes your shoulders drop and your breath come easier and your brain stop, for just a moment, calculating. I made three portions. We ate in the living room, and nobody said anything, and that silence was different from the silences before. It wasn't empty. It was full, in the way a mouth is full. --- After that, it became a routine. And I learned something about myself that I didn't know, or maybe that I'd always known but never had reason to examine: I am a cook. Give me an ingredient, and I will find a way. The second day, Kael brought a larger piece. The outer rind was tough, almost leathery, but the inner flesh was softer, more delicate. I treated it like calamari—a quick, hot sear, no more than twenty seconds a side. It curled at the edges, crisped slightly, and when I tasted it, there was a sweetness I hadn't expected. Like scallops, I thought again. Like the best scallop I'd ever had, if the scallop had grown in the dark and fed on nothing but time. The third day, I asked Kael to bring me a piece from closer to the base of the stalk. He gave me a look—the look, the one that said *I am doing this for you and I need you to know that I hate it*—but he brought it. This piece was different: denser, with a texture almost like braised beef. I cooked it low and slow on the last of the gas, and it fell apart in the pan, and the smell filled the cottage so completely that Finn came out of his corner to watch. "It smells like Sunday," he said. "Don't," I said. "It does." "I know it does. Don't." I was learning the anatomy of the things. The outer rind was good for nothing—too tough, too bitter, with a texture like boiled leather. But the inner layers varied. Close to the stalk, the flesh was dense and savory. Further out, near the fronds, it was lighter, more delicate, almost translucent. I found that if I sliced the translucent parts paper-thin and seared them for just a few seconds, they crisped like the skin on a roast potato, and the taste was— I was doing it again. Describing the taste. Building a vocabulary for something that shouldn't have a vocabulary. I caught myself, once, mentally pairing a piece of Growth with the word *umami*, and I had to put the knife down and press my palms against the counter until the urge passed. But it didn't pass. It never passed. It just got quieter, and then it got normal, and then it got easy, and that was the most frightening thing of all. --- "Where do you want the next one?" Kael asked, on the fourth morning. He was standing in the doorway, his knife on his belt, his jacket zipped to the chin. The gray scab on his arm was still there, still wrapped in cloth, but he'd stopped mentioning it. I'd stopped asking. That was part of the routine too—the things we didn't talk about. "Near the base again," I said. "But not from the same one. Find a different cluster." "Why?" "Different ones taste different. I want to compare." He stared at me. "You want to *compare*." "Flavor profiles vary. It's like mushrooms—what they grow on affects the taste." "You're talking about them like they're ingredients." "They are ingredients, Kael. That's what they are now." He left. I heard his boots on the path, the specific rhythm of his walk, and I stood at the counter with the knife in my hand and waited for the sound of it to fade. Finn was in the corner, watching me. He'd been doing that more—watching. Not with the wary, careful observation of a sick child, but with something else. Interest, maybe. Or patience. "You're humming," he said. I stopped. I hadn't realized I was. It was a tune without a tune—a fragment of melody that didn't go anywhere, circling back on itself like a path in a garden. "Sorry," I said. "Don't be sorry. I like it." "It's not a real song." "I know. That's why I like it." I looked at him. His color was better than it had been in months—the gray gone from his cheeks, his eyes clear and bright. His cough was almost gone. He was sitting up straight, his book open on his lap, and there was something in his posture that was new: a steadiness. A groundedness. Like he'd found something to hold onto. "How's the chest?" I asked. "Good. Really good." "Let me hear you breathe." He took a deep breath. It was clean—no rattle, no catch. Just air, going in and out, easy as anything. I put my hand on his forehead. Cool. Perfectly cool. "That's good," I said. "Yeah," he said. "It is." He went back to his book. I went back to the counter. The knife was in my hand, and the Growth was on the board, and I was humming again—quietly, so quietly I could barely hear it myself. A tune without a tune. A sound that didn't belong to me, but that felt, somehow, like mine. --- Kael was different. Not in the ways that mattered—not on the surface. He still did his perimeter checks. He still sat by the window, watching the Growths with that steady, unreadable expression. He still brought me what I asked for, left it on the step, knocked twice. But there were cracks. On the fifth morning, he came back without a piece. He stood in the doorway, his knife clean, his hands empty. "There weren't any," he said. "What do you mean, there weren't any?" "I mean I couldn't find any. The clusters by the rocks are gone." "Gone where?" "Just gone. Like they moved." "Growths don't move." "I know they don't move. I'm telling you what I saw." I looked at him. He was standing in the doorway with his hands at his sides, and there was something in his face I hadn't seen before—a flicker, quick and gone, like a fish turning in deep water. Not fear. Something else. Something that looked, for just a moment, like loss. "I'll try further up the coast," he said. "Be careful." "I'm always careful." He left. I stood at the counter, the knife in my hand, and I thought: *He couldn't find any.* And then I thought: *He didn't look.* And then I thought: *No. That's not fair. He looked. He just didn't want to find them.* That night, he slept by the door as usual, but I woke in the dark to a sound I didn't recognize—a low, rhythmic murmur, almost too quiet to hear. I lay still, listening. It was coming from Kael's corner. Not snoring. Not breathing. Something else. A sound like words, but without shape, like language before it learns to mean. I listened until it stopped. Then I listened a while longer, just in case. In his corner, Finn was not sleeping. I could see the gleam of his eyes in the dark, open and watchful, fixed on the ceiling. He was smiling. "It's okay," he whispered. "He's just talking to them." "Talking to who?" Finn didn't answer. He closed his eyes and turned to the wall, and the cottage settled around us, creaking and whispering and humming with a sound I was beginning to recognize as the sound of something becoming something else. Outside, the Growths pulsed in the darkness. One-two-three. One-two-three. I pulled the blanket up to my chin and listened to them breathe.

# Chapter 5: The Changes The stain appeared on a Tuesday. I think it was a Tuesday. The days had started to bleed together, marked only by meals—Growth in the morning, Growth at midday, Growth at night. Three meals a day. We were eating better than we had since before the Bloom, and the irony of that was not lost on me, but it was getting quieter, the way ironies do when they settle in and make themselves at home. I was reaching for the knife when I noticed. My fingertips, the first two on each hand, were gray. Not dirty-gray—the kind of gray you get on your hands from handling charcoal, which scrubs off. This was in the skin itself, a faint, permanent discoloration, like the ghost of a bruise. I held my hand up to the light from the window. The gray had texture, too—a faint roughness, barely perceptible, like very fine sandpaper. I rubbed my thumb against my forefinger. The sensation was muted. Not numb, exactly, but... distant. Like touching something through a thin glove. I looked at the knife. Looked at my fingers. Then I picked up the knife and cut the Growth on the board, because dinner wasn't going to make itself. --- The memory thing started around the same time. Kael was telling a story. He did that now, in the evenings—not because he wanted to, but because I think he needed to prove something. That the old world still existed, somewhere, in some form. That there was a before. "It was the herring season," he said. He was in his chair by the window, his hands wrapped around an empty mug he'd taken to holding, the way some people hold cigarettes. "Must have been... God, 2019? The boats were going out every morning, four, five in the morning, and the harbour stank of fish so bad you could taste it." "What did it taste like?" Finn asked. "Salty. Wet. Like money, if money was made of fish." Finn smiled. I tried to picture it—the harbour, the boats, the smell—but the image wouldn't form. Not the way it used to. I could remember that there *was* a harbour, that there *were* boats, but the details were gone. The color of the water. The sound of the ropes. The specific way the light hit the pilings at a certain hour. All of it dissolved into a general impression, like a photograph left in the sun. "What color was the water?" I asked. Kael looked at me. "What?" "The water. In the harbour. What color was it?" "Blue, El. The water was blue." "Dark blue or light blue?" "I don't... it was blue. Depending on the weather." I nodded. But the question had opened something—a door I hadn't meant to open. I tried to picture my mother's face and got as far as: dark hair, glasses, a shape that might have been a smile or might have been a frown. I tried to picture the kitchen in the flat—the one I'd cooked in for seven years, the one where I'd learned everything—and got: a counter. A stove. A window that looked out on something. All of it stripped of detail, reduced to a sketch. But the taste of Growth—that I could recall with perfect clarity. The specific sear of the first bite. The way the edges crisped. The warmth that spread through the blood like slow syrup. I could taste it right now, sitting here, with a precision that made every other memory feel like a watercolor in the rain. "El?" Kael was watching me. "You all right?" "Fine. Tell the story." "The herring—" "The harbor stank. You said. What happened next?" He kept talking. I kept listening. But the story slid off me like water, and what stayed was the taste in my mouth—not of the Growth I'd eaten hours ago, but of the one I'd eat tomorrow, already forming in my mind, already perfect. --- Kael's wound healed. Not in the way wounds heal—slowly, reluctantly, with scabs and itching and the gradual knitting of skin. It healed fast. Too fast. One morning the gray scab was there, textured and strange; the next, it was gone, replaced by a patch of skin that was smooth and pale and faintly luminous in certain light. He didn't unwrap the bandage for me to see. I saw it by accident—he was changing the cloth wrapping, his sleeve pushed up, and I caught a glimpse before he saw me looking and pulled the sleeve down. "It's fine," he said. "I saw it, Kael." "It's healed." "I saw what healed looks like." We looked at each other. The cottage was quiet. Finn was asleep, or pretending to be, his breathing even and deep, deeper than it used to be, like he was drawing air from somewhere further down. "It doesn't hurt," Kael said. "I know." "I can't feel it at all." "I know that too." He pushed his sleeve up. Held out his arm. The patch was maybe three inches long, smooth and pale, the exact color of the inner flesh of a Growth. It didn't look like scar tissue. It didn't look like skin. It looked like something in between—something that had made a decision about what it wanted to be. "Does it spread?" I asked. "I don't think so." "You don't *think* so?" "It's the same size as before. Maybe smaller." "Maybe." "El." His voice was quiet. Not angry. Not scared. Just... level. Like he was reading from a script he'd memorized. "I'm fine. We're fine. Finn is better. You're better. We're all better than we've been in months." He was right. That was the worst part. Finn's cough was gone. His fever was gone. He was eating with an appetite that was almost alarming, and his eyes were clear, and he was moving around the cottage with an energy he hadn't had since the Bloom. Kael was stronger, too—I'd seen him carry a full jerry can of water from the stream without breaking stride, something that would have winded him a month ago. And I— I felt good. That was the word, and it felt dishonest, but there was no other word for it. I felt good. My joints didn't ache. My head was clear. My hands, stained and rough as they were, were steady. I could stand at the counter for hours without fatigue. I could go without sleep and wake feeling rested. I was stronger and sharper and more myself than I had been in years, and the price of that was— The price was what? I looked at my fingertips. Gray. Rough. Muted. I picked up the knife. --- The dreams started that week. Not every night—every other night, maybe, the pattern unpredictable. But always the same dream. I'm standing in a field. There's no sky, or the sky is the same color as the ground, a uniform gray that goes on forever. The ground under my feet is soft, yielding, and when I look down, I see that I'm sinking—not fast, but slowly, like standing in wet sand. Roots are growing from my feet. Not my feet, exactly—from the ends of me, the places where I touch the earth. They're thin and pale, and they're reaching down, and as they go, I can feel what they feel: the texture of the soil, the temperature of the clay, the slow, patient pulse of water moving through rock. It should be terrifying. It isn't. It feels like— It feels like being held. I wake up with dirt under my fingernails. Not gray—brown. Real dirt. I check the floor around my bed. Nothing. I check my hands. The dirt is only there for a moment, then it fades, like a memory. I don't tell the others. Kael tells me, one morning, that he's been dreaming about the sea. Not the post-Bloom sea, but the old one—clean and blue and full of things that weren't trying to eat him. He says he wakes up with the taste of salt on his lips. "Do you think that's normal?" he asks. "I don't think anything is normal anymore." "No," he says. "I suppose not." He goes back to the window. The Growths sway in the wind, and I watch his reflection in the glass—the angle of his jaw, the set of his shoulders, the bandage on his arm, luminous in the morning light. "What were you doing at the window?" "Watching." "Watching what?" "The Growths. They were doing something interesting." "What were they doing?" He thinks about it. His expression is thoughtful, careful, like he's deciding how much to say. "They were reaching," he says. "Toward the house. Not the whole cluster—just a few of them. The ones closest to the wall. "They grow toward warmth." "Yeah," Finn says. "Maybe." He goes back to his book. But I see him, later, at the window, and his hand is pressed flat against the glass, and outside, the nearest Growth is swaying in a wind that isn't there, its stalk bending toward the cottage, toward the warmth, toward the hand. Toward the hand that is gray, and steady, and no longer trembling.

# Chapter 6: The Incident The one Kael brought home that morning was different. I knew it before he set it on the counter. The weight of it—heavier than the others, denser, with a heft that spoke of age. The outer rind was darker, almost brown, and when I turned it over in my hands, I saw something that made me stop. Eyes. Or what looked like eyes. Three of them, clustered near the top of the stalk, each one a small, dark circle in the pale flesh, like the eyes of a potato but smoother, more deliberate. They weren't moving. They weren't seeing. But they were *there*, and looking at them made something in my chest tighten in a way I couldn't name. "Where did you get this?" I asked. "Same place. The cluster near the rocks." "It's different." "They're all different, El. You said so yourself." I set it on the counter. The eyes looked up at the ceiling. Or they looked at me. There was no way to tell. "I don't know about this one," I said. "It's food." "I don't know about this one, Kael." He was standing in the doorway, his knife on his belt, his jacket dusted with gray spores. He hadn't taken it off. He was looking at the Growth on the counter with an expression I'd seen before—not on his face, but on the faces of people in the old world, in the old kitchens, when they'd watch me break down a chicken. Not disgust, exactly. Not fascination. Something in between. Something that was trying to decide what it was allowed to feel. "It's just food," he said again. But his voice was different this time. Quieter. Like he was trying to convince himself. I picked up the knife. --- I cooked it the way I'd cooked the others—thin slices, quick sear, the pan screaming with heat. But this one was different. The flesh was denser, resistant, and when the knife went through, there was a sound—not loud, but there. A faint, high sound, like a note on a glass. The smell was stronger too: earthier, older, with a new note underneath that I couldn't place. Something sweet. Something almost like rot, but not unpleasant. Like the smell of a forest floor after rain. I plated three portions. We sat in the living room. Finn ate first. He always ate first now—he'd stopped waiting for the ritual of starting together, and I'd stopped enforcing it. He took a bite, chewed slowly, and his eyes closed. "It's different," he said. "I know." "Older." "How do you know it's older?" He opened his eyes. Looked at me. In the low light, his irises were darker than they should have been—not brown, but something closer to black, with flecks of gray that might have been a trick of the light. "I can tell," he said. "Can't you?" I could. That was the thing. I could taste the age in it, the way you can taste the age in wine—a depth, a complexity, a sense of time folded into flesh. I didn't want to admit it. Saying it out loud would make it real in a way that eating it didn't. "It's good," Kael said. He was eating mechanically, the way he always did—eyes closed, jaw working, his mind somewhere else. But when he opened his eyes, he looked at the piece on his plate and said, quietly: "It's sad." "Sad?" "It tastes sad." Finn and I looked at each other. Kael stared at his plate, his fork halfway to his mouth, and there was something in his face that I hadn't seen before—a crack, not in his composure, but in his understanding. Like he'd tasted something that wasn't just food. Like he'd tasted a feeling. "Eat," I said. He ate. We all ate. The taste was good—better than good, deep and satisfying, the kind of taste that fills you up in places you didn't know were empty. But Kael's word stayed with me, lodging itself in a corner of my mind like a splinter. Sad. It tasted sad. --- After dinner, Finn went to the window. He did that now—stood there for long stretches, his hand pressed flat against the glass, watching the Growths sway in the darkness. He wasn't afraid of them. He'd stopped being afraid weeks ago, and I'd stopped being able to remember what his fear had looked like. "They're not trying to kill us," he said. Kael was cleaning the knife. He didn't look up. "They're not trying to do anything," I said. "They just grow." "No." Finn's voice was quiet, certain, the voice of someone stating a fact they'd verified through careful observation. "They're curious. I've been watching. They watch back." "Finn," Kael said. "They do. When I'm at the window, they stop moving. The ones closest to the glass—they stop. They reach, but they stop. Like they're waiting for something." "They're waiting for you to open the window so they can kill you," Kael said. His voice was flat. Not angry. Flat. "You don't believe that." "I believe they're monsters, Finn. I believe they destroyed everything. I believe they killed everyone we ever knew." "They didn't kill us." The silence that followed was thick, weighted, like the air before a storm. I put my fork down. The plate was clean. I'd eaten all of it without tasting the last few bites, my mind somewhere else, in a field with no sky, sinking slowly into the earth. "Finn," I said. "Come away from the window." "They're not monsters," he said. He was still looking out, his hand still on the glass. "They're just... here. Like we're here. We're all just here." "Finn." Kael's voice was sharp now. Sharp in a way I hadn't heard before—not the sharpness of anger, but of fear. "Come away from the window." Finn turned. His face was calm. His eyes were dark and clear and very, very steady. "I think they're lonely," he said. Kael stood up. The chair scraped against the floor. He crossed the room in three strides and grabbed Finn's arm—not hard, but firm, pulling him away from the glass. Finn didn't resist. He let himself be pulled, his eyes still on the window, his expression unchanged. "Don't," Kael said. "Don't say that." "Why not?" "Because they're not alive. They're not lonely. They're not *anything*. They're things that grow and kill and spread, and we are eating them because we have no choice, and that's it. That's the end of it." Finn looked at Kael's hand on his arm. Then he looked at Kael's face. Something passed between them—a current, invisible and fast, like the flash of a fish in deep water. "You're scared," Finn said. "I'm not scared." "You count things when you're scared. I've seen you. Your lips move. One-two-three-four." Kael let go of Finn's arm. Stepped back. His face was white. "I'm not scared," he said again. But his voice had changed. It was smaller now, and under the smallness, something was shaking. "You didn't have to eat it," I said. They both looked at me. The words had come out before I could stop them—sharp, precise, surgical. The kind of words I'd promised myself I wouldn't use anymore. The kind that leave marks. "What?" Kael said. "You heard me." "You're the one who cooked it. You're the one who—" "I know what I did. I'm talking about what you did." The silence was worse than before. Worse than any silence I'd ever heard. Kael stood in the middle of the room, his hands at his sides, his face stripped of everything but the one thing he'd been trying to hide for weeks: the knowledge that he'd chosen this. That every bite had been a choice. That he could have said no, and he didn't, and he'd never forgive me for making him realize it. "You didn't have to eat it," I said again. Quieter this time. Not sharp anymore. Just true. He turned. Went to his corner. Sat down with his back to the wall and his hands on his knees and didn't move. Finn went back to the window. I washed the plates. The water was cold. My hands were gray. The Growth with the eyes sat on the counter, the remaining slices already cooling, the flesh congealing in a way that looked, from certain angles, like it was breathing. --- That night, I dreamed of roots. Not the slow, gentle sinking of the previous dreams. This was different. I was standing in the field, and the earth was pulling me down, and the roots were growing from me—not from my feet, but from everywhere. From my hands, my fingers, the tips of my hair. They were thick and pale, and they were reaching, and I could feel what they felt: the soil, the clay, the water moving through rock, and beneath it all, a vast, silent network, connecting everything, pulsing with a rhythm I recognized. One-two-three. One-two-three. I woke with my hand on the wall. Not against it—*on* it. My fingers were spread, pressed flat, and the stone was warm under my palm, and I could feel— Something. A vibration. A pulse. The same rhythm from the dream, slow and steady, coming from inside the wall. From the other side. From the Growths that had been creeping closer, day by day, inch by inch, until they were right there, just on the other side of the stone, pulsing in the dark. I pressed my hand harder. The vibration grew stronger. Not a sound—a feeling. A feeling that traveled up my arm and settled in my chest, quiet and warm and familiar. I stood there for a long time, my hand on the wall, my eyes closed, listening to something that wasn't a heartbeat but felt like one. Outside, the Growths pulsed. Inside, I pulsed with them. It didn't feel like horror. It felt like coming home.

# Chapter 7: The Visitor The knock came at dawn. Not the scrape of a Growth against the wall, which we knew. Not the creak of the cottage settling, which we knew better. This was a knock. Knuckles on wood. Three raps, deliberate and human, a sound so foreign it took me a moment to place it. I was at the counter, preparing the morning meal. The knife was in my hand. Kael was in his chair, staring at nothing. Finn was at the window, his palm flat against the glass, his eyes on the Growths outside. Three raps. Then silence. We looked at each other. Kael's hand went to his knife. I put mine down. "Stay here," Kael said. He went to the door. I followed—not because I didn't trust him, but because I needed to see. The need was physical, a pull in my chest, and I didn't question it. I was past questioning things. Kael opened the door. The man was gaunt. Not starving-gaunt—past that. The kind of gaunt where the body has started to eat itself, where the skin hangs loose and the eyes are too big and the joints stick out like knots in rope. He was soaked from the rain, his clothes clinging to him, and there was a wildness in his eyes that I recognized: the look of someone who has been alone for too long. "Thank God," he said. His voice was cracked, dry, barely a voice at all. "Thank God. I saw the smoke. I didn't think anyone was—" "What do you want?" Kael's voice was flat. Not hostile. Just flat. "Water. Just water. I've been walking for—" "Where from?" "Alnwick. Or what's left of it. It's gone. Everything's gone. The whole town." He was swaying on his feet. Behind me, Finn had turned from the window and was watching with his dark, steady eyes. The stranger's gaze flicked past Kael, past me, to the counter where the Growth lay split open, its pale flesh glistening in the gray light. He went still. "What is that?" he said. "Food," I said. "That's not food." His voice changed. The desperation drained out of it, replaced by something harder. "That's one of them. That's one of the Growths." "It's food," I said again. "You're eating them." He looked at Kael, at me, at Finn. His eyes were wide, and the wildness in them had a new edge—not fear, but something worse. Recognition. "You're eating them. You know what they do to people? You know what happens?" "Do you want water or not?" Kael said. "I've seen it. I've seen what happens. There was a group in Alnwick, they started eating them too—said it was safe, said it was just like mushrooms. Two weeks later they were—God, they were—" "Water," Kael said. "Yes or no." The stranger looked at Kael. Then at me. Then at the Growth on the counter. His mouth was working, the words piling up behind his teeth, and when they came out, they were quiet. Defeated. "You're already gone, aren't you?" he said. Kael hit him. It was fast—a single movement, his fist connecting with the stranger's jaw, sending him stumbling back off the step. The stranger fell, his head hitting the stone path, and Kael was on him, his hands around the man's throat, and the sound he was making— It wasn't a human sound. It was low, guttural, rhythmic, and it came from somewhere deep in Kael's chest, somewhere that didn't have words. The stranger was struggling, his hands clawing at Kael's wrists, and I was standing in the doorway watching, and my first thought was not *stop him*. My first thought was: *He'll attract attention.* "Kael." My voice was calm. Too calm. "Kael, stop." He didn't stop. His hands tightened. The stranger's face was turning red, then purple, his mouth open, his eyes bulging. Finn was behind me, watching over my shoulder, his breathing steady. "Kael." I stepped forward. Put my hand on his shoulder. His muscles were rigid, vibrating, and under my palm, I felt— The pulse. The same rhythm. One-two-three. Coming from inside him, from his muscles, from his blood. "Kael, stop. He's not worth it." Kael's hands loosened. The stranger gasped, coughed, rolled away. He was scrambling backward on his hands and knees, blood running from his nose, his eyes fixed on Kael with an expression of pure terror. "Go," I said to the stranger. "Go now." He went. Stumbling, crawling, then running—down the path, into the gray, disappearing into the mist and the spores and the swaying stalks of the Growths that lined the coast. I watched him until he was gone. Then I looked at Kael. He was standing in the path, his hands at his sides, his chest heaving. His knuckles were bloody—not his blood. The stranger's blood. And in the blood, on his skin, gray spores were blooming. Tiny, delicate structures, like the first suggestion of mold on bread, spreading across his knuckles in real time. He looked at his hands. Looked at me. His face was white. "El," he said. "El, what—" "Come inside." "El, look at my hands—" "Come inside, Kael." He came inside. I closed the door. The cottage was quiet, the only sound the hum of the Growths outside and the slow, steady breathing of Finn, who was back at the window now, his palm on the glass, his eyes on the dark. I took Kael's hands. Washed them with the last of the water. The spores were gone—washed away with the blood—but the skin underneath was different. Softer. Smoother. The gray patch on his arm had grown. It was past his elbow now, a smooth, pale expanse that caught the light like silk. "It's spreading," he said. His voice was hollow. "I know." "What do we do?" I looked at my own hands. Gray fingertips. Rough skin. The muted sensation, the distant touch. "I don't know," I said. But that was a lie. I did know. I'd known since the first bite, since the taste that bypassed the tongue and went straight to the blood. I knew what we were doing. I knew what it was costing. I knew that the cost was rising, day by day, meal by meal, and that soon it would be too high to pay, and we would pay it anyway, because the alternative was a hunger so deep it had no bottom. "We eat," I said. "That's what we do." Kael looked at me. His eyes were wet. Not with tears—with something else, something thicker, something that caught the light. "I hit him," he said. "I know." "I wanted to kill him, El. I wanted to kill him and I don't know why." "I know." "He looked at us and he said we were gone, and I wanted to kill him for saying it." I took his hands. They were shaking. Under my palms, his skin was warm, too warm, and the pulse was there—one-two-three, one-two-three—steady and deep and not entirely his own. "Come," I said. "Sit down." I led him to his chair. He sat. I stood behind him, my hands on his shoulders, and I could feel the pulse traveling up my arms, syncing with my own, and the feeling was— Not right. Not wrong. Just true. The truest thing I'd felt in months. Finn was at the window. He hadn't moved. His hand was on the glass, and outside, the nearest Growth was pressed against the other side, its stalk flat against the pane, its surface pulsing in time with Finn's breath. "Finn," I said. He didn't turn. His eyes were fixed on the Growth, and the Growth was fixed on him, and between them, through the glass, something was passing. Not spores. Not heat. Something else. Something that had no name. "They're not lonely anymore," Finn said. His voice was quiet. Content. "None of us are." The cottage settled around us. The wind moaned. The Growths hummed. And I stood there, my hands on Kael's shoulders, feeling the pulse in his blood sync with the pulse in the wall sync with the pulse in the earth, and I thought: *This is what symbiosis feels like.* And then I thought: *No. This is what dinner feels like.* And then I didn't think at all. I just stood there, in the warm, humming dark, and listened to the sound of something becoming something else, and it sounded like breathing, and it sounded like home.

# Chapter 8: The Meal The stranger's blood was gone by morning. The stone where he'd fallen had been colonized overnight—not by the gray of the Growths, but by small, pale mushrooms, pushing up through the cracks in perfect rows. They looked intentional. Planted. I watched them from the door while the kettle boiled, and I thought: *He should have knocked softer.* Kael hadn't spoken since last night. He was in his chair, his hands on his knees, his eyes on the floor. The gray had spread past his elbow now, up toward his shoulder, visible where his sleeve had ridden up. He didn't cover it. He didn't seem to care. Finn was at the window. He was always at the window now. His palm on the glass, his eyes on the Growths, his lips moving faintly—silently, the way Kael used to count. But Finn wasn't counting. He was listening. I could tell by the tilt of his head, the slight furrow of concentration, the way his breathing slowed to match the rhythm of the things outside. One-two-three. One-two-three. I went back inside. The kettle was screaming. --- I made porridge. Real porridge. The last of the oats, mixed with the last of the water, heated on the last of the gas. It was a gesture—a reaching-back toward something that was slipping away, grain by grain, day by day. I stirred it slowly, watching the oats swell and soften, and the smell was— Nothing. That was the first thing I noticed. The smell was nothing. Not bad, not good. Just absent. Like stirring wallpaper paste. I served three bowls. Set them on the table. Called the others. Finn came first. He sat, looked at the bowl, picked up the spoon. He took a bite. Chewed. His face was blank. "How is it?" I asked. He swallowed. Put the spoon down. "It doesn't taste like anything," he said. "It's porridge. It tastes like porridge." "No. It doesn't." I picked up my own spoon. Took a bite. The oats were warm, soft, slightly gritty—exactly the texture of porridge. But the taste was gone. Not muted, not faint. *Gone.* Like eating the memory of food. Like chewing warm water. I swallowed. The porridge slid down my throat and settled in my stomach like a stone—not heavy, just present. Unwelcome. A foreign object in a space that had learned to expect something else. Kael hadn't touched his. He was staring at the bowl like it had insulted him. "Eat," I said. "Why?" "Because it's food." "It's not food." His voice was quiet. Not angry. Just factual. "It's not food anymore, El." "It's oats. It's water. It's what we used to eat." "We used to eat a lot of things." He pushed the bowl away. The porridge sloshed, thick and gray—everything was gray now, even the food, even the light—and settled back into a flat, featureless surface that reflected nothing. I looked at my bowl. Looked at Finn. Looked at Kael. The three of us sitting at the table with our bowls of nothing, and outside the window, the Growths swaying in the wind, their pale stalks bending and straightening, and the smell of them coming through the cracks in the walls—earthy, briny, alive. "I'll make something else," I said. "There's nothing else to make." "There's always something." I stood up. Went to the counter. The last piece of Growth was there—small, pale, from the inner stalk, the part I liked best. I'd been saving it. Not saving it. Resisting it. There was a difference, once. Now the difference was thin, and getting thinner. I picked it up. It was warm in my hand. Not the warmth of flesh—the warmth of something that was alive, that was breathing, that was connected to something larger, deeper, older than any of us. I could feel the pulse in it. One-two-three. Syncing with my own. "El," Kael said. His voice was different now. Not warning. Not protest. Something quieter. Something that sounded, if I listened closely, like hope. "I know," I said. I sliced it thin. The knife went through like butter, and the flesh parted with that familiar, faint sound—the note on a glass, the sigh of something letting go. The smell hit me: earth, sea, the sharp sweetness of something that should not have been beautiful but was. My mouth watered. My hands steadied. The porridge sat on the table, untouched, forgotten, a relic of a world that was slipping away like sand through fingers that had learned to prefer the feel of stone. I heated the pan. The gas caught on the first try. The slices hit the metal and sizzled, and the sound was— Right. The only right sound in the room. I cooked it the way I'd cooked it that first night—quick sear, no seasoning, just heat and flesh and the alchemy of transformation. The edges crisped. The center stayed pale, tender, barely cooked. The smell filled the cottage, and behind me, I heard Kael inhale. Heard Finn push back his chair. I plated three portions. Brought them to the table. Set them down where the porridge had been—pushing the bowls aside, making room for something that mattered. We looked at each other. The three of us, in the gray light of a morning that didn't feel like morning, with the Growths humming outside and the mushrooms pushing through the stone and the stranger's blood long since washed away but not forgotten, never forgotten. "Together," I said. We ate. The taste was— Home. That was the word. Not the old home—the flat, the kitchen, the harbor, the world that was gone. This home. This room. This table, scarred and stained. This air, thick with spores and salt and the faint, sweet smell of something growing. This body, gray-fingered and strange and no longer entirely mine, but *mine*, fed and full and alive in a way that the old life had never made me feel. I watched Kael take his first bite. His eyes closed. His shoulders dropped. The tension he'd been carrying for months—years—since before the Bloom, since before me, since the first time he'd realized that the world was a place that took things and never gave them back—drained out of him like water from a sink. His face changed. Not a lot. Just enough. The hard lines softened. The jaw unclenched. Something in his eyes, behind the closed lids, shifted from resistance to acceptance. He chewed. Swallowed. Opened his eyes. "Better?" I asked. He looked at me. Nodded. Didn't speak. Didn't need to. Finn was eating slowly, savoring each bite, his eyes half-closed. He looked— Peaceful. That was the word. Not happy, not sad. Peaceful. Like a creature in its element. Like a fish in deep water. Like a thing that had stopped fighting what it was and found, in the surrender, a kind of freedom. When we were done, the plates were clean. The cottage was warm. The porridge sat on the counter, congealing, forgotten. Outside, the Growths pulsed, and I could feel them—not see them, not hear them, but *feel* them, the way you feel your own heartbeat, the way you feel the ground under your feet. They were there. I was here. And the distance between there and here was narrowing, day by day, meal by meal, until it was just a line, and then a crack, and then nothing at all. I cleared the plates. Washed them. The water was cold, but I didn't mind. I didn't mind the cold anymore. I didn't mind the gray. I didn't mind the silence, or the spores, or the stranger who had come to the door and called us gone, because he was right, and being right hadn't saved him, and it wouldn't save anyone. I was at the counter, my hands in the water, when I felt it—a shift, deep and subtle, like the turning of a tide. The pulse in the wall quickened. The hum outside rose, just slightly, in pitch. I looked up. Through the window, I could see the Growths swaying faster, their stalks bending toward the cottage, toward the warmth, toward us. Kael saw it too. He was at the window, his hand on the glass, his gray arm luminous in the light. He wasn't afraid. I could see it in the set of his shoulders, the tilt of his head. He was watching them the way you watch something you understand. Finn was beside him. Their hands were side by side on the glass—Kael's large and scarred, Finn's small and gray, and mine, joining them, cool against the pane. Three hands, three pulses, three breaths, all synced to the same rhythm. Outside, the Growths swayed. Inside, we swayed with them. Not moving—not physically. But shifting, in some deeper way, in some way that had no language yet but was learning one, word by word, breath by breath. I looked at my reflection in the glass. My face was the same—plain, watchful, the scar on my chin, the dark hair escaping its tie. But my eyes were different. Darker. Steadier. The eyes of someone who had stopped looking for the way back and started, instead, to look forward. "El," Kael said. "Yeah." "Is this..." He didn't finish. He didn't need to. I looked at the Growths, swaying in the gray light. I looked at Finn, peaceful and strange and no longer a child, not really. I looked at Kael, who had followed me into this and would follow me out of it, if there was an out, and who would stay if there wasn't. I thought about the first bite. The taste that bypassed the tongue and went straight to the blood. The warmth that spread like slow syrup. The memory of hunger, already fading, already distant, like a story someone had told me about a life I'd lived a long time ago. "It tastes like coming home," I said. Kael's hand pressed harder against the glass. Finn's breathing slowed. Outside, the Growths pulsed—one-two-three, one-two-three—and the sound of it was the sound of my own heart, and the sound of the wall, and the sound of the earth, and the sound of something older and deeper and more patient than any of us, waiting, not with hunger, but with something that felt, if I listened closely enough, like invitation. I didn't pull away. The kettle had long since gone cold. The porridge sat untouched. The knife lay clean on the counter, its work done, its purpose fulfilled. And in the gray light of a morning that was no longer quite morning, the three of us stood at the window, our hands on the glass, our breath fogging the pane, and watched the world we had become part of sway and pulse and reach toward us, not to consume, but to welcome. It tasted like coming home. And the door, I realized, had been open for a long time.

Judge Response:
[Analysis] This is a strong final chapter that largely delivers on the plan's ambitions, though with some notable weaknesses worth examining carefully. The chapter opens with a genuinely unsettling image—the stranger's blood replaced by "small, pale mushrooms, pushing up through the cracks in perfect rows"—and the narrator's cold, almost sociopathic response ("He should have knocked softer") is exactly the kind of voice deterioration the plan called for. This is effective and earned. The porridge sequence is the chapter's strongest section. The idea that the old food has become tasteless—not bad, just absent—is a clever inversion of the expected horror. "Like eating the memory of food" is a phrase that genuinely lands. The clinical observation that the porridge "settled in my stomach like a stone—not heavy, just present. Unwelcome. A foreign object in a space that had learned to expect something else" is precise and disturbing without being overwrought. Kael's dialogue is sparse and effective: "It's not food anymore, El." This is one of the better lines in the chapter—factual, resigned, and carrying the weight of everything that's happened. The exchange is brief but does real work. However, the chapter has significant problems in its second half. The plan called for an ending that is "ambiguous but not beautiful" and explicitly warned against "neat thematic resolution" and "poetic transcendence." The chapter violates this repeatedly. The final third becomes increasingly purple and transcendent: "the sound of something older and deeper and more patient than any of us, waiting, not with hunger, but with something that felt, if I listened closely enough, like invitation." This is exactly the kind of symbolic, beautiful resolution the plan said to avoid. The final image—three hands on the glass, swaying in sync with the Growths, the door "open for a long time"—is visually striking but emotionally tidy. It resolves the ambiguity rather than sustaining it. The plan wanted the reader to feel uncertain whether Elara is still Elara; instead, the ending feels like a peaceful surrender, almost a benediction. "It tasted like coming home" repeated twice, with the final line about the open door, tips from ambiguity into something closer to acceptance-as-transcendence. The prose in the final section becomes noticeably more strained. "The distance between there and here was narrowing, day by day, meal by meal, until it was just a line, and then a crack, and then nothing at all" is the kind of accumulating metaphor that sounds profound but doesn't quite hold up to scrutiny—a line becoming a crack becoming nothing is a confused spatial metaphor. Similarly, "the alchemy of transformation" is redundant (alchemy is transformation), and "the hard lines softened. The jaw unclenched. Something in his eyes, behind the closed lids, shifted from resistance to acceptance" is telling rather than showing. The Finn characterization is consistent with his profile—peaceful, strange, no longer quite a child—but he's given very little to do in this chapter beyond sitting at the window and eating. His dialogue ("It doesn't taste like anything") is good, but he fades into the background for most of the chapter. The plan specified that Elara would serve porridge as "a gesture toward the old world," then cook Growth when it fails—this is followed faithfully. The plan also specified that the chapter should end with Kael's face showing "acceptance" and the final line about "coming home"—this is executed almost exactly as planned, which is both a strength (fidelity to plan) and a weakness (the plan's ending was always the most vulnerable to becoming too neat, and the execution doesn't find ways to complicate it). The voice deterioration is present but inconsistent. Early in the chapter, Elara's voice is appropriately flat and strange. By the end, it has become almost lyrical in a way that feels more like authorial intrusion than character voice. The plan called for the voice to "deteriorate or evolve in ways the reader can feel but not fully articulate"—instead, the evolution is quite articulable: she's become a nature mystic. The dialogue is generally sparse and functional, which suits the story. There's no weak dialogue per se, but there's also not much of it. Overall: a chapter that executes its plan faithfully and contains genuinely strong passages, but undermines its own stated goals in the final third by reaching for transcendence when it should have stayed in the uncomfortable, unresolved dark.
