# Chapter 1: In Which a Man Enters a Bookshop The rain came sideways off the estuary, and the Co-op bag was cutting into Rhys's fingers, and the man with the camera was standing by the car park wall pretending to look at his phone. Rhys knew the posture. You don't spend twenty years in front of cameras without learning the shape of a man who's waiting. The slightly turned body. The phone held at chest height. The stillness that isn't relaxed. He pulled his beanie down, turned his collar up, and pushed through the nearest open door. A bell. The smell of old paper and something warm — a wood burner, maybe, or just the particular enclosed smell of a room that's been full of books for a long time. Narrow aisles. Shelves to the ceiling. A cat on the counter — calico, unimpressed, watching him with the flat regard of something that's seen better things walk through that door. A woman was shelving paperbacks in the far aisle, her back to him. Brown hair, half-up with a clip that was losing its argument with gravity. Sleeves pushed up. "Sorry," Rhys said, and heard himself do the thing — the warmth switched on like a light, the voice pitched to charm. "Just getting out of the rain. Is that alright?" "Shop's open," she said, without turning around. "That's generally how it works." Right. He shifted the Co-op bag to his other hand and looked around properly. It was a good room. Small, cluttered in the way that suggested someone knew what they were doing, each shelf labelled in neat handwriting. A sign above the counter said *Bwthyn y Llyfrau*. Below it, sellotaped slightly crooked: *Yes, we have a cat. No, he doesn't like you.* "I like your cat," Rhys said. "He's not my cat. He's a freelancer." "Does he have a name?" "Dylan." "Of course he does." Rhys grinned. The grin that worked on chat show hosts, on directors, on everyone. "We're in Laugharne. I'm surprised he's not called Thomas." "He was. For the first week. Then we realised he answered to nothing, so it didn't matter." She turned. Shoved a paperback into the gap on the shelf without looking. Brown eyes. Watchful. She clocked him — he saw the recognition move through her face, not as shock or excitement but as a quiet piece of information received and filed. "Are you looking for something?" "Just browsing. If that's alright." "Browse away." He drifted down an aisle. Pulled a book out, looked at the cover, put it back. Turned another one over. Picked up a ceramic owl from a display shelf, examined it, put it back facing the wrong way. Did not notice. She did. "So," he said, from behind a shelf of crime fiction, "have you been open long?" "Three years." "And before that?" "Before that, the shop wasn't open." He laughed. She didn't. Not because she was trying not — she just didn't. He rounded the shelf and leaned against the end of it. "Look, I'll be honest. I'm not really browsing. I mean, I am, but — it's nice in here. It's warm. I've been walking around in that—" he gestured vaguely at the window, at the rain, at the general concept of weather, "—for about an hour." "The Co-op's warm too." "The Co-op doesn't have—" he gestured at the shelves, the cat, the room, searching for the word. "This." "Overpriced paperbacks and a cat with behavioural problems?" "Character," he said. "It's got character." She looked at him for a moment. Something in her face shifted — not softening, exactly, but a slight change of angle, as if she'd tilted the picture to see it differently. Then it was gone. "Do you want a cup of tea?" she said. "Yes. God, yes." "Kettle's through there. Milk's in the fridge. Mugs are on the hook." He blinked. "You want me to —" "You said you wanted tea. I told you where the kettle is. I'm not a waitress." He made the tea. Her mug said Cymru on it. He chose a plain blue one and made hers black, no sugar, because he'd seen her make one earlier. Brought them through. She was back at the counter now, stamping a date into the inside cover of a paperback, and didn't look up when he set the mug beside her. "You made it right," she said. "Black, no sugar. I noticed." "Most people don't." "Most people aren't paying attention." She looked up. Held his gaze for a beat — the first time she'd really looked at him directly, and it was like being read. Not admired. Not assessed. Read, the way she'd read the spine of a book: quickly, accurately, for information. "I should recommend something," she said. "Since you're here. Since you're not browsing." "I'm browsing now. I've got tea. I'm committed." She came out from behind the counter. Moved down a specific aisle, pulled a book from a specific place. She held it the way she held all of them — spine in her left hand, the pages fanned gently with her right thumb, like she was testing its pulse. "Here." He took it. Looked at the cover. A novel he'd never heard of, by a writer he'd never heard of. A woman standing on a coastline. The title was a single word he didn't recognise. "This is — what's this?" "Read it first. Then ask." "Can I at least know what it's about?" "You can know what it's about when you've read it. That's how books work." He looked at the book. Looked at her. The tea was too strong — he'd made it too strong — but he drank it anyway. "How much?" "Fiver." He gave her a tenner. She wrapped the book in brown paper from a roll under the counter, quick and practised, and handed it across. Their fingers touched. It was nothing — the ordinary, accidental contact of an exchange. He didn't feel anything. Except. The paper was smooth and her fingers were cool and the contact lasted a fraction of a second longer than it needed to. "Thanks," he said. "Thanks for the tea," she said. "Even though it was terrible." "It wasn't terrible." "It was very strong." "I like it strong." "That's not the defence you think it is." He was at the door when she spoke again. "That book." He turned. "Don't lend it to anyone. It's out of print." "How do you know I'd lend it to anyone?" "Because you look like the kind of person who passes things along. Don't. Keep it." Something in the way she said *keep it*. Not advice. Not a sales pitch. Something else. He tucked the book under his jacket and stepped out into the rain. The man with the camera was gone. The estuary was grey and the sky was lower than it had been and the Co-op bag was still cutting into his fingers. He walked fast, water in his boots, the book in its brown paper pressed against his chest. Behind him, the door of the bookshop closed. The bell went. Inside, the woman who ran it stood at the counter and looked at the space where he'd been standing. Listen to what, she didn't know. The cat jumped down and wound between her legs. She picked up his mug. Washed it. Put it back on the hook. Stood there with her hands on the edge of the sink, looking out the small back window at the rain. "Right," she said. To nobody. To the cat. To the kitchen, which had heard worse. She went back to the counter. Restamped a book she'd already stamped. Put it in the wrong pile. Noticed. Moved it. Sat down. Stood up again. The kettle had gone cold. She turned it on again without knowing why. Outside, the rain kept at it. The estuary didn't care. A man with a Co-op bag and a book walked faster than he needed to, and didn't look back, and the bookshop got smaller behind him until it was just a shopfront on a wet street in a town he'd come to hide in, and that should have been that. But he was holding the book too tight, and his fingers still felt cool where hers had been, and he had the unhinged thought that he might read it. He would read it. He didn't read books. He would read this one.

Let me work through the key elements critically. **Dialogue and Voice** The dialogue is the chapter's strongest element. The exchange between Rhys and Efa has the quality the plan promised: it sounds overheard rather than authored. Lines like "Shop's open. That's generally how it works" and "That's not the defence you think it is" are sharp without being clever-for-its-own-sake. The rhythm is right — Rhys fills space, Efa doesn't. The tea-making reversal (she tells him to make his own) is a small, perfect beat that shows rather than tells the power dynamic. The dialogue does real work: we understand both characters through what they say and, crucially, what they don't. The cat exchange ("He was. For the first week. Then we realised he answered to nothing, so it didn't matter") is excellent — it's funny, it's in character, and it tells us something about Efa's dry pragmatism without announcing it. **Character Consistency** Rhys is rendered faithfully to his profile: the charm switching on "like a light," the picking up of the ceramic owl and putting it back wrong, the compulsive warmth that lands on a surface that doesn't absorb it. His interior experience of charm failing is handled well — we feel his disorientation without being told about it. The detail of him making the tea too strong and defending it is exactly right for the character. Efa is equally well-rendered. Her watchfulness, her precision, the way she "reads" him rather than admires him — all consistent with the profile. The ending, where she restamps a book she's already stamped and can't explain why she's boiled the kettle again, is the best moment in the chapter: action doing emotional work without a word of interior explanation. **Show vs. Tell** The chapter is almost entirely show. The one moment that edges toward tell is "the warmth switched on like a light, the voice pitched to charm" — this is close-third-person narration that names what's happening rather than letting us see it. It's a minor infraction and arguably necessary to establish Rhys's self-awareness about his own performance. The line "Not admired. Not assessed. Read, the way she'd read the spine of a book: quickly, accurately, for information" is a slight overreach — it's the narrator explaining the metaphor rather than trusting the reader to feel it. But these are small complaints. **Prose Quality** The prose is clean and controlled. The opening paragraph — rain, Co-op bag, man with camera — is economical and effective. The description of the shop is specific without being indulgent. The physical details (the ceramic owl, the brown paper wrapping, the Cymru mug) are chosen well and do character work. There are a few moments where the prose reaches slightly too hard. "The estuary didn't care" is a bit of a cliché in this mode of writing — the indifferent landscape. "The bell went" is slightly awkward phrasing. The final section, after Rhys leaves, has a slightly over-engineered quality: "the bookshop got smaller behind him until it was just a shopfront on a wet street in a town he'd come to hide in, and that should have been that" — this is the narrator winking at the reader, which undercuts the restraint elsewhere. The ending with Rhys — "He didn't read books. He would read this one" — is effective but the triple-beat structure ("He would read it. He didn't read books. He would read this one.") is a touch too polished, too aware of itself as a closing rhythm. It's the kind of ending that knows it's an ending. **Chemistry and Undercurrent** The prompt asked for "an undercurrent of unspoken chemistry" and the chapter delivers this through accumulation rather than declaration. The finger-touch during the book exchange is handled with appropriate restraint — "It was nothing — the ordinary, accidental contact of an exchange. He didn't feel anything. Except." The "Except." is a good beat. The book recommendation scene, where she tells him to keep it and not lend it, has genuine charge without being overwrought. **Following the Plan** The chapter follows its plan closely and well. The key elements are all present: the charm offensive, the immunity, the book recommendation with specificity, the tea-making, the departure with the book. The plan promised "rendered entirely through dialogue and action" and the chapter largely delivers on this. The plan also promised Rhys's POV giving us "the interior experience of charm failing" — this is achieved, though the narration occasionally names the experience rather than purely dramatizing it. **Weaknesses** The main weakness is a slight over-tidiness. The chapter is very well-crafted, perhaps too well-crafted in places — the closing rhythm, the "Except." beat, the narrator's wink. The plan explicitly warned against this ("no line should sound like it's been written for a trailer") and most lines pass that test, but the closing paragraphs have a slight trailer quality. The chapter is also perhaps slightly too successful at its own goals — the chemistry is present but the "paradoxically provokes a genuine attraction and derails the charm offensive" element could be pushed further; we see the charm failing but the derailment of Rhys is only lightly sketched. Overall, this is a high-quality chapter that executes its brief with skill, restraint, and genuine wit. The dialogue is excellent, the characters are consistent and well-drawn, and the emotional undercurrent is present without being announced. Minor issues with over-polish and occasional narrative intrusion prevent it from being a masterpiece, but it's well above average work. # Chapter 2: Returns The shop opened at nine. Efa was there at eight-fifteen, which was normal, because she liked the quiet quarter-hour before the day started — the sound of the kettle, the particular creak of the floorboards, Dylan already on the counter having claimed it sometime before dawn. What was not normal was the thing she was doing with the front display, which had been fine yesterday and which she had now been rearranging for twelve minutes without improving. She stepped back. Considered it. Moved a stack of new hardbacks two inches to the left. Moved them back. "The heating's on too high," she told Dylan. Dylan didn't look up. At nine-oh-three, the bell rang and Rhys Griffith walked in again, and Efa felt something in her chest that she immediately identified as irritation and which was not entirely irritation. He looked less put-together today. The jacket was the same but the hair was doing something unmanaged, and there were dark bits under his eyes that hadn't been there yesterday, and he was carrying no Co-op bag, no prop, no excuse to be here except the actual reason, which made it worse. "Back," he said. "So I see." "I read the book." She had been straightening a pile of leaflets that didn't need straightening. She stopped. "You read it." "Last night. Well — most of it. I got to the bit where she finds the letter and then I couldn't — I had to put it down. I put it down and just sat there. Which isn't something I do. Sit there. You've probably noticed." "I've known you for one day. I haven't noticed anything." "Fair enough. But I don't sit well. As a rule. And I sat." Efa looked at him. He wasn't performing this — she could tell, the way you can tell when someone's reciting something versus saying it for the first time. He was slightly out of breath, not from the walk but from the having-said-it. From the admission that a book had made him stop. "What did you think of the language?" she asked. "The language." "The prose. The way she writes sentences." He considered this. Shifted his weight. Picked up a bookmark from the counter display, looked at it, put it back — on the wrong side. Efa moved it back without thinking. "I thought it was — look, I don't know the words. I'm not a — I don't review things. But there was this bit, early on, where she describes the sound a river makes at night. Not what it looks like. The *sound*. And I thought, yes. I know that sound. I've heard that sound. And then she kept doing it — finding the exact — I kept thinking, *how does she know that?* How does she know what that feels like?" "It's a man. The author." "What?" "Rhys Pritchard. The author. He's a man." "I — right. Okay. Yes. *He.* How does *he* know." Efa almost smiled. Not at him — at the cover of her own copy behind the counter, which she knew page-for-page, which she'd given to a stranger on instinct, and which the stranger had actually read. "So what else did you think?" "I think I need to read the rest of it." "That's not a thought about the book. That's a plan." "It's an honest plan." "Honesty from a man who walked in here yesterday and complimented my cat for forty-five seconds as a way of not telling me who he was." A beat. Rhys tilted his head. "You knew who I was? Yesterday?" "I know who everyone is. I read the papers. It's a bookshop. There's not much else to do between customers." "Right. And you didn't —" "I didn't what?" He gestured vaguely. "Most people — when they recognise me — there's a thing. A moment. A flicker. You didn't flicker." "I don't flicker. It's not something I do." "You're very calm for someone who's just had a Hollywood actor walk into her bookshop." "You're very confident for a man whose last film got two stars in the Guardian." The silence that followed was not empty. It was the silence of a ball landing in a place neither of them expected. Rhys's face did something complicated — a flinch, then a recovery, then something more honest underneath both. "That's — yeah. Fair enough. That's fair." Efa turned away. Began restacking a shelf that didn't need restacking. She hadn't meant to say that — it had come out the way things sometimes do when her mouth gets ahead of her defences. She'd read the review. She'd read all the reviews, actually, on an evening she would not be admitting to, and they had been unfair, most of them, and she'd thought so at the time, and she'd said the unfair thing anyway because — Because. "I shouldn't have said that," she said, to the shelf. "No, it's — it's true. It's what people are thinking. Better you say it to my face than —" He stopped. Something shifted in his expression. "Actually, that's the first time anyone's said it to my face. Everyone else is very careful about it. My agent says 'mixed response.' My mam says she fell asleep during the fight scenes. You just —" "Said what I was thinking." "Yeah." "You're welcome." He laughed. Not the talk-show laugh — a smaller one, surprised, involuntary. And Efa, despite herself, despite every alarm in her body telling her this was a man who made everyone laugh and therefore the laugh meant nothing — She laughed too. It came out before she could catch it. A real laugh, not performed, not polite, and it was louder than she expected, and it lasted a beat too long, and when she stopped it she felt exposed, as if she'd said something she hadn't meant to. Rhys was looking at her. Not with triumph — with something more like recognition. As if he'd just heard a sound he'd been listening for. "Don't," she said. "Don't what?" "Don't look at me like that." "Like what?" "Like you've won something." He put his hands up. "I'm not — look, I'm not trying to — I just came to read the book. I came to read the book and tell you it made me sit still for ten minutes, which is a medical event in my case, and maybe get another recommendation if you're — I mean, if you've got time. If you're not busy." She looked at the shop. Empty. Rain on the windows. A cat asleep on the counter. The shelves she'd been rearranging all morning because she'd known, on some level below thought, that he would come back. "I'm not busy," she said. "Right. Good. So — what else have you got?" She came out from behind the counter. Moved past him — close enough to smell the wet-wool scent of his jacket — and into the fiction aisle. He followed. She could feel him behind her, not close, but there — the particular weight of another person in a space that was usually hers alone. She stopped at a shelf. Ran her finger along the spines. Pulled out something harder this time — denser, less immediately winning. A Welsh novel, translated, demanding. She'd chosen it for him the way she chose books for people she cared about: not what they'd enjoy, but what they needed. "Try this," she said, holding it out. "It won't be easy." "I didn't come here for easy." Their eyes met. The book was between them, her hand on one side, his reaching for the other. "Clearly," she said. He took the book. She turned back toward the counter. "Same rules?" he called after her. "Don't lend it? Don't pass it along?" "Those were the rules for the last one. These are different rules." "What are the rules for this one?" "Read it properly. Don't skim. Don't skip to the end. If you get bored, push through — it's not boring, you're just not listening." "When do I come back to discuss it?" "I didn't say we'd discuss it." "You're going to discuss it. You're a bookseller. Discussing books is — it's the whole thing." "It's really not the whole thing. The whole thing is keeping the lights on and stopping that cat from eating the post." "When do I come back?" She was behind the counter now. Safe. The counter between them, like a desk, like a barrier, like the thing she put between herself and anything that — "Tomorrow," she said. "If you've read at least fifty pages." He held up the book. Grinned. The proper grin this time, the one that worked on everyone, and she saw it work and she felt it not-work and she didn't know which of those facts was more alarming. "Tomorrow," he said. The bell. The door. The rain. Gone. Efa stood behind the counter. Her heart was doing something she didn't care for. Dylan opened one eye, regarded her, closed it again. "Don't start," she said. She picked up the bookmark he'd put back in the wrong place. Moved it to the right place. Put it in her apron pocket instead, because it was simpler, because she didn't need it on the counter, because she wasn't keeping it. She was not keeping it. The shop was quiet. The rain was not. She sat down and opened her own copy of the book she'd just given him, to the page she knew he'd reach tonight, the one where it stops being a book and becomes a mirror, and she read the single paragraph that had once, years ago, made her put the book down and sit very still, just as he had described, and she thought: *Oh.* *Oh, no.* Dylan jumped off the counter and sat on her feet. "Still don't start," she said.

# Chapter 3: What the Mam Knows Gwynne Street smelled of Fairy Liquid and Welsh cakes, same as it always had, and Rhys's childhood bedroom still had the Wales poster on the wall — Tŷ Coch, Rhossili, the Brecon Beacons — curling at the edges now, twenty-five years of Sellotape leaving yellow marks on the magnolia paint. He'd been here four days and the room had already started to feel like a trap. "Are you eating?" Glenys said, from the kitchen. "Yes." "You're not eating." "I had a banana." "A banana." She appeared in the doorway, tea towel over her shoulder, hands on hips. The posture of a woman who had raised two children alone and did not consider a banana to be food. "When?" "Yesterday." "Yesterday." "To be fair, I also had toast." "When?" "This morning. Before you ask — yes, I used the butter. Yes, I know it's the good butter. I'm sorry about the butter, Mam." "The butter's not the point, Rhys bach." She went back to the kitchen. He followed, because she was making tea and because following Glenys into a kitchen where tea was being made was a law of nature, like gravity or *Pobol y Cwm* at half seven. The kitchen hadn't changed. Same table — the table, the one where Wyn had died, mid-sentence, forty-three years old, and Glenys had never replaced it and nobody had ever asked why. Same curtains, same pattern, new fabric. Same clock on the wall, five minutes fast. Rhys had asked about the clock once, when he was twelve. "So we're never late," she'd said. He hadn't asked again. "You look tired," she said, setting his tea down. No saucer. Mugs on the table, that's how it was done. "I'm fine." "You look tired and you're not eating and you've been here four days and you haven't once told me why you've come, and don't say the estuary. Nobody comes to Laugharne for the estuary." "I came to see you." "You came to hide." She sat down, wrapped her hands around her mug. Her hands — broad, capable, a grip like a mechanic. She was sixty-eight and could still open a jar that defeated him. "Which is fine. I don't mind you hiding. I mind you not eating." Rhys looked at his tea. There was nothing to say to this because it was true and because Glenys had always had the specific talent of saying true things in a way that made them sound like weather — not an accusation, just a fact of the atmosphere. "Have you been to the bookshop?" she said. "What?" "The bookshop. Bwthyn y Llyfrau. Down by the —" "I know where it is." "Well?" "I went in. Yesterday. To get out of the rain." "And?" "And I bought a book." Glenys looked at him with the look — the one he'd known since he was seven, the one that meant *I can see straight through you and we both know it*. "What book?" "A Welsh one. By — I've forgotten the name. Rhys Pritchard." "Never heard of him." "Neither had I. She recommended it." "She." "The woman who runs the shop." "Efa." "You know her?" "Everyone knows everyone. It's Laugharne. She comes into the post office. Keeps herself to herself. Nice enough. Good stock." Glenys sipped her tea. "Why?" "Why what?" "Why are you telling me about a woman in a bookshop?" "I'm not telling you about — I bought a book, Mam. People buy books. It's a bookshop. That's the transaction." "Mm." The *Mm* contained multitudes. It contained every conversation they'd had since he was fifteen, when he'd come home smelling of cigarette smoke and said he'd been "just standing outside" and she'd said *Mm* in exactly this tone, and they'd both known, and nothing more had needed to be said. "I like her shop," Rhys said, into the silence. "It's — it's a good room. It's quiet. There's a cat called Dylan." "Everyone's cat in Laugharne is called Dylan." "This one bites people." "They all do that as well." He laughed. She didn't, because she hadn't been joking, but her face did the thing it did when she was pleased with herself — a slight settling, like a house coming to rest. He stayed for lunch — cawl she'd already made, because she always already had cawl, because she knew he'd come without eating. He ate two bowls and bread and butter (the good butter) and she watched him with the quiet satisfaction of a woman whose primary love language was feeding people until they stopped moving. After, he helped her with a shelf that had been coming away from the wall in the front room. It took twenty minutes and a screwdriver from the drawer under the oven (everything was in the drawer under the oven) and when he finished she looked at it and said "That'll do" which was the highest praise available and they both knew it. He left at three. Walked the long way into town, past the brown estuary water, past the boat house, past the church where he'd been christened and Wyn had been buried. The sky was low and grey-green and the air tasted of salt and mud. He'd forgotten how the air tasted here. Or he hadn't forgotten — he'd just stopped noticing, which was different, and worse. He pushed through the door of the bookshop at half three. The bell went. Dylan opened one eye and closed it again, which Rhys was starting to understand was the cat's version of a standing ovation. Efa was behind the counter, stamping something. She didn't look up. "Fifty pages," she said. "I did more than fifty. I did a hundred." "And?" "This one's harder." "That's not an opinion. That's a complaint." "It's both." He leaned against the end of a shelf. "There's a chapter where nothing happens. He just — walks. For pages. He walks and looks at things and thinks about the past and I kept waiting for something to happen and it didn't and I was — I was annoyed. And then I wasn't. I was just... in it. I was walking with him. How does he do that?" Now she looked up. Held him with those brown eyes that stayed on things too long, that read. "You kept going," she said. "You said don't skim." "I said don't skip." "Same thing." "It's not the same thing at all." He conceded this with a tilt of his head. The conversation was easier today — not easy, never that, but the rhythm was different. Less sparring. More — he didn't know the word. Somewhere between arguing and listening. "The cat bit me again," he said. "I know." "Does he bite everyone?" "No." "So I should be flattered." "I wouldn't go that far." It was nearly closing time. He was still there. The shop was warm — the wood burner was lit, really lit this time, not smoking — and the rain was doing its thing on the windows and Efa had made two mugs of tea without being asked and Rhys was sitting on a wooden chair near the back, the one with the uneven leg, and she was on the one opposite, and between them was a crate being used as a table, and on it were two mugs and a plate of something she'd produced from the back room — biscuits, the kind that come in a tin, the kind his mam kept. "Where did you get Welsh cakes?" he said. "I didn't say they were Welsh cakes." "They're Welsh cakes. My mam makes these." "Everyone's mam makes these." "She'd be offended if she heard you say that. She thinks hers are unique. She thinks she's got a gift." "Has she?" "She has. Don't tell her I said that." The wood burner ticked. Rain on glass. Dylan asleep on a pile of unsold hardbacks. Rhys ate a Welsh cake and thought about the thing he'd been thinking about since yesterday, which was the specific quality of silence in this room, and how it was different from every other silence he'd known, because in every other silence — in his house in LA, in hotel rooms, in the back of cars — the silence was absence, the sound of nobody being there, and in this room the silence was presence, the sound of two people not needing to fill the space. "I keep meaning to visit more," he said. He didn't know he was going to say this until he said it. "My mam. I keep meaning to come back more often. And I don't. And every time I phone her I say 'next month' and every time it's six months and she never — she doesn't say anything. She just says 'when you're ready, bach' and I — yeah." Efa listened. She didn't say "that must be hard" or "I'm sure she understands" or any of the things people said when they were filling the gap between listening and responding. She just listened, and then she reached across and topped up his tea from the pot she'd brought through, and didn't say anything, and the not-saying was more than any saying could have been. He stayed until nearly six. When he left, it was dark, and the estuary was black and silver and the path was wet and he walked home along the water with his hands in his pockets, not thinking about the book or the reviews or the role Martin kept texting about. He was thinking about the way she'd topped up his tea. The quiet, automatic gesture. The fact that she'd noticed his mug was empty before he had. He let himself into the cottage. Sat on the bed. Took out the book — the first one, the one from yesterday — and opened it to where he'd left off, page forty-seven, the sound of a river at night. He read. He didn't check his phone once.

Judge Response:
[Analysis] This chapter is a strong piece of work that largely delivers on its ambitious plan. Let me examine it carefully across multiple dimensions. **Dialogue and Voice** The dialogue is the chapter's greatest strength. The opening exchange about the banana and the butter is pitch-perfect — it establishes Glenys's character through rhythm and repetition rather than description, and Rhys's defensive self-deprecation ("I'm sorry about the butter, Mam") lands with the ease of something overheard rather than written. The "Mm" moment is excellent: the narrative earns the observation that it "contained multitudes" because the reader has already felt it. The bookshop dialogue continues the established dynamic well — "I wouldn't go that far" is exactly the kind of line that does double work, being both a response to the cat question and a refusal of the larger compliment he's fishing for. The Welsh cake exchange is warm without being saccharine, and the line "Everyone's mam makes these" / "She'd be offended if she heard you say that" is a small, perfect piece of character work. **Character Consistency** Rhys is rendered faithfully to his profile: the defensive "To be fair," the picking up of things (implied in his restlessness), the compulsive charm that keeps trying to land, the genuine laugh. His admission about his mother — "I keep meaning to visit more" — is handled exactly as the plan specified: not a speech, just a dropped line, an admission he wasn't planning to make. The narrative doesn't editorialize about it. It just sits there. Glenys is the chapter's revelation. She is not a wisdom dispenser. She is a specific woman with specific habits — the five-minutes-fast clock, the cawl already made, the "That'll do" as highest praise. The detail about the table where Wyn died, never replaced, never explained, is quietly devastating and earns its place without being underlined. The "Mm" is her most characteristic moment. The line "You came to hide. Which is fine. I don't mind you hiding. I mind you not eating" is exactly right — it's blunt, loving, and refuses to be sentimental about either quality. Efa is present only briefly but her characterization holds: the not-saying, the tea-topping, the brown eyes that "stayed on things too long." The plan called for her to top up his tea without asking, and this is executed with restraint — no interior monologue explaining what it means, just the gesture and Rhys's recognition of it afterward. **Emotional Engagement** The chapter earns its emotional moments through accumulation rather than declaration. The tea-topping is the chapter's emotional climax, and it works because it's been set up by everything preceding it — the Glenys scene establishing what wordless care looks like in Rhys's life, and then Efa performing a version of the same gesture. The parallel is implicit, never stated. This is the chapter's best structural decision. The final image — Rhys reading, not checking his phone — is simple and effective. It doesn't announce itself as significant. It just is. **Where the Chapter Falls Short** The description of the estuary walk — "The sky was low and grey-green and the air tasted of salt and mud. He'd forgotten how the air tasted here. Or he hadn't forgotten — he'd just stopped noticing, which was different, and worse" — is the chapter's most self-conscious moment. "Which was different, and worse" is the kind of authorial underlining the plan explicitly said to avoid. It's not egregious, but it's the one place where the narrative tells us how to feel rather than letting the image do the work. Similarly, the observation about the silence in the bookshop — "the silence was absence... and in this room the silence was presence" — is slightly too neat, too articulated for a man who, we're told, doesn't have frameworks for what he's experiencing. It's the kind of thought Rhys might have, but the phrasing is too polished for his register. The plan warned against "emotional thesis statements disguised as dialogue" and this is an emotional thesis statement disguised as interior monologue. The chapter is also slightly longer than the plan's target of ~1,000 words, and the extra length is mostly in the Glenys section, which is the stronger half. The bookshop section, while good, covers ground already established in Chapters 1 and 2 (the cat biting, the rhythm of their exchange) without quite advancing the relationship as much as the plan suggested. The plan called for "a longer conversation. Quieter" and "they talk about Wales, about leaving, about what it means to come back" — the Wales/leaving conversation is gestured at but not fully developed. Rhys's admission about his mother is the closest we get, and it's good, but the plan's ambition for this scene was slightly larger than what's delivered. **Craft and Prose** The prose is clean and controlled. The physical details are specific and earned: the drawer under the oven, the clock five minutes fast, the uneven leg on the chair. These are the details of a writer who has thought about these people and this place, not a writer reaching for atmosphere. The Welsh cake moment is a small structural pleasure — connecting Glenys's kitchen to the bookshop without making the connection explicit. The chapter avoids purple prose almost entirely. The one near-miss is the estuary passage, but it's brief and the writing recovers quickly. **Overall Assessment** This is accomplished, disciplined work. It follows the chapter plan faithfully, renders the characters consistently with their profiles, and earns its emotional moments through restraint and specificity. Its flaws are minor: one or two moments of over-articulation, a slightly underdeveloped bookshop conversation, and the occasional authorial underlining. But these are the flaws of a writer who is mostly succeeding at something genuinely difficult — writing scenes that feel overheard rather than authored. # Chapter 4: What She Doesn't Say Something was wrong with the front display. Efa had rearranged it three times this morning — once because the hardbacks were uneven, once because the colour grouping was off, and once because Rhys had touched the ceramic owl yesterday and it was facing the wrong way and she'd only just noticed, and now the whole display felt contaminated by the wrongness of it, and she couldn't fix it, and it was ten past two, and he usually arrived around half past. She stepped back. The display was fine. It had always been fine. "He's not coming today," she told Dylan. Dylan was asleep. "He's probably gone back to London. Or LA. Wherever. People like that don't — they don't stay. They orbit. They pass through. That's what they do." Dylan continued to sleep with commitment. At half two, she made herself a coffee and drank it standing at the back window, looking at the small yard where nothing grew because she'd never planted anything, and she thought about the book she'd given him — the harder one, the second one — and the page she knew he'd be on by now, the one where the man in the book stands at a kitchen table and says the truest thing he's ever said and the woman across from him doesn't hear it, or hears it and can't hold it, and the chapter ends mid-sentence, and you turn the page and it's three years later and nothing is the same. She'd read that page for the first time in a flat in London, four years ago, her ring still in the bathroom where she'd left it, and she'd closed the book and opened it and closed it again and thought: *this is the most honest thing I have ever read about the way people fail each other.* She didn't know if Rhys would get there. She didn't know if he'd push through the walking chapter, the slow chapter, the chapter where nothing happens. She didn't know if he was the kind of reader who — The bell rang. He came in with rain in his hair and the second book in his hand and a look on his face that she recognised because she'd worn it herself, four years ago, in London. "Page one hundred and twelve," he said. She set down her coffee. "The kitchen table," he said. "The kitchen table." "He's standing there and he's saying — he's just *saying it*. Just out. Just the thing. And she's — and she doesn't —" He stopped. Ran a hand through his wet hair. Put the book on the counter like it was something that had burned him. "How does he know that? How does anyone know what that feels like from the outside?" "I think he's been inside it." "What?" "I think Rhys Pritchard has stood at a kitchen table and said something true and had it not land. I think that's how he knows." Rhys looked at her. The book between them on the counter. Rain on the windows. "Have you?" he said. "Have I what." "Stood at a kitchen table. Said something true." The question was too big and too direct and it came too fast and Efa felt her defences go up like blinds — the physical sensation of it, the snap. "I make tea for a living," she said. "I'm not sure I'm qualified for kitchen-table truths." "That's not an answer." "It's the one you're getting." He held his hands up. The gesture she was starting to know — the surrender, the retreat, the easy way out that wasn't easy for either of them. He picked up the book again. Turned it over. "I need to keep reading." "You do." "Can I — is it alright if I —" He gestured at the chair. The one with the uneven leg. The one he'd sat in yesterday. She should have said no. She knew she should have said no because the shop was open and there were things to do and the display still wasn't right and the window needed cleaning and she had a life that didn't include — "Put the kettle on," she said. He made the tea this time. Better than yesterday — not as strong, and he'd found the right mugs without asking. He brought them through and sat in the chair and she sat in hers and he opened the book and she opened hers — a different one, one she was reading for work — and for twenty minutes they sat in the back of the bookshop and read. It was the quietest twenty minutes of Efa's life that involved another person. She couldn't concentrate. She read the same paragraph three times. His page turned — a small, dry sound — and the sound went through her like a minor chord. She looked at him over the top of her book. He didn't notice. He was reading. His lips moved slightly — not with the words, but with the rhythm of them, as if his mouth was learning the shape of the sentences. His hands were still for once. Not picking things up. Not fidgeting. Still, on the pages, holding the book open, and she looked at his hands and then looked away and turned a page she hadn't read. He spoke without looking up. "What did you do before this?" "Before the shop." "Yeah." "Publishing. London." "What kind?" "Editorial. Academic first, then trade." "Why'd you leave?" She closed her book. Not marking the page. Just closing it. "Because I wanted a shop in Laugharne." "That's not why." "That's the one you're getting." He looked up now. Smiled — not the big one, not the talk-show one. Something smaller, sadder. "Fair enough," he said. Back to the book. Sixty pages later, he closed it. She heard the sound — the soft meeting of covers — and looked up before she could stop herself. "There's a woman in it," he said. "She's not the main character. She's just — she's there. In the background. Running a shop. And he describes her hands once — just once — and I thought —" He stopped. "You thought what." "Nothing. Forget it." The silence that followed was not the comfortable one. It was the other kind — the loaded kind, the kind that has edges. Efa could feel it pressing against the walls of the shop. She could feel the weight of whatever he'd been about to say, sitting in the air between them like heat. She stood up. Took the mugs to the sink. Washed them. Dried them. Put them back. Turned around. He was still sitting, the book open on his lap, looking at something she couldn't see. "I should go," he said. "You should." He stood. Set the book on the chair. Came to the counter where she was — closer than he'd been before, close enough that she could see the grain of the stubble on his jaw, the scar on his hand, the way his dark hair was drying in curls she wanted — She straightened a pile of leaflets. "Same time tomorrow?" he said. "You tell me." "Same time tomorrow." He moved toward the door. Stopped. Turned back. "Efa." "What." "After you left Cardiff. Where did you —" "I didn't leave Cardiff." He waited. "I left a person," she said. "Not a city." She didn't know why she'd said it. She heard the words come out of her mouth and felt the shock of them — the wrongness, the exposure, the way the sentence hung in the room like a confession she hadn't planned. Her face was hot. Her hands were gripping the counter edge. Rhys was very still. Not the actor-still, the performing-still. Still like a man who understood he'd been given something and was trying not to drop it. "Right," he said. Quiet. "Okay." "Don't —" "I won't." "I don't want you to —" "I know." He left. The bell. The door. The sound of his boots on the wet street, fading. Efa stood behind the counter. Her hands were shaking. She pressed them flat on the wood and breathed and breathed and Dylan jumped up and sat on her left hand and the weight of him was grounding, solid, real. "I didn't mean to say that," she told the cat. Dylan purred. "I *didn't*." She picked up the book Rhys had left on the chair. The second one. She fanned the pages with her thumb — the way she always did, spine in the left hand, the pulse of it — and a scrap of paper fell out. A receipt. His, from yesterday, from the Co-op. Bananas, bread, milk, biscuits. The mundane archaeology of a life. She put it back in the book. Put the book on the shelf behind the counter. Sat down. Her own copy — the book she'd given him, the first one — was on the shelf where she'd put it the other day. The wrong shelf. She reached for it, opened it to the page she knew, the one he'd reached last night, the sound of a river at night, and she read the paragraph and this time she didn't hear the river. She heard his voice saying *How does he know that?* She closed the book. Held it against her chest. The kettle had gone cold again. She didn't turn it on. She sat in the quiet shop and listened to the rain and the cat and the sound of her own breathing, and she was angry at herself — furious, actually, with a fury that was specific and precise and directed entirely inward — because she had built this life carefully, piece by piece, year by year, and it was good, and it was hers, and she could feel it shifting under her like ground that wasn't as solid as she'd thought. *I left a person, not a city.* Why had she said that? Why, of all the things she could have said, had she said the true one? Dylan stretched. Jumped off the counter. Walked to the door and sat in front of it, looking at it, as if expecting someone. "Don't wait for him," Efa said. Dylan waited. She pulled her sleeves down for once. Folded her arms. Sat in the back room of the bookshop she'd built to be safe, and felt the walls of it, and felt they were thinner than she'd believed, and heard the rain, and did not turn the kettle on, and did not cry, because she didn't do that, because she *didn't*. The rain kept at it. The estuary didn't care. A woman sat alone in a bookshop in a town she'd chosen because it was the opposite of everything that had hurt her, and held a book to her chest, and waited for nothing, and the nothing was the loudest sound in the room.

# Chapter 5: The Outside The text from Non came at ten past eight. Efa was opening the shop — keys in the lock, the particular pull of the old door, Dylan already winding between her legs wanting out, wanting in, wanting to make the process of opening a bookshop as difficult as possible. The second shot was through the window — the interior, the shelves, the counter, and there, slightly out of focus but unmistakably her, visible between the displays, behind the counter, in her shop. The comments underneath. *Who's the mystery woman?* *Bit plain for him isn't she lol* *Looks like his mum 😂* *She's a bookseller apparently. How very twee.* *I give it two weeks.* *Trading up from the wife? Couldn't be me* Efa put the phone down. Picked it up. Put it down again. Her hands were doing the thing they did when she was angry — the shake, the stupid involuntary shake that she couldn't control and that made her angrier than the thing itself. She read them again. She didn't know why. She read *plain* again and *his mum* and *twee* and *couldn't be me* and she felt each one land with the specific, grubby precision of someone she'd never met reaching into her life and handling it without permission. "Are you —" "Fine." "Because if you want me to —" "I'm fine, Megan." Megan stood in the doorway to the back room, bag still over her shoulder, the particular stance of a twenty-year-old who knew she was out of her depth and was going to stand there anyway. "The comments are rubbish," she said. "You know that, right?" "I know that." "You're not plain." "Megan." "Sorry. I just — I'm saying. They're wrong. About all of it." "They're strangers on the internet. I'm not — I'm not upset about strangers on the internet." "Okay." "I'm upset about —" She stopped. Because what she was upset about was too large and too complicated and had too many parts, and the strangers were only one part, and the other part was the fact that she was standing in a window, caught, seen, identified — the thing she'd come to Laugharne to stop being — and the other part, the largest part, the part she couldn't say to Megan or anyone, was that the photo of the bookshop interior showed the two chairs in the back, and the mugs on the crate, and the wood burner, and all of it looked like something it wasn't, or something it was, and she couldn't tell which was worse. "I'm going to rearrange the back room," she said. "It was rearranged yesterday." "It needs doing again." At eleven, Gareth from the Salutation Arms came in for a paperback. He always bought one on a Thursday — crime, usually, the same three authors in rotation. He picked one, brought it to the counter, and said, "Saw your picture on the internet, girl." "Gareth." "I'm not saying I Googled it. Dai showed me. On the phone. At the pub." "Of course he did." "Everyone's talking about it." "Everyone can —" "I told them it was nobody's business. I said, that Efa keeps herself to herself and whatever she gets up to with a film star is her own affair." "I'm not getting up to anything with a —" "That's what I said. I said, she's a private woman, that one, and you should all leave her be." "Thank you, Gareth." "Course, I also said he seemed like a nice lad. Good Welsh stock. His mam's Glenys from Gwynne Street. Known her thirty years." "Is there anything else, Gareth?" "Just the book, love." She rang it up. He left. She stood at the counter and counted to ten and then to twenty and then stopped counting because the numbers weren't helping. At half twelve, the bell rang and it was him. He looked terrible. Not styled-terrible — actually terrible. He'd seen the photos. She could tell from the way he was standing, slightly inside the doorway, like a man who wasn't sure he'd be welcome. "Efa." "Have you come to browse?" "I've come to — look, I've seen the photos. I'm sorry. I'm — I didn't — I don't know how they found —" "You don't know how they found you? Not —" "I should have warned you. That this happens. That it's — I should have said." "You should have said 'hello, nice bookshop, by the way the tabloids will photograph you through your own window'? Is that the conversation we should have had?" He stepped further in. The door closed behind him. The bell. "I'm sorry," he said again. "I know that doesn't —" "It doesn't." "What do you want me to do?" The question landed wrong. Not because it was insensitive but because it assumed she had an answer, and she didn't, and the not-having was the worst part. "I want you to not have brought this here," she said. "I want to not be on a website. I want people who've known me three years to not look at me differently because I'm standing next to someone who — who's —" "Who's what?" She looked at him. The man in her shop. The man who'd made her laugh, who'd read the book, who'd sat in the chair with the uneven leg and gone quiet over a paragraph. The man who was also a name, a face, a commodity, a thing that brought cameras and comments and strangers assessing you. "Your life contaminates everything it touches," she said. It was cruel. She knew it was cruel as she said it, and she said it anyway, because cruelty was a kind of honesty and honesty was all she had left in a morning where everything she'd built had been photographed and priced and judged by people who'd never set foot in this room. Rhys's face changed. The openness — the thing she'd been seeing all week, the unguarded, un-performing thing — shuttered. "That's —" "Don't." "No. You said something. I get to respond." He stepped forward. His voice was different — not charming, not warm. Flat. Hurt. "My life. My *life*. I didn't choose it. The stillness he'd learned to read — the contained, pulled-inward stillness that meant something had breached and was being repaired in real time. He went to the door. Stopped with his hand on the frame. "I shouldn't have said that." "No." "I'm sorry." "Leave." He left. The bell. A sound she would hear, afterwards, replaying in her head — the small, mechanical, unbearably cheerful sound of a bell on a door, as if nothing had happened, as if the world outside was just the world and not — She sat on the floor behind the counter. Stood on the path. The estuary was grey and the sky was grey and the rain was grey and he was soaked through and his phone was in his pocket buzzing with Martin's number and he didn't reach for it either. He thought: *if your life is that fragile.* He thought: *I said that. I said that to her face.* He thought about the look on her face — not the anger, which he could handle, which he knew, which was familiar from a hundred arguments with a hundred people in a hundred rooms — but the thing underneath the anger, which was worse, which was the look of someone who'd been hit in a place they'd spent years protecting, and the hitting had been exact, and he'd been the one to do it. The estuary lapped at the stones, in and out, in and out, the sound a river makes at night except it was daytime and it wasn't a river and the sound was nothing like the book and everything like the book and he put his head in his hands and sat there. [Analysis] Chapter 5 is the argument chapter, the moment where the story's carefully built tension breaks open into something ugly and real. Let me assess it across multiple dimensions. STRENGTHS: The chapter follows its plan with impressive fidelity. The gossip site photos, the comments (including "plain" and "his mum"), Gareth's well-meaning intrusion, the argument, and the dual ending with both characters alone in the rain — all of these are executed as planned. The model has not merely followed the plan mechanically; it has found specific, lived-in details to populate each beat. The dialogue is the chapter's strongest element. Gareth's scene is particularly well-handled — his combination of genuine loyalty ("I told them it was nobody's business") and complete inability to stop talking is both funny and true to the character profile. The exchange is economical and does real work. The argument itself is well-constructed: both characters say things that are partly right and partly wrong, as planned. Rhys's line about Efa "hiding in this shop long before I showed up" is genuinely cutting because it's accurate, and the model earns the cruelty by having Efa go first with "your life contaminates everything it touches." The Megan scene is brief but effective. Her persistence ("He's sad, isn't he?" is not in this chapter but her presence here is consistent with her profile), and her attempt to comfort Efa about the comments ("You're not plain") is both touching and slightly awkward in the right way. The physical details do emotional work without being announced: Efa sitting on the floor behind the counter rather than a chair, Dylan pressing against her thigh, the purr through her palm. These are earned and specific. The bell on the door — "the small, mechanical, unbearably cheerful sound" — is a good detail, though it edges toward the kind of prose that risks being over-written. The chapter's emotional logic is sound. Efa's anger is not simply about the photos; the model correctly identifies that it's about the permeability of the privacy she built, and the photo of the two chairs in the back room being visible — "all of it looked like something it wasn't, or something it was, and she couldn't tell which was worse" — is a genuinely good line that captures her ambivalence without explaining it. WEAKNESSES: The ending section, where Rhys walks the estuary, is where the chapter's discipline begins to slip. "The estuary was grey and the sky was grey and the rain was grey" is a competent sentence but it's doing the kind of atmospheric stacking that the writing plan explicitly warned against. More problematically, the final paragraph — "the sound a river makes at night except it was daytime and it wasn't a river and the sound was nothing like the book and everything like the book" — is the chapter's most significant failure. This is a callback to the book they discussed (presumably a passage about rivers at night), but it's rendered in a way that's self-consciously literary, slightly precious, and ultimately muddy. "Nothing like the book and everything like the book" is the kind of paradox that sounds meaningful but doesn't quite resolve into meaning. The plan specifically warned against "lyrical descriptions deployed for their own sake" and this passage is the closest the chapter comes to violating that principle. Rhys's interior monologue at the end — "He thought: if your life is that fragile. He thought: I said that. I said that to her face." — is effective in its repetition and self-recrimination, but the final image of him sitting on a rock with his head in his hands while "nobody came" is slightly melodramatic. The plan called for both characters "replaying what was said" and "each knowing they went too far" — this is achieved, but the execution for Rhys is slightly more theatrical than the plan's tone suggested. The line "cruelty was a kind of honesty and honesty was all she had left" is a moment where the narrative voice edges toward explaining rather than showing. It's not egregious, but it's the kind of interior thesis statement the plan warned against. The chapter is slightly less restrained in its final third than in its first two-thirds. The opening — the phone, the comments, the coffee, Megan's arrival — is excellent in its understatement. The argument is well-handled. But the aftermath reaches slightly too hard for resonance. CHARACTER CONSISTENCY: Both characters are consistent with their profiles. Efa's stillness as a response to being breached, her inability to articulate the full complexity of her anger, her sitting on the floor rather than performing composure — all of this is true to the character. Rhys's defensive pivot from apology to attack, his inability to stop himself once the reins slip, his immediate recognition that he's gone too far — this is exactly the character as designed. The "difficult" reputation having a kernel of truth is demonstrated rather than stated. OVERALL: This is a strong chapter that executes its plan with skill and mostly avoids the pitfalls the writing plan identified. The dialogue is the best element; the ending is the weakest. The emotional beats are earned. The argument is ugly in the right way. The chapter does what it needs to do in the story's arc without being neat about it. "You don't usually —" "I know. Gareth. Where is he?" "Which he?" "The one you told me about. Good Welsh stock. His mam's Glenys." Gareth set down the glass. Looked at her with the expression of a man who'd been running the Salutation Arms for twenty-two years and had seen every version of this conversation walk through his door. "He was here. Last three nights. Corner table. Gone now." "Gone where?" "Gone gone. Back, I think. His mam said he'd packed the car this morning." Efa stood in the doorway of the pub. The smell of old beer. The man with the racing form not looking up. Gareth watching her with kindness and something else — the professional discretion of a landlord who knew when to speak and when to let the silence do it. "Right," she said. "He left something for you, mind." "What?" Gareth reached under the bar. Brought out a paperback. The second book — *her* copy, the one she'd given him, the one he'd been reading in her shop. He'd left it at the pub. On the front cover, a sticky note in the same careful handwriting. *Finished. You were right about all of it. The chair was uncomfortable by the way. I don't know how you sit in that thing.* *Thank you. For the book. For the tea. For not asking for a photo.* *R* *P.S. I'm sorry about what I said. About your life being fragile. It isn't. It's the opposite. I said it because I was angry and because I'm a bastard when I'm hurt and none of that is your fault.* Efa held the book. The sticky note. The handwriting. "Are you alright, girl?" Gareth said. "Fine." "You don't look fine." "I'm going to go now, Gareth." "Right you are." She walked. Not back to the shop — along the estuary path, the way Rhys had walked three days ago in the rain, except it wasn't raining now and the sky was doing that thing it does in late October when the clouds break and the light comes through sideways and the water turns from grey to silver and the whole estuary looks like something you'd put on a postcard and resent for being beautiful. She walked to the boat house. Stood there. Opened her copy of the book — her copy, with his note — and read the note again. Read the P.S. Read *it isn't. It's the opposite.* She thought about the first edition wrapped in brown paper on her doormat. The seven words inside. The fact that he'd gone to find it, buy it, inscribe it, wrap it, walk it to her shop in the dark, slide it through the letterbox, and leave. No fanfare. No audience. No performance. Just a book, and a note, and a man who'd done something specific and quiet and then gone. She walked back. The light was changing. The estuary was doing its thing. She let herself into the shop, where Dylan was sitting in the window exactly where she'd left him, the Cymru mug untouched. "He's gone," she told the cat. Dylan looked at her. "He left books. Two books. And notes. And he's gone back to wherever he goes and I —" She stopped. Stood in the middle of her shop. The two chairs. The crate. The wood burner, cold now. The shelf where she'd put his book in the wrong place. She went to the shelf. Took down the copy she'd hidden between the Dylan Thomas biography and the water-stained *Bro Gaernarfon.* Sat in her chair — not his, hers — with both books, and the sticky note, and the inscription, and she read. Not the novels. The notes. The seven words. The *thank you for not asking for a photo.* The *I'm sorry.* The *it isn't, it's the opposite.* She put the books down. Took out her phone. No messages from him. She hadn't expected any. She didn't have his number. He didn't have hers. They'd never exchanged numbers, she realised, in ten days of conversation and tea and arguments and silence and rain, they'd never once done the most basic, practical, transactional thing and exchange a number, and there was something both absurd and perfect about that — two people who'd found something real and had no way to reach for it. She sat in the quiet shop. The light through the window was gold now, the last of the afternoon, and it hit the counter and the cat and the stack of books and the two mugs on the hook and the place where Rhys had once put the ceramic owl back wrong. She reached for the owl. Turned it to face the way he'd left it. Dylan stretched. Jumped off the counter. Sat by the door again, looking at it. "Don't," Efa said. The door didn't open. The cat waited. The light moved across the floor of the bookshop and the estuary breathed outside and a woman sat in a chair and held two books and didn't know what came next, and the not-knowing was terrifying, and the not-knowing was the first thing she'd felt in four years that wasn't safety or routine or the quiet satisfaction of a life she'd chosen because it couldn't hurt her. It could hurt her. She could feel it already. The possibility of it, the weight, the particular gravity of a man who'd listened to her and then left and left evidence that he'd listened. She picked up the sticky note. Read it one more time. *Thank you. For the book. For the tea. For not asking for a photo.* She folded it. Put it in her pocket. Not keeping it. Carrying it. There was a difference, and she was going to stand by that distinction for as long as she could.

[Analysis] This chapter is a strong piece of literary fiction that largely succeeds on its own terms. Let me examine it carefully across the relevant dimensions. **Craft and Execution** The chapter opens with a well-observed domestic detail — the negotiation of getting a bookshop open with a cat who has opinions about thresholds — that immediately grounds us in Efa's world and voice. The discovery of the parcel is handled with restraint: the narration doesn't over-explain the emotional significance, it trusts the reader to feel it through the accumulation of specific detail (the Co-op receipt she'd been "storing, not keeping," the recognition of the handwriting). The inscription itself — "Page 112. You were right about the kitchen table. R." — is genuinely excellent. It's specific, earned, and does exactly what the plan called for: a gesture that is personal and private rather than grand and performative. The brevity is the point. This is the chapter's strongest moment. The sticky note at the pub is slightly less successful. Where the inscription is seven words, the sticky note is considerably more verbose, and crucially, it contains the explicit apology that the plan suggested should be incomplete and messy. "I'm sorry about what I said. About your life being fragile. It isn't. It's the opposite. I said it because I was angry and because I'm a bastard when I'm hurt and none of that is your fault." This is articulate in a way that contradicts the character profile's insistence that Rhys "would never deliver a perfectly articulated monologue about his fear of being hollow" and that "if he comes close, he'll choke on it." The written apology is too clean, too self-aware, too complete. It does the emotional work that the plan explicitly said should be left undone. **Deviation from the Plan** The chapter plan called for Efa to go find Rhys at the pub, where he would be "nursing something," and for a face-to-face scene where his confession is "messy and incomplete" and her response is "a small, characteristic opening." Instead, the chapter has Rhys already gone — he's left books and notes and departed. This is a significant structural deviation. The plan's climactic scene — the two of them in the pub, the messy confession, the small opening — doesn't happen. Instead, we get Efa alone with objects and notes. This is a defensible creative choice, and in some ways it's more interesting — the absence is doing work, the notes are doing work — but it means the chapter doesn't deliver what the plan promised: the face-to-face reconnection, the "his face does something he can't control," the "why?" that is "genuinely asking." The emotional payoff is deferred rather than delivered, which may be artistically valid but represents a meaningful departure from the stated intention. **Dialogue and Voice** There is very little dialogue in this chapter, which is notable given that the plan specified 60-70% dialogue as the engine of the story. What dialogue exists (Efa and Gareth, Efa and Dylan) is good — Gareth's "Which he?" is a nice beat, and the Dylan exchanges are characteristic. But the chapter is primarily interior and descriptive, which is a significant tonal shift from the plan's stated approach. **Prose Quality** The prose is generally clean and controlled. The estuary description — "the clouds break and the light comes through sideways and the water turns from grey to silver" — is earned rather than purple, though the parenthetical "and resent for being beautiful" is slightly self-conscious. The "not keeping it, carrying it, there was a difference" callback to earlier character voice is well-executed and feels genuinely Efa. Some moments tip toward over-writing: "the particular gravity of a man who'd listened to her and then left and left evidence that he'd listened" is a bit labored. The final paragraph's accumulation of clauses ("the not-knowing was terrifying, and the not-knowing was the first thing she'd felt in four years that wasn't safety or routine or the quiet satisfaction of a life she'd chosen because it couldn't hurt her") is effective but slightly on-the-nose for a story that prides itself on not stating the theme. **Emotional Engagement** The chapter is emotionally effective. The first edition with seven words is genuinely moving. The owl turned to face the wrong way — Efa turning it back to how Rhys left it — is a beautiful, specific, earned detail that does more work than any interior monologue. The cat waiting by the door is perhaps slightly too neat as a symbol, but it's deployed with enough lightness to survive. **Character Consistency** Efa is largely consistent with her profile — the "not keeping it, carrying it" distinction, the talking to the cat, the precise observation of the handwriting. The moment where she fills the Cymru mug for the cat is charming and characteristic. However, as noted, Rhys's written apology is too articulate for the character as described. **Overall Assessment** This is accomplished literary fiction with a strong central gesture (the first edition inscription) and good control of Efa's interiority. Its main weaknesses are: the deviation from the chapter plan's promised face-to-face scene; the sticky note apology being too clean and articulate for Rhys's character; the relative absence of dialogue in a story that defined itself through dialogue; and occasional moments where the prose states what it should show. The owl detail at the end is the chapter's second-best moment — small, specific, and devastating in the right way. # Chapter 8: What Remains He came back on a Wednesday. Not with fanfare. Not with a plan. He drove from London in a car that wasn't hired, that was his, that he'd had shipped over because he was apparently the kind of man who had cars shipped, and he parked it on the street outside the bookshop at ten past three in the afternoon and sat in it for four minutes before getting out. Efa saw the car from the window. She saw him in it. She saw him sit there. She set down the book she was stamping and stood very still behind the counter and Dylan looked at her and she said nothing and the four minutes were the longest four minutes since the four minutes she'd stood in a London hallway looking at something she hadn't expected to see, except these were the opposite of those minutes, these were minutes of waiting for something she — The door opened. The bell. Same bell. Same sound. He looked different. Not better or worse — different. His hair was shorter. He was wearing a jacket she hadn't seen, one that was less careful, less bought-by-someone-else. He was carrying a plastic bag from the Co-op. "I brought biscuits," he said. She looked at him. The man in her shop. The woman behind the counter. The cat between them, on the floor, tail switching. "You left," she said. "I left." "You went back to London." "I did." "Your agent rang you. About the role." He blinked. "How did you —" "I heard you take the call. Outside. Through the window. You thought I couldn't hear." "Efa —" "And you went. You went back and you did whatever it is you do in London and you've come back with biscuits from the Laugharne Co-op like that's — like that's a gesture, like that's —" "I also came back with these." He reached into the bag. Not biscuits. Books. Three of them. He set them on the counter. "This one's recent, she's Welsh, I thought you might not stock her. This one's old, I found it in a shop in Hay-on-Wye. And this one —" He held up the third. A paperback. The same one she'd given him. The first one. The personal one. The one about the river. "This one I've read three times now and I need to talk to someone about it and the only person I know who's read it is you." She looked at the books on her counter. She looked at him. He was standing there with the Co-op bag crumpled in one hand and the book in the other and his face was doing something she hadn't seen before — not the charm, not the vulnerability, not the hurt. Something simpler. He was just standing there. Being a man in a bookshop with three books and a bag of biscuits and no performance, no audience, no script. "I don't have your number," he said. "I don't have yours." "We've been — for two weeks. We've never —" "I know." "That's — is that strange? That feels strange." "It's strange." He set the paperback on the counter. Looked at her. She looked at him. The rain started — sudden, the way it does in Laugharne, like someone's turned on a tap — and it hit the windows and the door and the roof and the shop was full of the sound of it. "I took the role," he said. "Okay." "I'm not saying that to — I'm telling you because it's true. I took it. It starts in February. I'm going back to London on Friday. I have to. That's the — that's the fact of it." "Okay." "And I don't know what this is. You and me. I don't know what to call it or what it means or where it goes or if it goes anywhere. I know I've read a book three times because you gave it to me and I know I drove four hours this morning to bring you biscuits and I know that I've been in a hundred rooms where everyone wanted me there and this is the only room where I want to be and I don't know what to do with that except —" He stopped. Ran out of words. She saw it happen — the moment where the vocabulary gave out and what was left was just a man, standing in the rain-light, holding a book. "Except bring biscuits," she said. "Except bring biscuits. Yes." She came out from behind the counter. Walked to where he was standing — three steps, four, the length of her shop, the gap between the counter and the door — and she stood in front of him and she was shorter than him and she had to look up and he had to look down and the difference was the right difference, the exact right difference, and she'd never in her life noticed the height difference between herself and another person and she noticed it now. "Your tea was terrible," she said. "I know." "Three sugars." "I've cut down." "To what?" "Two and a half." "That's not — that's not cutting down. That's rounding down." "I'm a work in progress." She almost laughed. She held it. Let it go. Felt it come out as something else — not a laugh but an exhale, a breath she'd been holding for four days, maybe longer, maybe since the first day he'd walked in with rain in his hair and a Co-op bag and a face that everyone trusted and she'd decided not to. "I'm not coming to London," she said. "I'm not asking you to." "I'm not — this shop. This town. This is where I am. This is what I have." "I know." "And I can't — I won't be the woman in the photo. The one they talk about. The one they assess. I won't." "I know." "So what is this?" He looked at her. The rain on the glass. The cat on the counter. The books between them. "I don't know," he said. "I honestly don't know." "Good." "Good?" "Good. Because if you knew, you'd be performing it. If you knew, you'd have a speech. The fact that you don't know means this might be real." He opened his mouth. Closed it. The man who always had something to say, who filled silences, who charmed and deflected and performed — standing in a bookshop in Laugharne with nothing. She reached out. Took the book from his hand — the paperback, the one she'd given him — and opened it. The pages were soft now, handled, read. She turned to the page — the kitchen-table page, 112 — and held it so they could both see. "This is what it is," she said. "This page. Two people. A thing said. A thing heard. That's all I can do. Right now. That's all I've got." He read the page. She watched him read it. His lips moved — not with the words, with the rhythm — and his hands were still and his face was open and she thought: *this is what he looks like when he's not trying to be seen. This is what it is.* "I'll take it," he said. "Don't lend it to anyone." "I won't." "Keep it." He nodded. She nodded. The rain went on. He was still holding the Co-op bag. She was still standing close enough to smell the wet-wool scent of his jacket, the same jacket from the first day, and it occurred to her that she knew the smell of this man's jacket and that knowing it was a specific, irrevocable thing that had happened to her without her permission and she was — "Tea?" she said. "God, yes." "Make it yourself this time." "I always make it myself." "You made it wrong every single time." "I'm aware." He went through to the back. She heard the kettle, the mugs, the sounds of a man navigating someone else's kitchen. He came back with two mugs. Hers was the Cymru one. His was the blue one. He'd made hers right — black, no sugar. They sat. The two chairs. The crate between them. The rain. The cat. "There's a chapter in the new one," she said, lifting the Welsh book he'd brought from Hay-on-Wye. "Page forty-something. There's a line about —" "Let me find it." "Let me finish." "Sorry." "There's a line about a man walking toward something he can't see. And I thought of you." "Is that good?" "I don't know yet." He smiled. Not the big one. The small one, the real one, the one that she was beginning to understand lived underneath the other one and had been there all along, waiting. The shop was warm. The wood burner was lit. The rain kept at it and the estuary breathed and a cat slept on a counter and two people sat in mismatched chairs and drank tea and talked about books and didn't talk about the future and didn't talk about what they were and let it be the thing it was, which was small and real and theirs, and the door was open — he'd left it open when he came in, the bell hadn't runed, the wet air came in off the street — and the afternoon light moved across the floor and neither of them watched it go. Outside, Laugharne did what Laugharne does. The Co-op sold groceries. Gareth opened the pub. The estuary came in and went out. A man walked past with a dog and didn't look in the window. The sky was grey and then gold and then grey again. It was just a Wednesday. It was the most ordinary day. Efa sat in her chair and looked at the man in the other chair and thought: *I will probably get hurt.* And thought: *I am already hurt.* And thought: *The hurt and the hope are the same thing. They have always been the same thing. I have been calling one of them safety and the other one danger and I was wrong. They are the same.* She picked up her tea. Drank it. Set it down. "You're holding that book wrong," she said. "I know." "Spine in the left hand. Like you're testing its pulse." "Show me." She reached across. Took the book from him. Held it the way she held all books — spine in her left hand, pages fanned with her right thumb, the pulse of it — and he watched her hands and she let him watch and the watching was the thing, the quiet, specific, irrevocable thing, and she handed it back. "Like that," she said. He tried. It was wrong. She laughed — the real one, the involuntary one — and he laughed with her, and the two laughs were different, his big and surprised and hers sharp and almost unwilling, and they mixed in the small room and Dylan opened one eye and closed it and the rain fell on Laugharne and the estuary didn't care and the bookshop stayed exactly where it was, warm and cluttered and imperfect and full, holding two people who had not planned to be there and did not know what came next and were, for once, not performing the not-knowing but simply in it, together, in the back of a bookshop in a small Welsh town on a Wednesday afternoon in late October, and the kettle was cold again, and neither of them minded.
